questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following features is not included in the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) classification system for grading splenic injuries?
questions.explanation: The AAST splenic injury scale is used to categorize the severity of trauma to the spleen based on specific anatomical and radiological findings. Its primary components include the depth and extent of parenchymal destruction or laceration (Option A), the presence and size of a subcapsular or intraparenchymal hematoma (Option D), and the degree of vascular involvement (Option B), such as active hemorrhage or hilar devascularization. While adjacent organ involvement (Option C) is a critical factor in the overall management of a trauma patient and determines the comprehensive injury severity score, it is NOT a specific component used to grade the injury to the spleen itself within the AAST organ-specific classification. The AAST system focuses strictly on the intrinsic damage to the splenic tissue and its immediate blood supply. Understanding this distinction is important for surgeons to accurately stage injuries and decide between non-operative management and surgical intervention like splenectomy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presents with weight gain, cold intolerance, and painless enlargement of the thyroid gland. Which of the following antibodies is not likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. TSH receptor autoantibody

Recognize the antibody profile of Hashimoto thyroiditis, the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions. Patients typically present with weight gain, cold intolerance, and a painless diffuse goiter. The disease is characterized by anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin (anti-Tg) antibodies, while TSH receptor–stimulating autoantibodies are characteristic of Graves disease, not Hashimoto thyroiditis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Anti-TPO antibody: Most sensitive marker for Hashimoto thyroiditis; present in >90% of cases.
• B. Anti-thyroglobulin (Anti-Tg) antibody: Present in many patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis, though less sensitive than anti-TPO.
• C. TSH receptor blocking antibody: May be present in a subset of Hashimoto patients and contributes to hypothyroidism by inhibiting TSH action.
• D. TSH receptor autoantibody (stimulating antibody/TSI): Characteristic of Graves disease, causing hyperthyroidism by stimulating the TSH receptor; not expected in Hashimoto thyroiditis.
questions.learning: TSH receptor autoantibody Recognize the antibody profile of Hashimoto thyroiditis, the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: An 18-year-old female was sexually assaulted by a 20-year-old male. There was presence of white stains on the clothes of the victim. Barberio's test was performed on the stains. Which of the following is detected by this test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spermine

Barberio's test detects the presence of spermine which is present in prostatic secretions and thus helps in the identification of seminal fluid.

In Barberio's test, a saturated aqueous or alcoholic solution of picric acid is added to the spermatic fluid. This produces yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals of spermine picrate.

Option B: Acid phosphatase test is a quantitative test for the presence of acid phosphatase enzyme. High levels of acid phosphatase from prostatic secretions are present in seminal stains (The normal vaginal secretions have low levels of acid phosphatase). Positive reactions are found till 36 hours after which the enzyme levels fall and disappear within 72 hours. In the absence of demonstrable sperms or aspermia, this test can be considered conclusive.

Option C: Florence test detects choline which is secreted by seminal vesicles. The suspected seminal stain is extracted with 10% hydrochloric acid and a drop of it is placed over a slide. A coverslip is placed over it and a drop of Florence solution (potassium iodide, iodine, and water) is made to run under the coverslip. If semen is present, dark brown rhombic or needle-shaped crystals of choline iodide appear immediately. The test is not confirmatory for the presence of semen, however, a negative reaction rules out the presence of semen.

Option D: Fructose acts as an energy source for sperm. Its presence in seminal fluid indicates a patent efferent ductal system, as fructose will be absent in its obstruction.

The absolute proof of semen is finding at least one unbroken spermatozoon or electrophoretic LDH isoenzyme detection of sperms.
questions.learning: Spermine Barberio's test detects the presence of spermine which is present in prostatic secretions and thus helps in the identification of seminal fluid.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: How would you define a post-term neonate?
options: Neonate born after 37 weeks of gestation
Neonate born between 37-40 weeks of gestation
Neonate born after 40 weeks of gestation
Neonate born after 42 weeks of gestation
questions.explanation: The standard clinical definition of a post-term neonate is any infant born at or beyond 42 weeks (294 days) of completed gestation. This is distinct from a "term" neonate, which is born between 37 weeks 0 days and 41 weeks 6 days of gestation. Option A and B describe "term" babies; 37 weeks marks the transition from preterm to term. Option C (after 40 weeks) is "post-dates" but not yet technically "post-term" according to international neonatal standards. Post-term infants are at a higher risk for complications like meconium aspiration syndrome, placental insufficiency, and fetal macrosomia due to the aging placenta's inability to provide adequate oxygen and nutrients. Therefore, the strict cutoff for the definition of post-term is exactly 42 completed weeks of pregnancy. Clinicians prioritize this definition to manage the unique risks associated with post-maturity syndrome
questions.learning: The standard clinical definition of a post-term neonate is any infant born at or beyond 42 weeks (294 days) of completed gestation. This is distinct from a "term" neonate, which is born between 37 weeks 0 days and 41 weeks 6 days of gestation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old female presents with recurrent episodes of right flank pain, hematuria, and a history of urinary tract infections. Urine analysis shows alkaline urine with a pH of 8.0. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Triple phosphate stones

The given clinical scenario and microscopic image showing coffin lid shaped crystals are suggestive of triple phosphate stones. They are also known as staghorn or struvite stones.

This is caused due to infection with urea-splitting organisms, such as Proteus, Klebsiella, Serratia, or Enterobacter species.They are usually formed in alkaline urine.

Staghorn calculi are radio-opaque stones that grow in a branching pattern along the pelvicalyceal system. The above organisms metabolize the urea into ammonium and bicarbonate. Increased metabolism of urea results in alkalinity of the urine, and precipitation of magnesium, ammonium, and phosphate - resulting in the formation of struvite stones.

Complete removal of a staghorn calculus is essential, as any remaining fragments after treatment can lead to a rapid recurrence and continued presence of bacteriuria. Following the successful removal of the infection stone, long-term chemoprophylaxis is required for several months.
questions.learning: Triple phosphate stones — The given clinical scenario and microscopic image showing coffin lid shaped crystals are suggestive of triple phosphate stones.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient undergoes surgery for a pilonidal sinus. Which type of flap is typically used in this procedure?
questions.explanation: The image shows a curved, double-lobed flap closure, which is characteristic of a bilobed flap. This technique is commonly used in pilonidal sinus surgery (e.g., off-midline closure procedures) to redistribute tension and flatten the natal cleft, reducing recurrence. A bilobed flap consists of two adjacent flaps that are transposed sequentially to close a defect, allowing: 1. Tension-free closure 2. Better cosmetic outcome 3. Reduced risk of recurrence in pilonidal disease Why other options are incorrect: (A) Fasciocutaneous rotation flap: Involves a broad arc rotation, not the characteristic double-lobed design (C) Transposition flap: Single flap moved across defect; does not show the two-lobed pattern (D) Random pattern flap: Refers to blood supply type, not a specific flap design The distinct double-lobed appearance confirms this as a bilobed flap, commonly used in pilonidal sinus surgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All are true about intestinal transplantation except ______.
options: Most of the grafts are multi-visceral grafts.
It is not widely used due to vigorous rejection reactions.
The most dangerous complication is sepsis.
The most common indication is the ischemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Most of the grafts are multi-visceral grafts.

Multivisceral grafts are rarely used in intestinal transplantation. The most common intestinal graft is small bowel graft, with or without the colon or a combined liver and small bowel graft.

All the other statements are correct.

Small bowel transplantation is the final treatment option after the outcome of reconstruction and lengthening procedures are unsatisfactory.

The small bowel transplant is highly immunogenic since it contains a large amount of gut-associated lymphoid tissue, donor dendritic cells, and macrophages. Acute rejection has been reported in 56–75% of patients, with small bowel transplant limiting the overall survival to only one-third of recipients.
questions.learning: Most of the grafts are multi-visceral grafts. Multivisceral grafts are rarely used in intestinal transplantation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Respiratory distress syndrome is due to the deficiency of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dipalmitoyl Phosphatidylcholine

Respiratory distress syndrome is due to the deficiency of dipalmitoyl-phosphatidyl-choline(DPPC) /dipalmitoyl lecithin. It is the major pulmonary surfactant.

Clinical relevance- Test to assess fetal lung maturity is L/S ratio - lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio. A ratio of ≥ 2 is considered normal.
questions.learning: Dipalmitoyl Phosphatidylcholine Respiratory distress syndrome is due to the deficiency of dipalmitoyl-phosphatidyl-choline(DPPC) /dipalmitoyl lecithin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Hamman sign is seen in
questions.explanation: Hamman's sign, also known as Hamman's crunch, is a clinical finding characterized by a "crunching" or clicking sound heard during auscultation of the heart. This sound is synchronous with the heartbeat and is best heard over the left sternal border with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position. It is caused by the heart beating against air that has escaped into the mediastinal tissues (Pneumomediastinum). Pneumomediastinum can result from alveolar rupture (Macklin effect), esophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndrome), or trauma. Pneumoperitoneum (Option A) involves air in the abdominal cavity. Pneumopericardium (Option B) is air specifically within the pericardial sac and might produce similar sounds but is much rarer. Hydropneumothorax (Option D) involves air and fluid in the pleural space, which would cause decreased breath sounds and succussion splash, but not a precordial crunch. Hamman's sign is often associated with subcutaneous emphysema in the neck or chest. Therefore, it is a hallmark clinical indicator of air in the mediastinum
questions.learning: Hamman's sign, also known as Hamman's crunch, is a clinical finding characterized by a "crunching" or clicking sound heard during auscultation of the heart.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not included in the SAFE strategy for trachoma?
questions.explanation: The WHO-recommended "SAFE" strategy is a comprehensive approach to eliminate trachoma, the world's leading infectious cause of blindness. Each letter represents a specific intervention: S Surgery for individuals with trichiasis (in-turned eyelashes) to prevent corneal scarring. A Antibiotics (typically oral azithromycin) to treat active Chlamydia trachomatis infection in the community. F Facial cleanliness to reduce the transmission of the bacteria via fingers and flies. E Environmental improvements, such as increased access to water and improved sanitation, to eliminate breeding sites for flies. While "Evaluation of the control program" (Option D) is an essential administrative task for any public health initiative, it is not one of the four technical pillars that constitute the "SAFE" acronym. The strategy addresses both the immediate clinical needs of patients and the underlying socio-environmental factors that allow the disease to persist in endemic regions

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What does the magnified number marked on the Foley catheter correspond to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Outer tube diameter

The number shown in the above image of the Foley catheter indicates the outer diameter.

"Fr" stands for French scale and refers to the external diameter of the catheter. 1Fr is 0.3 mm in diameter.

An 18 Fr. catheter will have a circumference of approximately 18 mm and a diameter of 6 mm.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a history of penetrating chest trauma. On examination, marked tracheal deviation is noted. What is the immediate step in management?
questions.explanation: Severe tracheal deviation following penetrating chest trauma is a pathognomonic sign of a tension pneumothorax. This occurs when air trapped in the pleural space shifts the mediastinum and compresses the heart and opposite lung, leading to rapid obstructive shock. Immediate needle decompression using a large-bore cannula (typically in the 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line) is mandatory and life-saving. Waiting for a chest X-ray (Option B) or performing an E-FAST ultrasound (Option C) is dangerous because it delays critical intervention in a clinically diagnosed emergency. While 100% oxygen (Option D) is part of general stabilization, it will not relieve the mechanical pressure causing the tracheal shift and circulatory collapse. Once the pressure is relieved by a needle, a definitive intercostal chest drain (ICD) must be placed. Thus, clinical diagnosis and immediate decompression are the priorities

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 54-year-old woman presents with heartburn and shiny, tight, thickened skin over her hands associated with non-pitting edema. Serological testing is positive for anti–topoisomerase I antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient displays the core features of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), including skin thickening (sclerodactyly) and esophageal symptoms (heartburn). The definitive diagnostic marker is the Topoisomerase I (Anti-Scl-70) antibody, which is highly specific for the Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis subtype (Option B). This subtype is characterized by rapid skin involvement that extends proximal to the elbows and knees, and a high risk of internal organ disease like interstitial lung disease, as noted in this patient. Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (Option A) (CREST syndrome) is associated with Centromere antibodies and limited skin involvement. Raynaud's phenomenon (Option C) is a symptom (color change in fingers) that is often the first sign of scleroderma but is not the diagnosis for the full clinical picture. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (Option D) involves GI polyps and pigmentation . Thus, the specific antibody profile confirms the diffuse type
questions.learning: The patient displays the core features of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), including skin thickening (sclerodactyly) and esophageal symptoms (heartburn).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 38-year-old man presents to a Suraksha clinic with complaints of anorectal discharge. Under the syndromic management approach for sexually transmitted infections, which color- coded treatment kit is recommended for this condition?
questions.explanation: Under India's Syndromic Case Management (SCM) approach for STIs, color-coded treatment kits are used for standardized management. The Grey kit is specifically recommended for anorectal discharge syndrome. The Grey kit contains medications targeting the common causative organisms of anorectal infections including Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. Why other options are wrong: (B) Green kit is incorrect because the Green kit is used for vaginal discharge syndrome in women, targeting common vaginal infections including bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, and cervicitis. (C) White kit is incorrect because the White kit is designated for genital ulcer disease syndrome, targeting conditions like syphilis, chancroid, and herpes genitalis causing ulcerative lesions. (D) Blue kit is incorrect because the Blue kit is used for urethral discharge syndrome in males, targeting gonorrhea and chlamydial urethritis — distinct from anorectal discharge which requires the Grey kit
questions.learning: Under India's Syndromic Case Management (SCM) approach for STIs, color-coded treatment kits are used for standardized management. The Grey kit is specifically recommended for anorectal discharge syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following drugs decreases the serum parathyroid hormone levels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcitriol

Correct answer is B because calcitriol (active vitamin D) increases intestinal calcium absorption and raises serum calcium, which suppresses parathyroid hormone via negative feedback.

Key regulators of PTH:

| Factor | Effect on PTH

| ------ | -------------

| Low Ca²⁺ | ↑ PTH

| High Ca²⁺ | ↓ PTH

| Calcitriol | ↓ PTH

| Phosphate | ↑ PTH

Calcitriol acts on:

| Organ | Effect

| ----- | ------

| Intestine | ↑ Ca absorption

| Kidney | ↑ Ca reabsorption

| Bone | ↑ remodeling

Risedronate reduces bone resorption but does not directly suppress PTH. Lithium can increase PTH and cause hyperparathyroidism. Diuretics have variable effects and are not primary PTH suppressors.
questions.learning: Calcitriol Correct answer is B because calcitriol (active vitamin D) increases intestinal calcium absorption and raises serum calcium, which suppresses parathyroid hormone via negative feedback.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with complaints of vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss. An audiogram is provided for evaluation. Based on the audiometric findings shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and progressive hearing loss is characteristic of Meniere's disease. The provided audiogram shows a low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (the line is lower on the left side of the chart), which is pathognomonic for the early stages of this condition. BPPV (Option A) causes brief, position-triggered vertigo but no hearing loss or tinnitus. Vestibular neuronitis (Option C) causes sudden, severe, prolonged vertigo but hearing remains normal. Presbycusis (Option D) is age-related hearing loss that characteristically affects high frequencies (the right side of the chart) and is always bilateral. Meniere's disease is caused by endolymphatic hydrops—excess fluid pressure in the inner ear. Episodes typically last minutes to hours and are often preceded by a feeling of ear fullness. Management involves a low-salt diet, diuretics, and medications like betahistine to reduce the frequency and severity of attacks. Accurate audiometric assessment is essential for confirming the sensorineural nature and specific frequency pattern of the hearing loss

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Malar telangiectasia is classically associated with diseases such as scleroderma. Such an association of malar telangiectasia can also be seen with which of the following cardiac lesions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic mitral stenosis

Malar telangiectasia (malar flush) is a characteristic facial finding seen in chronic severe mitral stenosis due to long-standing pulmonary hypertension, reduced cardiac output, and peripheral vasodilatation. Although telangiectasia is classically associated with connective tissue disorders such as systemic sclerosis, a similar malar flush is a well-recognized clinical sign of advanced mitral stenosis.

• Chronic mitral stenosis causes:

• Low cardiac output
• Pulmonary hypertension
• Peripheral vasodilatation

• This produces the characteristic pinkish-purple malar flush (“mitral facies”) over the cheeks.

Why not the other options?

• B. Aortic regurgitation: Characterized by bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, Corrigan pulse, Quincke’s sign, etc., not malar flush.
• C. Constrictive pericarditis: Presents with raised JVP, Kussmaul sign, and pericardial knock, not malar telangiectasia.
• D. Dilated cardiomyopathy: Causes features of heart failure without the characteristic mitral facies.
questions.learning: Chronic mitral stenosis Malar telangiectasia (malar flush) is a characteristic facial finding seen in chronic severe mitral stenosis due to long-standing pulmonary hypertension, reduced cardiac output, and peripheral vasodilatation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A newly renovated operating theatre is having essential anesthesia equipment installed. During routine inspection of the anesthesia workstation, the technician suddenly develops lightheadedness and nausea. He immediately switches off the anesthesia machine and leaves the room. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Leakage of Nitrous Oxide

Nitrous oxide exposure causes:

• dizziness
• nausea
• euphoria / disorientation
• headache
• diffusion hypoxia (with sudden discontinuation)

It is also the most common anesthetic gas associated with chronic occupational exposure issues, especially in poorly scavenged OTs.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 60-year-old female patient presented with purplish, itchy, flat-topped lesions on his shins for the past 3 months. The patient also gives a history of chewing tobacco for 20 years. She occasionally drinks alcohol and smokes. On examination, the lesions are seen as in the image below. Which of the following is the first line of management for the condition seen in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Topical corticosteroids

The clinical features and characteristic lesions showing fine white lacework in buccal mucosa called Wickham's striae shown in the image are diagnostic of lichen planus. The first line of management is potent topical corticosteroids like clobetasol propionate ointment 0.05%.

Lichen planus is a type of lichenoid disorder affecting the papillary dermis. It is a T-cell mediated autoimmune disease against the basal keratinocytes. The primary lesions of lichen planus are described by the characteristic "6 Ps": planar (flat-topped), purple, polygonal, pruritic, papules, and plaques. These well-defined areas of purple-coloured, itchy, flat-topped papules may be with interspersed lacy white lines known as Wickham's striae(shown below). It may present with mucous membrane lesions in the absence of skin lesions, commonly involving the tongue and buccal mucosa.

Various factors that can precipitate the disease are:

* Viruses like Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, Human herpesviruses (HHV-6, HHV-8), Varicella zoster

* Betel quid which contains areca nut and tobacco leaf

* Environmental factors like:

* Drugs like antimicrobials, antihypertensives, antimalarials, antidepressants, anticonvulsants

* Radiotherapy

* Anxiety, depression, stress

Histology: Most useful investigation to confirm the diagnosis. Basal epidermal cell degeneration/destruction by dermal CD8+ T lymphocytes is characteristically seen in lichen planus. Other findings are:

* Hyperkeratosis

* The degeneration leads to the formation of spaces in the epidermis known as Max-Joseph spaces.

* Saw-toothed appearance of the Rete ridges

* Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate is present at the dermo-epidermal junction.

Other options:

Options A and C: Ciclosporin, and methotrexate are used in third-line management and not first-line management of the disease.

Option D: Oral corticosteroids are used in the second-line management of the disease.
questions.learning: Topical corticosteroids — The clinical features and characteristic lesions showing fine white lacework in buccal mucosa called Wickham's striae shown in the image are diagnostic of lichen planus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A Patient had dietary Cu deficiency, which is required by lysyl oxidase to cross link the collagen, what is the diagnosis of the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Menkes Disease

Copper is an essential cofactor for the enzyme lysyl oxidase, which catalyzes the oxidative deamination of lysine and hydroxylysine residues in collagen and elastin, allowing cross-linking of connective tissue fibers. Role of lysyl oxidase:

• Requires Cu²⁺ (copper) as a cofactor
• Forms cross-links between collagen and elastin fibers
• Provides tensile strength and structural stability to connective tissue

Menkes disease:

• X-linked recessive disorder
• Caused by mutation in ATP7A gene → defective copper transport
• Leads to systemic copper deficiency and reduced lysyl oxidase activity
• Weak connective tissue
• Kinky (steely) hair
• Neurodegeneration
• Failure to thrive
• Hypopigmentation

Differentiation from other options:

• Scurvy → Vitamin C deficiency → impaired hydroxylation of collagen
• Ehlers–Danlos syndrome → collagen structure/synthesis defects
• Scoliosis → spinal curvature disorder, not enzyme-related
questions.learning: Menkes Disease Copper is an essential cofactor for the enzyme lysyl oxidase, which catalyzes the oxidative deamination of lysine and hydroxylysine residues in collagen and elastin, allowing cross-linking of connective tissue fibers.

questions.text: The risk of genetic diseases in consanguineous marriage between first cousins is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 4-8%

The risk of genetic diseases in consanguineous marriage between first cousins is 4-8%.

The risk of genetic diseases in non-consanguineous marriage is 2-4%.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient hailing from an area infested with mosquitoes presents with fever, chills, and myalgias. WBC count was 4000 cells/cu.mm, RBC was normal, and platelets were 90000 cells/cu.mm. He also had a maculopapular rash. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dengue

The given clinical scenario with a patient hailing from a mosquito-infested area with fever and decreased platelet counts is diagnostic of dengue.

Symptoms of severe dengue are headache, myalgias, retroorbital pain, end-organ damage, pleural & ascitic effusions and thrombocytopenia (<100,000/ uL). Complications include mild hepatic injury, seizures, arrythmias and acute kidney injury.

Diagnosis is made by NS1 antigen detection and IgM antibody assays. Treatment includes crystalloid infusion in mild cases and colloid infusion in severe cases, oxygen administration and close monitoring.

Dengue is classified into dengue with or without warning signs and severe dengue. Dengue is to be suspected when a high fever (40°C/104°F) is accompanied by any two of the following symptoms during the febrile phase (2-7 days) which include severe headache, retro-orbital pain, arthralgia or myalgia, nausea, vomiting and maculopapular rash.

Warning signs in dengue are:

• severe abdominal pain
• persistent vomiting
• tachypnea
• bleeding gums or nose
• fatigue
• restlessness
• hepatomegaly
• malena or hematemesis
questions.learning: Dengue — The given clinical scenario with a patient hailing from a mosquito-infested area with fever and decreased platelet counts is diagnostic of dengue.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of zileuton?
questions.explanation: Zileuton is an oral medication used for the maintenance treatment of asthma. Its specific mechanism of action is the inhibition of the enzyme 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX). This enzyme is responsible for the first step in converting arachidonic acid into pro-inflammatory leukotrienes (, , , and ). By blocking 5-LOX, Zileuton prevents the formation of leukotrienes, which are potent bronchoconstrictors and mediators of inflammation in the airways. This distinguishes it from Montelukast, which is a leukotriene receptor antagonist. Cyclooxygenase inhibitors (Option A) are NSAIDs like aspirin. 5-phosphodiesterase inhibitors (Option C) include Sildenafil for erectile dysfunction. Mast cell stabilizers (Option D), such as Cromolyn sodium, prevent degranulation but do not target the 5-LOX enzyme. Zileuton is particularly useful in patients with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD). Therefore, 5-lipoxygenase inhibition is the definitive biochemical mechanism for Zileuton
questions.learning: Zileuton is an oral medication used for the maintenance treatment of asthma. Its specific mechanism of action is the inhibition of the enzyme 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The most common drug which causes physical dependence is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Heroin

Heroin is the most common drug which can cause physical dependence.

Physical dependence is defined is a condition where withdrawal of a drug after its prolonged use causes physiological and emotional illness, often referred to as the withdrawal syndrome. Neither physical dependence nor withdrawal symptoms occur with hallucinogens. Although it is necessary to note that a user can develop a psychological dependence on the insight-inducing experiences of episodes of hallucinogen use. Hence, all 3 hallucinogens - ketamine, LSD, and Phencyclidine (PCP) does not cause physical dependence.

According to the world drug report 2019, released by the United Nations office on drugs and crime (UNODC), the most common drugs used across the world (in decreasing order) include:

• Cannabis
• Opioids
• Amphetamine and prescription stimulants
• Ecstacy
• Cocaine

Among the opioids, the commonly used group of drugs are opiates which include drugs like opium, morphine, and heroin.
questions.learning: Heroin Heroin is the most common drug which can cause physical dependence. Physical dependence is defined is a condition where withdrawal of a drug after its prolonged use causes physiological and emotional illness, often referred to as the withdrawal…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Mark the incorrect statement reagrding Nipah virus:
options: It is transmitted through bat's urine
questions.explanation: Nipah virus (NiV) is a zoonotic virus that characteristically causes severe encephalitis (brain inflammation) and, in some cases, severe respiratory disease. It is not a typical cause of hemorrhagic fever (Option B); viral hemorrhagic fevers are caused by different families of viruses like Ebola, Dengue, or Lassa. Statement A is correct; the virus is carried by fruit bats (Pteropus species) and is transmitted through bat urine, saliva, or feces, often by consuming contaminated fruit or date palm sap. Statement C is correct; NiV is present in India, with several documented outbreaks, particularly in Kerala and West Bengal. Statement D is correct; it is classified as an emerging infectious disease with high epidemic potential and no currently available vaccine or specific treatment. Clinically, NiV presents with fever, headache, and rapid progression to confusion, coma, and death. High mortality rates and the risk of human-to-human transmission make NiV a significant public health priority
questions.learning: Nipah virus (NiV) is a zoonotic virus that characteristically causes severe encephalitis (brain inflammation) and, in some cases, severe respiratory disease.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A farmer presents with a swelling on the palm that developed several months after sustaining a thorn prick injury. What is the most likely medical diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of a palm swelling following a penetrating injury (like a thorn prick) is the "textbook" presentation of an implantation dermoid cyst. This occurs when a fragment of surface epithelium is driven into the deeper subcutaneous tissues during trauma. Over time, this trapped tissue grows and desquamates keratin, forming a cyst. Farmers are particularly susceptible due to occupational exposure to thorns and splinters. Ameloblastoma (Option A) is a tumor of the jaw. Embryogenic (Option B) and sequestration dermoids (Option C) are congenital cysts that occur along embryonic fusion lines (e.g., the midline or outer angle of the eye) rather than resulting from trauma. Implantation dermoids are typically firm, non-tender, and move with the skin. Surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Therefore, the traumatic origin in the palm confirms the diagnosis of an implantation dermoid
questions.learning: The clinical history of a palm swelling following a penetrating injury (like a thorn prick) is the "textbook" presentation of an implantation dermoid cyst.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following findings is characteristic of Frey’s syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sweating & flushing over preauricular region

Frey’s syndrome occurs due to aberrant regeneration of auriculotemporal nerve fibers after parotid gland injury or surgery.

Parasympathetic fibers meant for salivation instead stimulate sweat glands, causing gustatory sweating and flushing over the preauricular area.

The other options describe features of Horner syndrome, not Frey’s syndrome.
questions.learning: Sweating & flushing over preauricular region Frey’s syndrome occurs due to aberrant regeneration of auriculotemporal nerve fibers after parotid gland injury or surgery.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A woman underwent surgery, but the surgeon discovered a cyst and removed her ovaries. She is of reproductive age with an incomplete family. What consent was violated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Informed consent

This kind of consent is informed consent since the patient has been made aware of the benefits and complications and has agreed to the procedure.

Informed consent is one given by the patient after understanding the nature of the condition, proposed treatment, outcomes of the recommended treatment, alternative options to treatment, and the risks and benefits involved. The patient can accept or reject the procedure. This is also called the rule of full disclosure.

"Consent" refers to a voluntary agreement, compliance, or permission. It can be expressed or implied. Expressed consent can be oral or written and refers to consent in which the terms are clearly stated in distinct and explicit language.

"Opt out" refers to a patient's refusal of the procedure, test, or treatment. It is the physician's duty to disclose the risks or consequences of refusal adequately and appropriately to the patient.

Option B: Implied consent is that which is not written or expressly stated. It is implied that the patient is giving consent to examination in a general sense. For example, when a patient visits the hospital with an illness, it implies that he has given consent to a physical examination to find out the nature of his illness. Another example of implied consent is when a patient exposes his arm for injection. It is legally effective.

Option C: The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur (the thing or the act speaks for itself) is a situation whereby an obvious gross act of negligence leads to damage to the patient. For example, prescribing high doses of NSAIDs to a patient with a history of perforated peptic ulcer. The negligent act is so obvious that the patient need not prove the negligence.

Option D: According to BNS Section 30 (IPC 92), a doctor is permitted to perform life-saving procedures on a patient with life-threatening injuries. For example, in a case where conservative measures have failed to control intractable postpartum haemorrhage, an emergency hysterectomy can be performed without obtaining consent in order to save the patient's life. The guiding principle is whether the delay in treatment in order to obtain consent would result in harm to the patient. This is the doctrine of anticipation. Under some circumstances, like emergencies, informed consent may be neither possible nor necessary.
questions.learning: Informed consent — This kind of consent is informed consent since the patient has been made aware of the benefits and complications and has agreed to the procedure.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient taking multi-drug therapy (MDT) presents with worsening of existing lesions and nerve involvement. What will be your next best step of action?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Continue MDT, start systemic steroids

The given scenario of worsening of existing lesions in the context of leprosy treatment with multi-drug therapy (MDT) is suggestive of a type 1 lepra reaction. The next best step in the management would be to continue MDT and start systemic steroids.

Type 1 lepra reactions present with inflammation of existing skin lesions. The lesions become red, painful, and edematous. They may rarely ulcerate. New lesions may occur but are very rare. It is associated with acute neuritis, with the tenderness and loss of sensory and motor function.

MDT is never stopped in patients with lepra reactions. For pain, NSAIDs can be supplemented along with oral steroids.

The use of thalidomide is restricted to severe forms of type-2 lepra reaction or erythema nodosum leprosum. These are characterized by systemic effects like iritis, orchitis, and eruption of new skin lesions.

The summary of lepra reactions is attached in the pearl below.
questions.learning: Continue MDT, start systemic steroids — The given scenario of worsening of existing lesions in the context of leprosy treatment with multi-drug therapy (MDT) is suggestive of a type 1 lepra reaction.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged male presents to the emergency room after a road traffic accident. Upon examination, the external auditory meatus has blood clots. What is the investigation of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CT Temporal bone

The clinical history of a road traffic accident causing bleeding through the ears is highly suggestive of a basilar skull fracture or ring fracture. Hence, the investigation of choice in the given clinical vignette is a CT scan of the temporal bone

Signs of basilar skull fractures:

* Haemotympanum: Pooling of blood behind the tympanic membrane, associated with fracture of the temporal bone. It is one of the earliest signs of a basilar fracture.

* Periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes): Pooling of blood surrounding the eyes, associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa.

* Mastoid ecchymosis (Battle’s sign) refers to the collection of blood in the posterior aspect of the ear (mastoid region), indicating a middle cranial fossa fracture.

* CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea: Double target sign, a double-ring pattern described with CSF-containing bloody fluid from the ear or nose, when dripped onto paper or linen.

Following a head injury, the battle’s sign and raccoon eyes are usually delayed findings, developing between 6 hours to 3 days post-trauma.

The onset of CSF leaks following trauma may be delayed by several hours to days. Suspected fluid is confirmed as CSF by testing for β2-transferrin. Most CSF leaks are conservatively managed. Persistent leaks >7 days have a heightened risk of meningitis and are often surgically repaired.

Nasopharyngeal airways and nasogastric tube insertion are relatively contraindicated in basilar skull fractures due to the risk of intracranial placement. NIPPV is avoided due to the risk of pneumocephalus.

The image below shows raccoon eyes and a battle sign.

Pearl PF0368: Types of skull vault fracture

Diastatic fracture - Separation of sutures due to blow with blunt weapon or from cerebral edema. It is also called sutural fracture.

Fissured fracture/Linear fracture:

* Linear skull fractures are breaks in the bone that traverse the full thickness of the skull from the outer to inner table.

* They are usually fairly straight with no bone displacement.

* The common cause of injury is blunt force trauma where the impact energy transferred over a wide area of the skull.

Pond fracture - Occurs in children due to elasticity of bones. It is also known as indented fracture.

Depressed fracture - Caused by a heavy weapon with a small striking surface. Its shape indicates the type of weapon which is produced. So it is also called 'signature fracture'.

Comminuted fracture - It is also called spider web fracture and has a stellate appearance where there is no displacement of fracture.

Pearl PF1160: NICE Guidelines for CT in Head Injury

National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) Guidelines for Computed Tomography (CT) in Head Injury

Indications for CT imaging within 1 hour of following risk factors being identified:

* Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) <13 at any point

* GCS <15 at 2 hours after injury on assessment in emergency department

* Focal neurological deficit

* Suspected open, depressed, or basal skull fracture

* More than one episode of vomiting

* Post-traumatic seizure

Indications for CT imaging within 8 hours

* Age >65 years

* Coagulopathy (e.g., aspirin, warfarin, or rivaroxaban use)

* Dangerous mechanism of injury (e.g., fall from a height, road traffic accident)

* Retrograde amnesia >30 minutes

Though there is no steering wheel to impact into the chest, its absence also denies the slight protection offered to the driver in reducing the collision with the windscreen, perhaps by giving him something to brace against.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a history of missed abortion subsequently develops amenorrhea, despite having a negative urine pregnancy test. Hysterosalpingography shows the abnormality illustrated in the provided image. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of secondary amenorrhea following a pregnancy-related procedure (like curettage for a missed abortion) is highly suggestive of Asherman syndrome (Option C). Asherman syndrome is characterized by the formation of intrauterine adhesions or synechiae that obliterate the uterine cavity. The provided hysterosalpingogram (HSG) confirms this diagnosis, showing characteristic irregular filling defects and a diminished, jagged uterine cavity where the contrast cannot flow smoothly. Pyometra (Option A) involves an accumulation of pus in the uterus, usually presenting with pain and fever. Endometriosis (Option B) involves extra-uterine implants and would not show these specific intra-cavity HSG defects. Sheehan syndrome (Option D) is a form of pituitary necrosis following postpartum hemorrhage that causes amenorrhea through hormonal failure, but the HSG in Sheehan’s would show a normal uterine cavity. Therefore, the structural scarring seen on HSG confirms Asherman’s
questions.learning: The clinical history of secondary amenorrhea following a pregnancy-related procedure (like curettage for a missed abortion) is highly suggestive of Asherman syndrome (Option C).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male presents with purulent discharge from a perianal opening. Examination in the lithotomy position reveals an external opening at the 11 o’clock position, about 4 cm from the anal verge. What is the most likely location of the internal opening, and from where does it originate?
options: 12 o'clock and at external anal sphincter
11 o'clock and at internal anal sphincter
6 o'clock and crypt of the dentate line
questions.explanation: The management of a fistula-in-ano is guided by Goodsall’s Law. According to this rule, an external opening located posterior to a transverse line through the anus (such as the 11 o'clock position) will have a curved tract that enters the anal canal at the midline posterior (6 o'clock position). Furthermore, most fistulae originate in an infected anal crypt at the dentate line . Option B describes a straight tract, which according to Goodsall's law, only applies to anterior fistulae located within 3 cm of the anus. Option A and C do not follow standard anatomical tract guidelines. Because the external opening is both posterior and relatively far from the anus (4 cm), the track is expected to be complex and curved, meeting at the midline posterior crypt. Understanding these landmarks is essential for successful fistulectomy or seton placement

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a hospital, the management wants to know how much time each doctor is spending with a patient on an average. They want to increase or decrease the number of doctors, as per the requirement, to improve the quality of care. What management technique should they use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Work sampling

Work sampling is a systematic observation and recording of activities of one or more individuals carried out at predetermined or random interval and thus it has to be used to evaulate the time that each doctor spends per patient.

It is a type of quantitative method of management. It helps in standardizing the methods of performing the jobs and determining the need for manpower.

Model

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a painless swelling of the neck. The histology of the tissue is as given in the image below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hashimoto's thyroiditis

The slide shows the histopathology of Hashimoto thyroiditis, with:

• Follicular destruction
• Reduced colloid with increased interstitial connective tissue
• Small lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltration
• A well-developed germinal centre may be seen
• Hurthle (Askanazy) cells that have abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm lining the follicles

Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. It is also known as struma lymphomatosa or lymphocytic thyroiditis. It is an autoimmune disease that results in the destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual & progressive thyroid failure.

Clinical features:

• Most prevalent between 45-65 years of age
• More common in females
• Painless enlargement of the thyroid
• Hashitoxicosis: When the auto-antibodies attack and damage the follicles, there is a sudden release of thyroid hormones from these follicles. This leads to a transient phase of thyrotoxicosis.
• Hypothyroidism: Since the follicles are damaged and cannot form the hormones anymore, these patients tend to be in a state of hypothyroidism.

Diagnosis:

• T3 and T4 are low
• TSH is raised
• Autoantibodies against:

• Thyroid receptors
• Thyroid peroxidase (TPO)
• Thyroglobulin

These patients are managed with thyroid hormone replacement therapy.

In patients with long-standing goiter, there is a risk of compressive features and the development of thyroid lymphoma. Such cases can be treated with total thyroidectomy. It may also predispose to papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Other options:

Option A: Histological features of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid include polygonal to spindle-shaped cells in the form of nests, trabeculae or follicles. Small, round anaplastic cells may be found in some cases and amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin polypeptides are present in the stroma.

The given slide below shows medullary carcinoma of thyroid:

Option C: Grave's disease is an autoimmune disorder characterized by hyperthyroidism due to circulating autoantibodies. The thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins bind to the TSH receptors, causing overgrowth of the thyroid gland and increased thyroid hormone synthesis. Histologically, there is acinar cell hypertrophy and hyperplasia with the absence of normal colloid in the tall columnar epithelium (normally the epithelium is flat with colloid). Lymphoid infiltrates, consisting predominantly of T cells, along with scattered B cells and mature plasma cells, are present throughout the interstitium. Germinal centers are common.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient is found to have elevated blood pressure along with a reduced heart rate. Which physiological mechanism most likely explains this response?
questions.explanation: The physiological response of a decreased heart rate (bradycardia) in response to high blood pressure (hypertension) is mediated by the baroreceptor reflex. High pressure stretches baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch, which send increased signals to the medulla. The medulla responds by increasing parasympathetic (vagus) outflow and inhibiting sympathetic outflow, leading to a drop in heart rate and systemic vasodilation. Inhibition of baroreceptors (Option B) occurs during hypotension, resulting in compensatory tachycardia. The Bezold-Jarisch reflex (Option C) causes bradycardia and hypotension but is typically triggered by ventricular ischemia, not high blood pressure. Chemoreceptors (Option D) primarily respond to hypoxia and hypercapnia, generally leading to sympathetic activation and increased heart rate. The baroreceptor reflex is the body's fastest-acting mechanism for short-term blood pressure stability, such as during positional changes. This reflex helps counteract hypertension to maintain internal homeostasis
questions.learning: The physiological response of a decreased heart rate (bradycardia) in response to high blood pressure (hypertension) is mediated by the baroreceptor reflex.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the investigation of choice for detecting enteric fever in the first week?
questions.explanation: Enteric fever (Typhoid) is caused by Salmonella Typhi. The diagnostic yield of various tests changes significantly as the disease progresses. During the first week of illness, blood culture is the investigation of choice, with a sensitivity of . As the bacteria move into the lymphoid tissue, stool culture (Option C) becomes more useful in the second and third weeks. Urine culture (Option D) is generally positive in the third week. Antibody detection (Option D), such as the Widal test, only becomes positive after the first week and is notoriously unreliable due to many false positives. A useful mnemonic for the timing of cultures is "BASU": Blood (1st week), Antibody/Widal (2nd week), Stool (3rd week), and Urine (4th week). Bone marrow culture is actually the most sensitive test overall (up to ), even if the patient has already started antibiotics, but it is rarely done due to its invasiveness
questions.learning: Enteric fever (Typhoid) is caused by Salmonella Typhi. The diagnostic yield of various tests changes significantly as the disease progresses.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the most suitable dietary modification for a middle-aged man with a rare form of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency presenting with high anion gap metabolic acidosis?
options: High protein and low carbohydrate intake
High carbohydrate and low fat intake
High fat and low carbohydrate intake
questions.explanation: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) is the enzyme complex that converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle. A deficiency in PDH leads to the shunting of pyruvate into lactic acid, causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis. The most effective dietary management for these patients is a ketogenic diet, which is characterized by high fat and low carbohydrate intake. This diet provides an alternative fuel source by generating ketone bodies that can be converted into acetyl-CoA bypassing the defective PDH step. High carbohydrate intake (Options B and D) would exacerbate the condition by increasing pyruvate and lactic acid levels. While high protein (Option A) is part of many diets, it is not the primary mechanism for bypassing the PDH defect. Therefore, a high-fat, low-carbohydrate regimen is the specific dietary therapy used to manage metabolic acidosis in PDH deficiency
questions.learning: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) is the enzyme complex that converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle. A deficiency in PDH leads to the shunting of pyruvate into lactic acid, causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 32-year-old male chronic smoker presents with several months of persistent finger pain. Examination reveals gangrenous ulcers on his fingers, while recent blood tests show normal glucose and lipid levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a young male chronic smoker with persistent finger pain and digital gangrene is highly diagnostic of Buerger's disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans). This is a non-atherosclerotic inflammatory vasculitis that specifically affects small and medium-sized vessels in the extremities. The patient's normal glucose and lipid profiles are critical, as they rule out diabetic ulcers (Option B) and typical atherosclerosis. Raynaud's phenomenon (Option D) involves reversible vasospasm with triphasic color changes but rarely progresses to permanent gangrene in an isolated manner without underlying disease. Acute paronychia (Option C) is a localized bacterial infection around the nail, not widespread digital gangrene. Buerger's disease is uniquely and strongly linked to tobacco use; the only effective treatment is the absolute cessation of smoking. Therefore, based on the age, smoking history, and the presence of gangrene as shown in the image, Buerger's disease is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a young male chronic smoker with persistent finger pain and digital gangrene is highly diagnostic of Buerger's disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As per the POCSO Act, who is defined as being entitled to protection under the law?
options: Girl child less than 16 years age
Girl child less than 18 years age
Any child less than 16 years age
Any child less than 18 years age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Any child less than 18 years age

Under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, a child is defined as any person below 18 years of age, irrespective of gender.

The Act provides gender-neutral protection against sexual offences and mandates child-friendly procedures during reporting, investigation, and trial.

This uniform age definition ensures comprehensive legal protection for all minors.
questions.learning: Any child less than 18 years age Under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, a child is defined as any person below 18 years of age, irrespective of gender.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
A child presented to the OPD with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness while exercising. Laboratory investigations found that LCFA oxidation was affected. A muscle biopsy was done which revealed the presence of fat vacuoles. What is the probable diagnosis?

LCFA- Long-chain fatty acid

LPL- Lipoprotein lipase

LDL- Low-density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carnitine deficiency

The clinical scenario of a child with fatigue and muscle weakness on exercise with laboratory findings of LCFA oxidation deficiency and fat vacuoles on muscle biopsy suggests a diagnosis of carnitine deficiency.

Carnitine deficiency is a defect in fatty acid oxidation that leads to hypoketotic hypoglycemia and hyperammonemia. Carnitine transports activated LCFA (long chain fatty acyl CoA) from the cytoplasm to the mitochondria for beta-oxidation (as they cannot cross the mitochondrial membrane), carnitine deficiency impairs this transport causing accumulation of lipids (skeletal muscle weakness). This excess fatty acid inhibits the urea cycle causing hyperammonemia. Since beta-oxidation cannot occur, energy production is reduced, and there is hypoglycemia without a corresponding increase in ketone bodies (hypoketotic) during times of glucose depletion such as exercise.

The role of carnitine in the metabolism of fatty acids is demonstrated in the image below:

Clinical features of carnitine deficiency begin in childhood and include poor feeding, lethargy, liver dysfunction and hepatomegaly, hypotonia, and dilated cardiomyopathy. Treatment involves oral supplementation of carnitine.

Other options:

Option A: An increase in LDL can cause hyperlipoproteinemia, and reduced LDL can cause defective absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

Option B: LPL is involved in hydrolysis of lipoproteins in the blood to free fatty acid and glycerol which are then taken up by the tissues. A defective LPL can cause type 1 familial chylomicronemia syndrome presenting as pancreatitis.

Option C: Fatty acid synthase is a multienzyme complex involved in fatty acid synthesis in the cytosol which when defective may impair energy production, essential fatty acids, and affect metabolic pathways. There is no accumulation of fat vacuoles since fatty acids are not synthesised.
questions.learning: Carnitine deficiency — The clinical scenario of a child with fatigue and muscle weakness on exercise with laboratory findings of LCFA oxidation deficiency and fat vacuoles on muscle biopsy suggests a diagnosis of carnitine deficiency.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A scientist is studying the invasion of malignant colon cancer cells into surrounding tissues in an experimental model. Over time, the cancer cells are observed to detach from each other and degrade the extracellular matrix, allowing the tumor cells to invade the basement membrane and access nearby blood vessels. Which of the following substances is most likely upregulated to facilitate basement membrane invasion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metalloproteinases

Tumor invasion and metastasis require cancer cells to degrade the extracellular matrix (ECM) and basement membrane to spread into surrounding tissues and blood vessels. A key mechanism is the upregulation of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), which are enzymes that break down components of the ECM, including:

• Type IV collagen (major component of basement membrane)
• Laminin
• Proteoglycans

This degradation allows tumor cells to penetrate the basement membrane and invade adjacent tissues, facilitating metastasis.

Why not the other options:

A. Acid hydrolases: Lysosomal enzymes involved in intracellular digestion, not the main enzymes degrading the basement membrane during tumor invasion.

B. E-cadherin: A cell adhesion molecule. In cancer invasion it is typically downregulated, allowing tumor cells to detach from each other.

C. Hyaluronic acid: A component of extracellular matrix that helps tissue hydration and cell migration but does not degrade the basement membrane.
questions.learning: Metalloproteinases Tumor invasion and metastasis require cancer cells to degrade the extracellular matrix (ECM) and basement membrane to spread into surrounding tissues and blood vessels.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with features suggestive of acute rheumatic fever. Microscopic examination reveals gram- positive cocci arranged in chains. What is the most likely etiological agent?
questions.explanation: Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) is a non-suppurative inflammatory complication that occurs 2-4 weeks after a pharyngeal infection. The specific etiological agent responsible for triggering this autoimmune response is Streptococcus pyogenes, also known as Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcus (GABHS). Microscopically, these are characterized as gram-positive cocci arranged in chains. Streptococcus viridans (Option A) is a common cause of subacute bacterial endocarditis but does not trigger ARF. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option C) causes pneumonia and meningitis and typically appears as gram-positive diplococci. Enterococcus (Option D) is associated with urinary tract and abdominal infections. ARF results from molecular mimicry between the streptococcal M-protein and human heart tissue. Diagnosis is made clinically using the Jones Criteria. Long-term penicillin prophylaxis is required for these patients to prevent recurrent attacks and subsequent chronic rheumatic heart disease

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Paralysis of which muscle causes ptosis in Horner syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Superior tarsal muscle

Ptosis in Horner syndrome is due to paralysis of the superior tarsal (Müller’s) muscle, which is a sympathetically innervated smooth muscle.

This causes mild ptosis, unlike complete ptosis from levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) palsy.

Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelid, and orbitalis has no role in eyelid elevation.
questions.learning: Superior tarsal muscle Ptosis in Horner syndrome is due to paralysis of the superior tarsal (Müller’s) muscle, which is a sympathetically innervated smooth muscle.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presents with difficulty in smoothly transitioning between voluntary movements, along with involuntary, uncontrolled movements of the hands. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Difficulty in switching between rapid alternating movements, such as pronation and supination of the hands, is termed dysdiadochokinesis. This clinical sign is a classic manifestation of cerebellar dysfunction or ataxia. Intentional tremor (Option B) also occurs in cerebellar disease but specifically refers to tremors that worsen as the hand approaches a voluntary target. Metamorphosis (Option C) typically refers to visual distortions (metamorphopsia) and is unrelated to motor coordination. Resting tremor (Option D) is characteristic of Parkinson's disease, occurring when the limb is at rest and improving with voluntary movement. Other cerebellar signs include ataxia (drunken gait), dysmetria (overshooting), and dysarthria (jumbled speech). The inability to perform these smooth, rapid alternating movements helps localize the lesion to the cerebellum, which normally coordinates the timing and sequencing of motor activities
questions.learning: Difficulty in switching between rapid alternating movements, such as pronation and supination of the hands, is termed dysdiadochokinesis. This clinical sign is a classic manifestation of cerebellar dysfunction or ataxia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 5-year-old child with Wilson's disease is being considered for liver transplantation. Which of the following is not a parameter in the selection criteria for transplantation?
options: Jaundice less than 7 days before development of encephalopathy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Jaundice less than 7 days before development of encephalopathy

A 5-year-old child with Wilson's disease is a case of non-paracetamol-induced acute liver failure and jaundice for more than 7 days before the development of encephalopathy is one of the parameters in the King's College criteria for liver transplantation.

It includes the following parameters:

Non-paracetamol-induced acute liver failure:

• PT >100 s (INR >6.5)

or/and

• Any three of the following:

• Age <10 years or >40 years
• Etiology non-A, non-B hepatitis, or idiosyncratic drug reaction
• Jaundice more than 7 days before the development of encephalopathy i.e., not hyperacute
• PT >50 s (INR > 3.5)
• Bilirubin > 18 mg/dl (300 μmol/L)

Paracetamol-induced acute liver failure:

• pH <7.30 (irrespective of the grade of encephalopathy)

or/and

• All three of the following:

• Prothrombin time >100 s (INR >6.5)
• Serum creatinine >3.4 mg/dl (300 μmol/L)
• Grade 3 or 4 hepatic encephalopathy

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In Integrated child development services (ICDS), intersectoral coordination is seen with which organization?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NHM

In Integrated child development services (ICDS), intersectoral coordination is seen with NHM(National Health Mission).

The ICDS overlaps with many of the programs of NHM of which the Anemia Mukt Bharat Scheme  is an example, where prophylactic iron and folic acid is given to children, adolescents, women of reproductive age, and pregnant women, irrespective of anemia

ICDS:

The blueprint for the scheme was prepared by the Department of Social Welfare in 1975. The Government of India decided to expand the project to cover 100 areas by 1978-79. UNDP (United Nations Development Programme): It is the main source of funds for technical assistance. Its main objective is to help poorer nations develop their human and natural resources to their potential.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is brought with complaints of poor vision in one eye. On examination, there is no obvious squint. Visual acuity is 6/6 in the right eye and 6/24 in the left eye. Cycloplegic refraction reveals +1.00 D in the right eye and +5.50 D in the left eye. Fundus examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anisometropic amblyopia

Anisometropia is defined as a difference in refractive error between the two eyes, leading to unequal image clarity.

Difference in myopia, hypermetropia, or astigmatism between eyes.

Clinical significance:

• Can cause anisometropic amblyopia (lazy eye) in children
• Due to unequal image size/clarity (aniseikonia) → brain suppresses one eye
• Important cause of unilateral amblyopia

Types of Amblyopia (Lazy Eye)

A. Isoametropic Amblyopia

Occurs when both eyes have high but equal refractive error.

• Brain receives blurred images from both eyes.
• Usually due to high:

• hypermetropia,
• myopia,
• or astigmatism in both eyes equally.

Example:

Both eyes have +7D hypermetropia → bilateral blurred vision → amblyopia develops in both eyes.

B. Strabismic Amblyopia

Occurs due to squint (strabismus).

• Brain suppresses image from deviated eye to avoid diplopia.
• Suppressed eye becomes amblyopic.

Example:

Child with esotropia suppresses input from one eye → reduced vision in that eye.

C. Anisometropic Amblyopia

Occurs when there is unequal refractive error between the two eyes.

• Brain prefers clearer image from better eye.
• Blurred eye gets suppressed and becomes amblyopic.

Example:

One eye +1D, other eye +6D hypermetropia → poorer eye develops amblyopia.

D. Deprivation Amblyopia

Occurs when visual stimulus is blocked during visual development.

• Most severe form.
• Due to obstruction of visual axis.

Causes:

• Congenital cataract
• Ptosis
• Corneal opacity

Example:

Unilateral congenital cataract prevents image formation → amblyopia.
questions.learning: Anisometropic amblyopia Anisometropia is defined as a difference in refractive error between the two eyes, leading to unequal image clarity. Difference in myopia, hypermetropia, or astigmatism between eyes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presented with recurrent oral ulcers since one year, episodes of redness of eye and genital ulcers. Which one of the following tests is of diagnostic value?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pathergy test

Behçet’s disease is a chronic multisystem inflammatory vasculitis characterized by the classic triad of:

• Recurrent oral aphthous ulcers
• Genital ulcers
• Ocular involvement (uveitis)

The Pathergy test is a useful bedside diagnostic test that demonstrates cutaneous hyperreactivity. A sterile papule or pustule develops 24–48 hours after a needle prick, reflecting an exaggerated inflammatory response.

Why not the other options?

• A. Mantoux test: Used to detect tuberculosis infection, not Behçet’s disease.
• B. Drug-sensitivity test: Used to determine antimicrobial susceptibility and has no role in diagnosing Behçet’s disease.
• D. Patch test: Used to diagnose allergic contact dermatitis (Type IV hypersensitivity).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer from the sub-Himalayan belt had a thorn prick injury a year back and developed a warty, verrucous growth at the site of prick. A skin biopsy sample was taken and sent for histopathological examination. The characteristic microscopic body as shown in the image was seen. Which of the following could be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chromoblastomycosis

The history of a slowly spreading warty, verrucous lesion following a thorn prick injury and the histopathological image showing medlar bodies is suggestive of chromoblastomycosis.

Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is a subcutaneous mycotic infection that is usually caused by traumatic inoculation. Over months to years, the primary lesion becomes verrucous and wart-like with extension along the draining lymphatics.

Histologically, the lesions are granulomatous and the dark sclerotic bodies may be seen within leukocytes or giant cells called medlar/copper penny bodies.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents to you with anemia, thrombocytopenia, and bony pain. On examination, hepatosplenomegaly was noticed. If light microscopy of bone marrow aspirate reveals "crumpled tissue paper" appearance, what is the enzyme defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glucocerebrosidase

The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of Gaucher's disease, where there is a defect in the enzyme glucocerebrosidase.

Gaucher's disease is a lysosomal storage disease with autosomal recessive inheritance. The condition results due to the deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase. This results in the accumulation of glucosylceramide (glycolipid substrate) in the reticuloendothelial cells. There is progressive infiltration of the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

There are three clinical types:

• Type 1: Adult (non-neuronopathic) form
• Type 2: Infantile (acute neuronopathic) form
• Type 3: Juvenile (subacute neuronopathic) form

Type 1 is the most common. It presents with a myriad of symptoms, such as bruising secondary to thrombocytopenia, fatigue due to anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone pain. Pathologic fractures and lytic lesions of the femur, ribs, and pelvis may also be seen. A few patients may have pulmonary involvement. Growth retardation may be observed in cases presenting in the first decade.

Type 2 is rare, and presents with hypertonia, strabismus, and organomegaly. Neurodegeneration is the characteristic feature. Stridor and failure to thrive can also be the presenting features. Ultimately, death can occur due to respiratory arrest.

Type 3 presents with intermediate symptoms, as seen in the other two types. By the age of 10–15 years, the child succumbs to death.

The Gaucher cells, which are the reticuloendothelial cells with glucosylceramide, have a wrinkled-paper appearance due to intracytoplasmic substrate inclusions. These cells stain strongly with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain. This is characteristic of Gaucher's disease.

Other options:

Option B - Acid sphingomyelinase deficiency results in Niemann-Pick disease types A and B. Both are autosomal recessive conditions. Type A has a neurodegenerative course, while type B is non-neuronopathic. The former presents with hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and psychomotor retardation. Death occurs by the age of 3 years. Type B is associated with hepatosplenomegaly and mild pulmonary involvement.

Option C - Hexosaminidase deficiency causes Sandhoff disease. It has an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. Clinical features include ataxia, dysarthria, and mental retardation.

Option D - Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency leads to von Gierke disease, which is a glycogen storage disorder.  It is an autosomal recessive condition. The affected children have characteristic doll-like facies. Hyperuricemia, lactic acidosis, and triglyceridemia can be seen. Hepatomegaly and renal enlargement is also associated.
questions.learning: Glucocerebrosidase — The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of Gaucher's disease, where there is a defect in the enzyme glucocerebrosidase. Gaucher's disease is a lysosomal storage disease with autosomal recessive inheritance.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following clinical features is not commonly associated with Ménière’s disease?
questions.explanation: Meniere's disease is an inner ear disorder characterized by endolymphatic hydrops. The classic clinical tetrad includes episodic vertigo (Option B), fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus (Option A), and a sense of fullness in the affected ear (Option C) . Ear pain (otalgia) (Option D) is not a feature of Meniere's disease; its presence should prompt an investigation into other conditions such as otitis media, external ear infections, or referred pain from the throat. Tinnitus in Meniere's is typically low-pitched and described as a "roaring" sound. The vertigo is usually spontaneous and lasts for several hours. Because Meniere's involves a build-up of fluid pressure within the vestibular and cochlear compartments rather than an infectious or inflammatory process in the pain-sensitive outer structures, it remains a painless condition. Therefore, ear pain is the correct "not" answer for this diagnosis
questions.learning: Meniere's disease is an inner ear disorder characterized by endolymphatic hydrops. The classic clinical tetrad includes episodic vertigo (Option B), fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus (Option A), and a sense of fullness in the affected ear…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is a correct statement regarding retroperitoneal trauma?
options: All zone 1 injury to be treated conservatively
Zone 3 injury whether blunt or penetrative should always be explored
Zone 2 injury with expanding hematoma should be treated surgically
Mattox maneuver is when the ascending colon is mobilized to the right to visualise the aorta
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zone 2 injury with expanding hematoma should be treated surgically

A zone 2 retroperitoneal injury with expanding hematoma should be treated surgically.

Zone of retroperitoneal injury
Type of viscera
Differential management

Zone 1
Central
Always explored, after proximo-distal vascular control

Zone 2
Lateral

Only explored if the hematoma is pulsatile or expanding, else conservative/ angioembolization

Zone 3
Pelvic
Only explored if the hematoma is pulsatile or expanding, else conservative/ angioembolization

Surgical exploration is done in cases of penetrating injuries to any zone.

Other options:

Option A: Zone 1 injuries are always explored.

Option B: Depending on the situation, zone 3 injuries can be managed with surgical exploration or conservatively.

Option D: Mattox manoeuvre is left medial visceral rotation to expose the aorta, while the Cattell-Braasch manoeuvre is done by right medial visceral rotation to expose IVC.
