questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with palpitations, headache, and sweating. His BP is 180/100 mmHg. 24-hour urinary metanephrine values are elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pheochromocytoma

The above clinical scenario of palpitations, headache, and sweating, with BP is 180/100 mmHg, 24-hour urinary metanephrine values are elevated, is consistent with the diagnosis of Pheochromocytoma.

It is a catecholamine-secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.It can be sporadic or hereditary. Hereditary pheochromocytoma occurs in association with syndromes such as MEN 2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), familial paraganglioma syndrome, Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, and neurofibromatosis (NF) type 1.

Clinical features:

It most commonly presents as a classic triad of intermittent headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating along with hypertension. The patient can also present with anxiety, panic attacks, nausea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and weakness. Symptoms may be precipitated by surgery, pregnancy, position changes, exercise, and medications such as metoclopramide and tricyclic antidepressants.

Investigations:

* Biochemical screening test—measurement of urinary and plasma levels of catecholamines and metanephrines.

* MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor. It is preferred over a CT scan, as the contrast used in CT scans can precipitate paroxysms.

* Other imaging modalities like MIBG scintigraphy and DOPA- or FDG-PET scans are used in identifying the primary tumor as well as the extra-adrenal tumors and metastases.

Surgical resection of the tumor is the definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma. Preoperatively, hypertension is managed initially with alpha-blockers followed by beta-blockers.

Other options:

Option B: Carcinoid Tumor usually presents with flushing, diarrhea, wheezing, and elevated 5-HIAA (not metanephrines).

Option C: Neuroblastoma usually occurs in children, presents with abdominal mass with hypotonia, ataxia, behavioral symptoms and elevated urinary VMA/HVA, not metanephrines.

Option D: Adrenocortical Tumor secretes cortisol/aldosterone/androgens, not catecholamines.

Pearl PF1539: Pheochromocytoma

Features:

* When pheochromocytoma is associated with the MEN syndrome it is rarely malignant.

* Phaeochromocytomas are greyish-pink on the cut surface and are usually highly vascularised.

* Zellbalen cells and nuclei with salt and pepper chromatin are seen.

Factors indicating more chances of malignancy:

* An increased PASS (phaeochromocytoma of the adrenal gland scale score)

* High number of Ki-67-positive cells

* Vascular invasion or a breached capsule

Diagnosis:

* Urinary catecholamine and VMA level assay are most sensitive screening test.

* MRI is the IOC.

* Biopsy and CT Contrast scan are contraindicated in order to avoid Hypertensive crisis.

Treatment:

* Adrenalectomy is preferred TOC.

* Size<5 cm -  Laparoscopic adrenalectomy

* Preop Alpha blockers should be given

* Mitotane should be started as adjuvant or palliative treatment
questions.learning: Pheochromocytoma — The above clinical scenario of palpitations, headache, and sweating, with BP is 180/100 mmHg, 24-hour urinary metanephrine values are elevated, is consistent with the diagnosis of Pheochromocytoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is cannabinoid oil not indicated in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rett syndrome

Cannabinoid oil is not indicated in Rett syndrome.

The FDA recently approved cannabidiol oral solution for the treatment of seizures associated with tuberous sclerosis complex in patients one year of age and older. It was previously approved for the treatment of seizures associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and Dravet syndrome.

Cannabinoid oil is an oral derivative of the cannabis plant. The mechanism by which it improves seizure threshold is not understood yet and there are various studies ongoing to survey its use. The cannabinoid receptors are G protein-coupled receptors located predominantly in the presynaptic nerve terminals.

The CB1 receptor is located in the central nervous system. Activation of CB1 receptor results in euphoria and alleviation of pain (anti-nociceptive effect). The CB2 receptor is located mainly in the periphery and their activation does not have a euphoric effect.

The endogenous cannabinoid system is a potential target for use in the treatment of chronic pain. The most common adverse effects of CBD at doses used for treating epilepsy include somnolence, fatigue, decreased appetite, diarrhea, and elevated hepatic transaminases. The elevations in liver transaminases are dose-related.
questions.learning: Rett syndrome Cannabinoid oil is not indicated in Rett syndrome. The FDA recently approved cannabidiol oral solution for the treatment of seizures associated with tuberous sclerosis complex in patients one year of age and older.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with sedation, respiratory depression, and altered level of consciousness suggestive of benzodiazepine overdose. What is the appropriate antidote in this situation?
questions.explanation: Flumazenil is the specific and standard antidote for benzodiazepine overdose. It acts as a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site on the receptor complex. By displacing benzodiazepines from the receptor, it rapidly reverses their sedative and respiratory depressant effects. Flurazepam (Option B) is actually a long-acting benzodiazepine and would worsen the overdose. Barbiturates (Option C) act on a different site of the receptor and would further compound the CNS depression. Buspirone (Option D) is a non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic that acts on serotonin receptors and has no role in managing benzodiazepine toxicity. While flumazenil is effective for acute reversal, its use must be cautious in chronic users, as it can precipitate life-threatening withdrawal seizures. Furthermore, it has a shorter half-life than many benzodiazepines, meaning the patient may require repeated doses or an infusion if "re-sedation" occurs once the flumazenil wears off. It is primarily used for acute poisoning or to reverse conscious sedation post-procedure
questions.learning: Flumazenil is the specific and standard antidote for benzodiazepine overdose. It acts as a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site on the receptor complex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the underlying cause of hypoxia in a newly arrived resident in a high-altitude region?
questions.explanation: At high altitudes, the total barometric pressure decreases, which results in a corresponding decrease in the partial pressure of inspired oxygen (PO2). This lower PO2 in the atmosphere leads to a lower PO2 in the alveoli and consequently in the arterial blood, causing hypoxia. This is the primary physiological challenge for anyone ascending to high altitudes. Low hemoglobin levels (Option A, anemia) can cause hypoxia, but it is not the cause of altitude-related distress; in fact, the body eventually increases hemoglobin as an adaptation. Low blood lactate (Option C) is not a cause of hypoxia. High partial pressure of CO2 (Option D) would indicate hypoventilation, but at high altitudes, residents typically hyperventilate to compensate for the low oxygen, leading to low CO2 levels. Understanding this fundamental relationship between atmospheric pressure and PO2 is essential for grasping the pathophysiology of acute mountain sickness and the subsequent process of acclimatization
questions.learning: At high altitudes, the total barometric pressure decreases, which results in a corresponding decrease in the partial pressure of inspired oxygen (PO2).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding neutrophil extracellular trapping (NET)?
options: It is detected in blood during sepsis
It is produced in response to bacterial infection.
It is chromatin with antibacterial enzymes.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mitochondrial DNA is seen.

Bacterial infection

↓

Neutrophil activation

↓

Nuclear chromatin decondensation

↓

DNA + enzymes released

↓

NET formation → traps microbes

Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) consist of decondensed nuclear chromatin decorated with antimicrobial enzymes like elastase and myeloperoxidase.

They are released in response to bacterial infections and are detectable in sepsis.

NETs are composed primarily of nuclear DNA, not mitochondrial DNA.

Hence, the statement regarding mitochondrial DNA is false.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Arrange the sequence of lactation in the right order * Mammogenesis * Lactogenesis * Galactokinesis * Galactopoiesis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 - 2 - 3 - 4

The correct order of lactation is: Mammogenesis – lactogenesis – galactokinesis – galactopoiesis

Function
Definition
Hormone

Mammogenesis
Breast growth and development

Estrogen (ductal growth)

Progesterone (alveolar growth)

Lactogenesis
Initiation of milk secretion
Prolactin

Galactokinesis
Ejection of milk
Oxytocin

Galactopoiesis
Maintainence of lactation
Prolactin

Mammogenesis: This refers to the development and growth of the mammary glands. It occurs during puberty and pregnancy under the influence of hormones like estrogen and progesterone.

Lactogenesis: This is the process of milk production. There are two phases:

* a. Lactogenesis I: Also known as colostrum secretion, it begins during late pregnancy and continues after birth for a few days. The mammary glands produce colostrum, a thick, yellowish fluid rich in antibodies and nutrients.

* b. Lactogenesis II: Also known as transitional milk secretion, it begins around 2-5 days after birth. The mammary glands switch to producing mature milk.

Galactokinesis: This involves the movement of milk through the mammary ducts towards the nipple. It is facilitated by the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli in response to oxytocin release.

Galactopoiesis: This refers to the maintenance and regulation of milk production. It involves hormonal regulation, primarily prolactin, which stimulates milk synthesis and secretion. Additionally, factors like frequent breastfeeding or milk removal help maintain milk production.

So, the correct sequence is Mammogenesis (development of mammary glands) – Lactogenesis (milk production) – Galactokinesis (movement of milk) – Galactopoiesis (maintenance of milk production.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the branch of statistics dealing with describing the internal collection of data?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Descriptive statistics

Descriptive statistics is the branch that deals with describing the internal collection of data.

Statistical methods are mainly of two types

• Descriptive statistics is a type of statistical method which helps to describe, organise or summarise the data. It refers only to the actual data. They are described by the measures of central tendency and the degrees of dispersion.
• Inferential statistics involves going beyond the actual data and making inferences to test the hypothesis.

Other types of statistics:

• Analytical statistics is mainly used to test the hypothesis.
• Theoretical statistics is a mathematical approach which involves describing, predicting the events or analyzing the relationship between things.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 28-year-old dentist presents with painful grouped vesicular lesions on the distal phalanx of her right index finger. She reports a burning sensation followed by the appearance of fluid-filled blisters that ruptured into shallow ulcers. She denies systemic symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Herpetic whitlow

The given clinical vignette of a dentist with fluid-filled, painful grouped vesicular lesions, with a burning sensation on the distal phalanx of a dentist, is suggestive of herpetic whitlow infection.

Clinical features include painful, deep vesicles at the site of inoculation (in this case, the fingertips), which coalesce to form large bullae or a honeycomb appearance, which is most commonly contracted by dental workers and medical workers exposed to oral secretions. Fever and constitutional symptoms are mild. HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause this condition.

Whitlow can lead to necrosis of the distal 4/5th of the terminal phalanx. It does not cause necrosis of the entire phalanx because the proximal 1/5th escapes, as in this part, the artery does not cross the fibrous septa.The pulp space of fingers contains subcutaneous fat arranged in tight compartments. These compartments are formed by fibrous septa extending from the skin to the periosteum of the terminal phalanx.

Diagnosis of herpes simplex virus:

* Most sensitive test- HSV DNA- PCR (can differentiate between HSV 1 and 2)

* Most definitive test- virus isolation using human diploid fibroblast in which cytopathic changes can be observed as early as 24 - 48 hours.

* Microscopy - Tzanck smear, which is a rapid, diagnostic method, shows Tzanck cells. These are multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and homogenously stained ground-glass chromatin. Intranuclear type A inclusion bodies may also be seen.

The image given below shows Tzanck cells:

The image below shows the characteristic lesions of herpetic whitlow (The presence of vesicles and cloudy blisters at the pulp of fingers)

Topical acyclovir therapy can be initiated in cases of primary herpetic whitlow. Primary HSV infection at multiple sites and recurrent herpetic whitlow require oral acyclovir therapy. Intravenous acyclovir is recommended in immunocompromised patients.

Other options:

Option A: Molluscum contagiosum is a common, self-limiting viral disease of the skin caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus(MCV), which is classified within the poxvirus family. Usually, it occurs as scattered lesions on discrete areas of the body, appearing as shiny, pearly white, umbilicated papules(shown below).

Option B: Paronychia refers to an infection of the proximal & lateral nail folds. It results from the disruption of the protective barrier between the nail and the nail fold, introducing pathogens and predisposing the area to infection. Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus(shown below).

Option C: Verruca vulgaris or common wart is caused by human papilloma virus 2 (HPV-2), but is also closely related to types 27 and 57 as well as types 1 and 4. These present as firm papules with a rough, horny surface and are most commonly situated on the backs of the hands and fingers, and in children, frequently on the knees, though they may occur anywhere on the skin.
questions.learning: Herpetic whitlow — The given clinical vignette of a dentist with fluid-filled, painful grouped vesicular lesions, with a burning sensation on the distal phalanx of a dentist, is suggestive of herpetic whitlow infection.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the most common clinical effect observed with cannabis use?
questions.explanation: Cannabis is a psychoactive substance derived from the hemp plant. Its most characteristic and predominant manifestation is the induction of a dream-like state or "high," marked by altered perception of time, heightened sensory awareness, and euphoria. Other common acute features include conjunctival injection ("red eyes") and a significant increase in appetite (the "munchies"), making Option D incorrect. While anxiety (Option A) can occur—especially in high doses or "bad trips"—it is not the typical primary desired effect. Depressed mood (Option B) is generally not the immediate effect of cannabis use. Long-term use is associated with an "amotivational syndrome" characterized by apathy and social withdrawal. In a psychiatric and forensic context, recognizing this dream-like state and the characteristic physical signs is essential for identifying cannabis intoxication. The primary active component, THC, acts on receptors in the brain to modulate neurotransmission and produce these classic psychological effects
questions.learning: Cannabis is a psychoactive substance derived from the hemp plant. Its most characteristic and predominant manifestation is the induction of a dream-like state or "high," marked by altered perception of time, heightened sensory awareness, and euphoria.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old female patient presents with a 3-day history of fever, headache, ataxia, nausea, and vomiting. On examination neck rigidity is present and there is hip and knee flexion on passive flexion of the neck. A lumbar puncture was done and CSF findings are as shown below. What is your diagnosis? Opening pressure - Increased Colour- Cloudy white WBCs - 7000/µl; neutrophil predominant Sugar- 15 mg/dl CSF/serum glucose ratio - 0.2 Protein - 70 mg/dl Latex agglutination - positive Limulus lysate test - negative
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bacterial meningitis

The clinical picture and CSF examination findings are suggestive of bacterial meningitis.

The classic clinical triad of fever, headache, and neck rigidity is suggestive of meningitis. Other common complaints are nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. Nuchal rigidity (“stiff neck”) is the pathognomonic sign of meningitis. Hip and knee flexion on passive flexion of the neck is called Brudzinsky's sign.

>180 mmH2O

WBC

10/μL to 10,000/μL; neutrophils predominate

RBC
Absent in non-traumatic tap

Glucose

<2.2 mmol/L (<40 mg/dL)

CSF/serum glucose
<0.4

Protein

>0.45 g/L (>45 mg/dL)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Wasting in a child is assessed by which of the following measures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Weight for height

A low weight for height indicates wasting in a child.

Nutritional status is often assessed in terms of anthropometry

* Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition.

* High weight for height indicates overweight.

* Low height for age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.

* Low weight for age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

Note:

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is an age-independent parameter used for screening wasting in children.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A neuron is receiving 400 inputs from 150 sensory neurons. This is an example of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Convergence

A single neuron receiving 400 inputs from 150 sensory neurons is an example of convergence.

Convergence means signals from multiple inputs uniting to excite a single neuron. It can be of 2 types:

• Convergence from a single source
• Convergence from multiple sources

The importance of convergence is that neurons are almost never excited by an action potential from a single input terminal. However, action potentials converging on the neuron from multiple terminals provide enough spatial summation to bring the neuron to the threshold required for discharge.
questions.learning: Convergence — A single neuron receiving 400 inputs from 150 sensory neurons is an example of convergence. Convergence means signals from multiple inputs uniting to excite a single neuron.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All among the following are clinical features of necrotizing enterocolitis except _________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metabolic alkalosis

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) can cause metabolic or respiratory acidosis (not alkalosis).

Acidosis can be attributed to sepsis, lactic acidosis due to decreased perfusion of the abdominal wall, decreased reabsorption of bicarbonate from the intestine, and reduced respiratory compensation due to apnea.

NEC is the most common life-threatening gastrointestinal disorder in the newborn period. It is characterized by various degrees of mucosal or transmural inflammation and necrosis of the intestinal tract. It most commonly affects the distal ileum and proximal colon.

Three major risk factors implicated are prematurity (greatest risk factor), formula feeding, and bacterial colonization of the intestine. Incidence and mortality increase with decreasing birth weight and gestational age.

It usually presents within the 2nd or 3rd week of life with abdominal distension and tenderness, feed intolerance, and occult/gross blood in the stool. Systemic features include hypotension, bradycardia, lethargy, and temperature instability. Other signs and symptoms include vomiting, changes in stool pattern, abdominal mass, apnea, respiratory distress, hyponatremia, shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Diagnosis can be made with a plain abdominal X-ray. Pneumatosis intestinalis (air in the bowel wall) is diagnostic. Portal vein gas is a sign of severe disease. Pneumoperitoneum indicates perforation of the intestinal wall.

Management of NEC includes supportive measures - nil per oral, nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and inotropic support if indicated. Perforation is an absolute indication for surgery. The most effective preventive strategy is the use of human milk. Prebiotics and probiotics can be used with variable efficacy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the imaging modality given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. PET CT

The above imaging modality is a PET CT scan.

PET (positron-emission tomography) CT scan is a hybrid technique that combines PET and CT scan that is used for targeted imaging of tumor physiology and biology. It is based on the principle that tumor cells generally have high metabolic activity compared with normal tissues.

A small dose of the radiopharmaceutical agent 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG). This enters cells and is phosphorylated to FDG 6-phosphate which cannot be metabolized further. Since it is a highly polar molecule, it cannot easily diffuse back out of the cell. After intravenous injection of FDG, it continuously accumulates in the metabolically active cell.

The main advantage of PET-CT is the identification of distant metastatic disease not seen on CT alone. The disadvantages of PET scans are radiation burden, poorer spatial resolution when used alone, and high cost.

Other options:

Option A: Cerebral blood flow scan refers to the perfusion MRI that uses gadolinium as contrast and provides information about the cerebral blood flow and volume.

Option B: The sestamibi scan is used for parathyroid localization and is now considered the most accurate and reliable method for imaging the parathyroid glands. Sestamibi accumulates in mitochondria. Parathyroid adenomas often have a high concentration of oxyphilic cells with high mitochondrial content. These retain sestamibi tracer and adenomas are therefore associated with a slow washout when compared with the thyroid gland.

Option D: The full body MDCT scan refers to the multidetector CT scan which is an advanced CT imaging technique that uses multiple detector elements that provide improvement in speed, quality, and scope.
questions.learning: PET CT — The above imaging modality is a PET CT scan. PET (positron-emission tomography) CT scan is a hybrid technique that combines PET and CT scan that is used for targeted imaging of tumor physiology and biology.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female, P2L2, presents with a mass per vaginum. On examination, infravaginal elongation of the cervix is noted. How will you treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fothergill surgery

The appropriate treatment for a 30-year-old female with infravaginal elongation of the cervix is Fothergill surgery.

Fothergill surgery, or the Manchester operation, involves performing an anterior colporrhaphy combined with the amputation of the cervix. During the procedure, the Mackenrodt ligaments are sutured in front of the cervix, and the operation concludes with a colpoperineorrhaphy. This surgical approach is particularly suitable for women under 40 years old who wish to maintain reproductive function, although it’s important to note that fertility may be reduced following the procedure.

Various other surgeries were performed for the management of uterovaginal prolapse:

1. Anterior colporrhaphy: This is done for cystocele or cystourethrocele.
2. Posterior colporrhaphy/ colpoperineorrhaphy: This is done for posterior defects like rectocele or rectal defects with perineal laxity.
3. Le Forte's repair(option B): This is preferred only in elderly women with advanced prolapse, or those unfit for surgery. Women wanting an active sexual life are poor candidates for this procedure as it creates an adhesive area in the midline.
4. Abdominal sling surgeries: Young women desirous of retaining menstrual and reproductive functions are ideal candidates. These surgeries use tapes as slings to prevent organ descent. These include:

1. Abdominal wall cervicopexy (modified by Purandare and Mathre) - sling attached to cervix posteriorly near uterosacral ligaments.
2. Shirodkar's sling surgery - the sling fixes the cervix to the lumbosacral fascia.
3. Khanna's sling surgery - sling fixed to the anterior superior iliac spine, strengthening the Mackenrodt's ligament.

5. Fothergill surgery (Manchester operation)
6. Ward-Mayo surgery: This is a combination of vaginal hysterectomy + pelvic floor repair. It is done in women >40 years, not desiring reproductive function.
7. Moschowitz surgery: This is performed for enterocele repair where the pouch of Douglas is obliterated.

Management of Vault prolapse:

• If the patient is fit for abdominal surgery: Transabdominal sacral colpopexy, i.e., suspending the vault to the sacral promontory extraperitoneally. It is best suited for younger women since coital difficulty following vaginal surgery is avoided
• If the patient is not fit for abdominal surgery: Right Transvaginal sacrospinous colpopexy. It is usually preferred in obese and elderly women, who are not fit for abdominal surgery.
• Colpocleisis is permissible if sexual activity is not desired.

Other options:

Option A: McCall culdoplasty is primarily used to prevent enterocele formation and provide support to the posterior vaginal apex, particularly following vaginal hysterectomy.

Option D: The Latzko procedure is a surgical technique used to treat vesicovaginal fistula. It involves removing the vaginal epithelium around the fistula and approximating the edges to promote healing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with a clinical scenario of obstructive jaundice. Which of the following results can be seen on Van den bergh's reaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Direct positive

In a patient with obstructive jaundice , van der bergh reaction gives direct positive result due to conjugated  hyperbilirubinemia .

Van den Bergh reaction is used to determine the serum bilirubin level.

Van den Bergh reaction is a colorimetric method to measure serum bilirubin. It is based on the formation of red azodipyrroles when diazotised sulfanilic acid reacts with bilirubin.

Interpretation:

• In the absence of methanol, the water-soluble conjugated bilirubin reacts rapidly with the reagent and is called direct bilirubin.
• In the presence of methanol, both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin react, providing the total bilirubin.
• Unconjugated (Indirect) bilirubin = Total-direct bilirubin
questions.learning: Direct positive — In a patient with obstructive jaundice , van der bergh reaction gives direct positive result due to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia . Van den Bergh reaction is used to determine the serum bilirubin level.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 30-year-old man develops auditory hallucinations and is unable to identify the source of the voices approximately seven hours after undergoing an appendectomy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A patient developing auditory hallucinations 7 hours post-surgery is classic presentation of postoperative delirium — an acute confusional state caused by physiological disturbance following surgery including anesthesia effects, hypoxia, electrolyte imbalance, or pain medications. Key features pointing to Delirium: 1. Acute onset after surgery 2. Hallucinations — perceptual disturbances 3. Postoperative setting — classic trigger 4. Unable to identify source — disorientation characteristic of delirium Why other options are wrong: (A) Delirium tremens is incorrect because delirium tremens occurs 48-72 hours after alcohol withdrawal — not 7 hours post-surgery. No history of alcohol dependence or withdrawal is mentioned here. (B) Acute transient psychotic disorder is incorrect because ATPD requires symptoms lasting at least 1 day with sudden onset psychosis — postoperative hallucinations have a clear organic physiological cause making delirium more appropriate diagnosis. (D) Alcoholic hallucinosis is incorrect because alcoholic hallucinosis occurs in chronic alcoholics experiencing withdrawal, typically 12-24 hours after stopping alcohol — no alcoholism history is mentioned and surgical context clearly points to delirium

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the histological image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Transitional epithelium

The above image shows transitional epithelium.

The deepest layer has columnar cells, the middle layers are made up of polyhedral cells and the surface layer has cells that are large and shaped like an umbrella.

Transitional epithelium is found in the renal pelvis and calyces, the ureter, the urinary bladder, and part of the urethra. Because of this distribution, it is also called urothelium. In the urinary bladder, it is usually observed that transitional epithelium can be stretched considerably without being damaged. When stretched it appears to be thinner and the cells become flattened or rounded.

Pearl PF1699: Various Types of Epithelium, Their Location and Functions

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male with Marfanoid features presented with sudden onset breathlessness. The chest X-ray is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pneumothorax

The chest X-ray demonstrating tracheal deviation and displacement of the heart away from the affected side along with the partial collapse of the left lung in the above condition points to a diagnosis of left-sided pneumothorax.

Marfan's syndrome is one of the causes for seconday spontaneous pneumothorax in adults.

Pneumothorax refers to the collection of air in the pleural space.

Chest radiograph in spontaneous pneumothorax demonstrates:

• Thin, sharp white line, demarcating the visceral pleural edge
• Absence of lung markings seen peripheral to this line
• Peripheral space radiolucent compared to adjacent lung
• Complete lung collapse, as well as subcutaneous emphysema and pneumomediastinum, may be seen
• Deep sulcus sign (on supine chest radiograph)

Deep sulcus sign: On a supine position(common in the ICU), air collects anteriorly and basally, within the non-dependent portions of the pleural space, abnormally deepening the costophrenic angle. This sign is indicative of pneumothorax in such patients and may be the only visible clue, especially when patient can not be imaged upright.

The image below is plain chest x-ray showing pneumothorax with deep sulcus sign (shown by arrow):

When there is a progressive accumulation of air intrapleurally in the thoracic cavity (caused by a valve effect during inspiration and expiration), it is called Tension pneumothorax. It can result in compression of mediastinal structures and compromise cardiopulmonary function. It is life-threatening and requires emergency intervention.
questions.learning: Pneumothorax — The chest X-ray demonstrating tracheal deviation and displacement of the heart away from the affected side along with the partial collapse of the left lung in the above condition points to a diagnosis of left-sided pneumothorax.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the name of the sign demonstrated in the contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head shown below?
questions.explanation: The Holman Miller sign (or antral sign) is a classic radiological feature observed in juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA). It refers to the anterior bowing or displacement of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus by the tumor mass, which originates in the sphenopalatine foramen. This sign is highly characteristic of JNA, which typically affects adolescent males and presents with recurrent, severe epistaxis and nasal obstruction. Aquino Sign (Option A) involves the blanching of a tumor upon carotid compression. Teardrop sign (Option C) and Hanging drop sign (Option D) are associated with orbital blowout fractures where orbital contents herniate into the maxillary sinus. In the context of a 14-year-old male with severe spontaneous nasal bleeding, the Holman Miller sign on CT provides definitive evidence of the expansive nature of a nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not a branch of the external carotid artery in Kiesselbach’s plexus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior and posterior ethmoidal

Anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries are branches of the ophthalmic artery which in turn is a branch of the internal carotid artery.

Kiesselbach’s plexus is an arterial anastomosis at the anterior inferior part of the nasal septum (Little's area). It includes the anterior ethmoidal artery, septal branch of the superior labial artery, septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery, and septal branch of the greater palatine artery. It is the usual site of epistaxis in children and young adults.

The blood supply of the nasal septum can be divided into two main systems, the internal carotid system, and the external carotid system.

• Internal carotid system: Branches of the ophthalmic artery, anterior ethmoidal artery, and posterior ethmoidal artery.
• External carotid system: Sphenopalatine artery (branch of the maxillary artery) gives nasopalatine and posterior medial nasal branches, septal branch of the greater palatine artery (branch of the maxillary artery), and septal branch of the superior labial artery (branch of the facial artery).
questions.learning: Anterior and posterior ethmoidal Anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries are branches of the ophthalmic artery which in turn is a branch of the internal carotid artery.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A research group conducted a placebo-controlled clinical trial to assess whether a new drug to treat acute migraine with or without aura in adults is more effective than standard therapy. During the data analysis phase, the researchers decide to set alpha at 0.01 rather than 0.05. Which of the following is the most likely result of this change?
options: Any significant findings will be reported with greater confidence
There will be a higher probability of a type I error
There will be a higher probability of finding statistically significant results
The study will have more statistical power
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Any significant findings will be reported with greater confidence

Reducing alpha makes the test more stringent, lowering Type I error. As a result, any statistically significant findings are reported with greater confidence, but power may decrease. Hence, option A is correct.
questions.learning: Any significant findings will be reported with greater confidence Reducing alpha makes the test more stringent, lowering Type I error. As a result, any statistically significant findings are reported with greater confidence, but power may decrease.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following compounds is predominantly responsible for the disinfecting property of bleaching powder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypochlorous acid

The disinfectant property of bleaching powder is predominantly due to the action of hypochlorous acid. It is 70-80 times more effective than hypochlorite ions.

Bleaching powder, also known as chlorinated lime (CaOCl2), has 33 per cent of chlorine in it. When chlorine is added to water, there is the formation of hydrochloric and hypochlorous acids. The hydrochloric acid is neutralized by the alkalinity of the water. The hypochlorous acid ionizes to form hydrogen ions and hypochlorite ions, as follows:

H2O + Cl2 → HCl + HOCl

HOCl → H + OCl
questions.learning: Hypochlorous acid — The disinfectant property of bleaching powder is predominantly due to the action of hypochlorous acid. It is 70-80 times more effective than hypochlorite ions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden-onset headache, palpitations, and profuse sweating, with a history of recurrent similar episodes. During these episodes, blood pressure is elevated and 24-hour urinary metanephrine levels are raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic paroxysmal triad of sudden headache, palpitations, and profuse sweating in the presence of severe hypertension is highly suggestive of Pheochromocytoma. This tumor, usually arising in the adrenal medulla, secretes excessive catecholamines. The definitive laboratory clue in this case is the elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrine levels, which are end-metabolites of catecholamines and have very high diagnostic sensitivity. Addison's disease (Option A) involves adrenal insufficiency and results in hypotension. Renal artery stenosis (Option B) causes persistent secondary hypertension but lacks the episodic sweating and high metanephrine profile. Hyperthyroidism (Option D) can cause tachycardia and sweating but is not associated with paroxysmal hypertensive crises or high metanephrines. Diagnosis is localized via CT or MRI of the abdomen. Preoperative management requires careful alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) followed by beta-blockade to prevent a life-threatening crisis during surgery. Pheochromocytoma is often referred to as the "10% tumor" as 10% are extra-adrenal, 10% are bilateral, and 10% are malignant
questions.learning: The classic paroxysmal triad of sudden headache, palpitations, and profuse sweating in the presence of severe hypertension is highly suggestive of Pheochromocytoma.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A labourer's younger child is brought to the OPD with a swollen belly and dull face. He has been fed rice water (rice milk) in his diet mostly. On investigations, the child is found to have low serum protein and low albumin. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kwashiorkar

A poor diet history (rice water) and a swollen belly are suggestive of Kwashiorkor.

Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) characterized by oedema and apathy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient was prescribed an antipsychotic drug following which he developed parkinsonism. Which of the following drugs can be given?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trihexiphenidyl

Trihexyphenidyl is the drug of choice for drug-induced parkinsonism. It is a central anticholinergic.

Drug-induced parkinsonism is a condition caused by certain drugs having D2 antagonistic action (typical antipsychotics). The decrease in dopaminergic activity results in an unbalanced cholinergic activity. Anticholinergics act by restoring the balance.
questions.learning: Trihexiphenidyl Trihexyphenidyl is the drug of choice for drug-induced parkinsonism. Drug-induced parkinsonism is a condition caused by certain drugs having D2 antagonistic action (typical antipsychotics).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the primary surveillance tool in the Growth Restricted Fetus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Umbilical artery Doppler

• Umbilical artery Doppler is the first-line and most important surveillance modality in FGR. ⭐
• It evaluates placental blood flow by measuring:

• Pulsatility Index (PI)
• Resistance Index (RI)
• Systolic/Diastolic (S/D) ratio

• Progressive deterioration is indicated by:

• Increased PI
• Absent End-Diastolic Flow (AEDF)
• Reversed End-Diastolic Flow (REDF)

Why not the other options?

• A. Uterine artery Doppler: Used primarily as a screening tool in the second trimester (20–24 weeks) to predict FGR and preeclampsia, not for ongoing surveillance.
• B. Umbilical venous pulsation: Abnormal umbilical venous pulsations occur late and indicate severe fetal compromise.
• C. Middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler: MCA Doppler detects the brain-sparing effect (reduced PI due to cerebral vasodilatation) and complements umbilical artery Doppler but is not the primary surveillance tool.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The false statement about cystic masses of the neck is:
options: Type 3 Branchial fistula has its internal orifice on cricopharynxgeus
Cystic hygroma is filled with clear lymph
Thyroglossal cyst moves upwards on swallowing and tongue protrusion
Fluctuation is positive in branchial cyst
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type 3 Branchial fistula has its internal orifice on cricopharynxgeus

Branchial fistulas may be congenital or acquired. The external orifice of the Type 3 Branchial fistula is seen at the junction of the middle and lower third of the sternomastoid and the internal orifice is present on the pyriform sinus of the pharynx and the tract courses between internal and external carotid arteries . An acquired fistula is usually seen in cases of incomplete excision for the branchial cyst or spontaneous rupture, and it is seen at the same site as the cyst.

Treatment is complete excision of the cyst or fistula to avoid recurrence.

Branchial cysts are fluctuant.

The below image shows a large right-sided branchial cyst.

Cystic hygroma is a cystic swelling due to the sequestration of a portion of the jugular lymph sac. It usually presents in the early infancy or at birth which may obstruct labor. The cyst contains clear lymph and is lined by a single layer of epithelium with a mosaic appearance.

Below is an image showing a child with cystic hygroma.

Thyroglossal cysts originate from persistent thyroglossal duct tracts. They move upwards on swallowing and tongue protrusion, as they are usually located anywhere along the base of the tongue to the thyroid isthmus.

Below is the image of a thyroglossal cyst.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with a previous history of myocardial infarction and ventricular arrhythmia is on treatment for a few months. He developed fatigue, dyspnea, and weight gain. He had also developed pulmonary fibrosis. Which of the following drugs is responsible for the above-mentioned side effects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amiodarone

The drug that is responsible for the above-mentioned side effects is amiodarone.

Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic drug. The most serious adverse effect during chronic amiodarone therapy is pulmonary fibrosis, which is rapidly progressive and fatal. The side effects of amiodarone include:

• Pulmonary fibrosis
• Hypotension, depressed myocardial function
• Corneal microdeposits
• Hepatotoxicity
• Neuropathies
• Photosensitivity
• Hypo- or hyperthyroidism

Other options:

Option B: Atenolol is a beta-1 selective antagonist. Bradycardia, fatigue, and cold extremities are common adverse effects. It is used in combination with a diuretic, in elderly patients with isolated systolic hypertension. CNS side effects like depression and nightmares are seen.

Option C: Aspirin is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that blocks the formation of thromboxane A2 by acetylation of COX1. Through this mechanism, it shows antipyretic, analgesic, and anti-inflammatory actions. Higher doses can result in bleeding.

Option D: Spironolactone is a potasium-sparing diuretic. It is a competitive inhibitor of the mineralocorticoid receptor in the late distal tubule and collecting duct of the kidneys. It promotes sodium diuresis but maintains the body's potassium levels. It is contraindicated in patients with hyperkalemia. Side effects are gynecomastia, impotence, decreased libido, and menstrual irregularities.
questions.learning: Amiodarone — The drug that is responsible for the above-mentioned side effects is amiodarone. Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic drug.

questions.text: A 42-year-old man is found to have persistent mild hypercalcemia during a routine health check-up. He is asymptomatic and has no history of renal stones or fractures. Laboratory investigations reveal low urinary calcium excretion, and a positive family history of similar biochemical findings in multiple first-degree relatives. Genetic analysis confirms a mutation in the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) gene. Which of the following laboratory and genetic findings is most consistent with this diagnosis?
options: Low PTH level with CaSR inactivating mutation
Normal PTH level with CaSR activating mutation
High PTH level with CaSR activating mutation
High PTH level with CaSR inactivating mutation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High PTH level with CaSR inactivating mutation

Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia (FHH) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by an inactivating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR).

The CaSR is expressed in:

• Parathyroid glands (regulates PTH secretion)
• Kidneys (regulates urinary calcium excretion)

Pathophysiology

Normally:

• High serum calcium activates the CaSR.
• This suppresses PTH secretion and increases urinary calcium excretion.

In FHH:

• The CaSR is inactivated, so the parathyroid gland perceives serum calcium as being "low."
• Consequently:

• PTH secretion is not adequately suppressed (normal or mildly elevated).
• Kidneys increase calcium reabsorption, resulting in hypocalciuria despite hypercalcemia.
questions.learning: High PTH level with CaSR inactivating mutation Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia (FHH) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by an inactivating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A Mother of a breastfeeding child only eats vegetables. Which deficiency is common in this case?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is uniquely synthesized by bacteria and is found almost exclusively in animal-based foods, such as meat, eggs, and dairy. A mother who follows a strict vegan diet (only eating vegetables) is at extremely high risk of Vitamin B12 deficiency. This is particularly critical during breastfeeding, as the infant’s B12 stores are primarily derived from maternal milk. Deficiency in the infant can lead to megaloblastic anemia, developmental delays, and permanent neurological damage. Vitamin A (Option B) is readily available in orange and green vegetables as beta-carotene. Vitamin D (Option C) is synthesized via sunlight, though supplementation is often required regardless of diet. Vitamin K (Option D) is found in green leafy vegetables and synthesized by gut flora. Therefore, strict vegetarianism without supplementation most predictably results in B12 depletion. Vegan mothers must be counseled on B12 supplementation to protect their own health and ensure their infant’s proper growth and brain development

questions.text: A guy was sitting on the balcony which was overlooking a park. He always used to sit nude on his balcony and derived sexual gratification by observing the people that look at him. This is best described as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Exhibitionism

The given scenario is suggestive of exhibitionism.

It involves behaviors over a period of 6 months or more, involving the exposure of one’s genitals to an unsuspecting stranger. The individual obtains sexual gratification from this. This is a punishable offense (Section 294 IPC/ Section 296 BNS) with imprisonment up to 3 months or a fine.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with 12 weeks amenorrhea presents with vaginal bleeding. On examination, the cervical os is open and the uterus is of 14 weeks size. USG shows a snowstorm appearance. The next best step in the management is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Suction and evacuation

The clinical scenario of vaginal bleeding, an enlarged uterus exceeding the corresponding period of amenorrhea, and a snowstorm appearance on USG strongly indicates a diagnosis of a hydatidiform mole. Suction and evacuation is the next best step in the management of this patient.

Hydatidiform mole is an abnormal condition of the placenta, characterized by partly degenerative and partly proliferative changes in the chorionic villi. It may be either partial or complete.

The patient presents with a characteristic history of abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or spotting, and vomiting during the first trimester. Also, there may be a history of passing grape-like vesicles vaginally. On examination, the size of the uterus is larger for gestational age and the fetal heart sounds are absent.

A USG scan shows a snowstorm appearance which is characteristic of a complete mole.

Suction and evacuation is the treatment of choice. Hysterectomy (option D) is done only if there is uncontrolled hemorrhage or perforation during surgical evacuation or if the age of the patient is above 35 years and has completed her family.

Serum hCG levels (option B) are checked within 48 hours of evacuation and are used as a baseline for future comparisons. It is then checked every week till it normalizes, which usually takes around 4 to 8 weeks. After the hCG values return to normal, a regular follow-up is done monthly for 6 months.
questions.learning: Suction and evacuation — The clinical scenario of vaginal bleeding, an enlarged uterus exceeding the corresponding period of amenorrhea, and a snowstorm appearance on USG strongly indicates a diagnosis of a hydatidiform mole.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child with a history of strabismus (squint) presents for a routine eye examination. Visual acuity testing shows reduced vision in the squinting eye compared to the other eye. Which drug is commonly used to perform refraction in children with squint?
questions.explanation: For a child with a squint (strabismus) and suspected amblyopia ("lazy eye"), a precise refractive evaluation is the most critical first step. 1% Atropine (Option A) is the gold standard cycloplegic agent used for refraction in this population. Atropine provides the most potent and consistent paralysis of the ciliary muscle, ensuring that the child's active accommodation is completely neutralized to reveal the true refractive error. Cyclopentolate (Option B) and Homatropine (Option D) are also cycloplegics but are less potent and typically reserved for older children without squint. Tropicamide (Option C) is a short-acting mydriatic used primarily for fundus examination rather than cycloplegic refraction in young children. Atropine is typically applied as an ointment for three days prior to the examination. Clinicians must warn parents about potential systemic side effects like facial flushing or fever. Correcting the full hypermetropic error revealed by atropine refraction is often the primary treatment for accommodative squints
questions.learning: For a child with a squint (strabismus) and suspected amblyopia ("lazy eye"), a precise refractive evaluation is the most critical first step. 1% Atropine (Option A) is the gold standard cycloplegic agent used for refraction in this population.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Craniopagus is defined as the fusion of ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Head only

Craniopagus is a type of conjoint twin where there is a fusion of the head or cranium.

Foramen magnum or the skull base never fuses in the case of craniopagus. They usually will have fused skulls and meninges. A shared cerebral cortex may occasionally be found.

Craniopagus has an incidence of 5%, and separation of the twins has a poor prognosis.

Dizygotic/fraternal twins result from the fertilization of two separate ova. Monozygotic/identical twins arise from the division of a single fertilized ovum. The outcome of the monozygotic twinning process depends on when division occurs.

Monozygotic types
Time of zygote division

Dichorionic diamniotic
<72 hours

Monochorionic diamniotic (more common)
4 to 8 days

Monochorionic monoamniotic
8 to 12 days

Conjoined twins
>12 days

Types of conjoined twins:

• Thoracopagus: united at the thorax
• Craniopagus: united at the head
• Cephalothoracopagus: fusion of both head and thorax
• Omphalopagous or xiphipagous: united anteriorly from the xiphoid to the umbilicus
• Parapagus: lateral fusion with two heads, sharing a single thorax, abdomen, and pelvis
• Ischiopagus: united at the pelvis
• Pygopagus: united in the sacral region
• Heteropagous: asymmetric forms

questions.text: A 43-year-old male presented with right-sided rib pain and shortness of breath. A chest X-ray showed a significant right-sided pneumothorax with cardio-mediastinal shift to the left. Which of the following changes will be seen?
options: Increased lung volume, Increased thoracic volume
Decreased lung volume, Increased thoracic volume
Decreased lung volume, thoracic volume remains unaffected
Lung volume remains unaffected, Decreased thoracic volume
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decreased lung volume, Increased thoracic volume

A large pneumothorax with mediastinal shift indicates a tension pneumothorax.

Air accumulation in the pleural space causes collapse of the affected lung (decreased lung volume) and expansion of the hemithorax (increased thoracic volume).

The raised intrathoracic pressure leads to mediastinal displacement to the opposite side.

Air enters pleural space (one-way valve)

↑ Intrapleural pressure

Lung collapses → ↓ lung volume

Thoracic cavity expands outward → ↑ thoracic volume

Mediastinum shifts to opposite side

↓ Venous return → shock risk

| Parameter | Change | Why

| --------- | ------ | ---

| Lung volume | ↓ Decreased | Lung collapses due to pressure

| Thoracic volume | ↑ Increased | Chest wall expands outward due to trapped air

| Option | Lung Volume | Thoracic Volume | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | ----------- | --------------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Increased lung + thoracic volume | ↑ | ↑ | Hyperinflation (emphysema) | ❌ Lung actually collapses here | Seen in COPD

| B. Decreased lung, Increased thoracic volume ✅ | ↓ | ↑ | ✔ Tension pneumothorax | ✔ Correct |  Classic combo

| C. Decreased lung, thoracic same | ↓ | No change | Simple collapse (atelectasis) | ❌ Thorax expands in pneumothorax | No mediastinal shift

| D. Lung same, thoracic decreased | Same | ↓ | Restrictive disorders | ❌ Opposite of pneumothorax | Seen in fibrosis

| Type | Key Feature

| ---- | -----------

| Simple pneumothorax | No mediastinal shift

| Tension pneumothorax |  Mediastinal shift + hemodynamic compromise

| Traumatic | Due to injury

| Spontaneous | Young tall males

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with symmetrical flaccid weakness of the lower limbs along with absence of spinal cord reflexes. This clinical presentation is suggestive of which condition?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of symmetric lower limb flaccidity and areflexia (no cord reflex) are characteristic of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS). GBS is an acute, autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy that causes demyelination of peripheral nerves. It typically presents as a "ground-to-brain" ascending paralysis, beginning with weakness in the legs. Multiple sclerosis (Option B) is a central nervous system disorder that usually presents with upper motor neuron signs like spasticity and hyperreflexia. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Option C) involves both upper and lower motor neuron signs but typically presents with asymmetric onset and fasciculations. Spinal cord injury (Option D) usually presents with a clear sensory and motor level and, after the initial shock phase, leads to spasticity rather than persistent flaccidity. Thus, the rapid onset of symmetric flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes is a clinical hallmark of the peripheral nerve involvement seen in GBS
questions.learning: The symptoms of symmetric lower limb flaccidity and areflexia (no cord reflex) are characteristic of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS). GBS is an acute, autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy that causes demyelination of peripheral nerves.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with a painless, palpable hard mass arising near the metaphyseal region of a long bone. Radiographic evaluation shows characteristic X-ray features associated with this lesion. Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A painless, palpable bony mass located near the metaphysis is the classic clinical presentation of an Osteochondroma (exostosis). It is the most common benign bone tumor and is essentially an outgrowth of the growth plate. The pathognomonic radiographic finding is a bony projection that is continuous with the cortex and medullary cavity of the host bone, often pointing away from the nearest joint. Osteosarcoma (Option A) is a highly malignant tumor that presents with severe pain, swelling, and aggressive bone destruction (e.g., "sunburst" appearance). Multiple myeloma (Option B) typically presents in older adults with systemic bone pain and "punched-out" lytic lesions. Osteoid Osteoma (Option D) is a very small lesion ( cm) that characteristically causes intense night pain which is relieved by aspirin. Osteochondromas typically stop growing once skeletal maturity is reached. While generally benign, a sudden increase in size or pain after puberty may signal a rare malignant transformation into a chondrosarcoma
questions.learning: A painless, palpable bony mass located near the metaphysis is the classic clinical presentation of an Osteochondroma (exostosis). It is the most common benign bone tumor and is essentially an outgrowth of the growth plate.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presented with vague abdominal pain. On USG, he was found to have a renal cyst of Bosniak class III. CECT was done, as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal angiomyolipoma

The CT image showing renal lesions that has hypoattenuating components consistent with macroscopic fat is highly suggestive of renal angiomyolipoma.

Imaging in renal angiomyolipoma: Demonstration of macroscopic fat is the main part of making a diagnosis. USG may show hyperechoic lesions in the cortex with posterior acoustic shadowing. In patients with tuberous sclerosis, the entire kidney is affected, producing an echogenic appearance with loss of normal corticomedullary junction.

CT findings:

• Cortical lesions that demonstrate macroscopic fat (less than -20 HU)
• Absence of ossification or calcification
• The presence of macroscopic fat is strongly suggestive of this condition, but not pathognomonic as RCC may rarely demonstrate macroscopic fat.
• Approximately 5% may be fat poor.

MRI: It is an excellent tool to demonstrate intramural fat components. Two sequences are used:

• Fat-saturated techniques
• Phase-in and phase-out imaging that shows India ink artifact at the junction between fat and non-fat components.

Digital subtraction angiography: They are hypervascular lesions showing 'sunburst appearance' in the arterial phase and 'onion peel appearance' in the venous phase.

Angiomyolipomas are benign tumors that occur sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis. The mean age of presentation is 43 years and there is a female predilection. It can present as spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage, especially with larger tumors. The patient can present with flank pain, palpable mass, hematuria, urinary tract infections, hypertension, or renal failure. They usually do not require any intervention. mTOR inhibitors like everolimus can be used to decrease the size of the lesion.

Bosniak classification:

It classifies the renal cystic lesions mainly into four classes based on the CT characteristics.

Class I and II are benign and do not require follow-up imaging or surgery.

Class IIF requires follow-up for about 5 years to exclude malignancy.

Class III needs to be biopsied or surgically explored due to a higher risk of malignancy.

Class IV lesions are clearly malignant and need appropriate treatment.

Other options:

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC): It is the most common malignant tumor of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50-70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It is a differential for angiomyolipoma but it is important to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

Renal oncocytoma: They are relatively benign in nature and usually present in the 6th to 7th decade. An important point regarding this tumor is its similarity with RCC and hence it is very difficult to differentiate between them preoperatively. A sharp central stellate scar may be seen in one-third of the cases. But RCC may also show this stellate scar appearance in some cases.

Renal cyst: It is a broader term that includes the cystic lesions of the kidney. They can be simple cysts that are benign. Complex or complicated cystic lesions need evaluation and can be malignant. Bosniak classification of renal cysts is given above.

questions.learning: Renal angiomyolipoma — The CT image showing renal lesions that has hypoattenuating components consistent with macroscopic fat is highly suggestive of renal angiomyolipoma.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient is admitted with symptoms suggestive of hydrophobia, raising suspicion for rabies infection. To confirm the diagnosis, the clinician plans to perform tests on a corneal scraping. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate and accurate for confirming rabies in this patient?
questions.explanation: Rabies is a fatal viral encephalitis, and early diagnosis in a living patient is crucial. In suspected rabies (e.g., hydrophobia), samples such as saliva, CSF, nuchal skin biopsy, and corneal scrapings can be used for diagnosis. RT-PCR (Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction) is the most sensitive and specific test for detecting rabies viral RNA in these samples. It allows early detection, even before antibody formation, and is highly accurate. Because it directly identifies viral genetic material, it is considered the best confirmatory test in modern practice, including for corneal scrapings. Why Other Options Are Wrong (B) Viral culture: Rarely used due to slow growth and biohazard risk (C) ELISA: Detects antibodies, which appear late → not useful early (D) DFA test: Commonly used but less sensitive than RT-PCR, especially in corneal samples
questions.learning: Rabies is a fatal viral encephalitis, and early diagnosis in a living patient is crucial. In suspected rabies (e.g., hydrophobia), samples such as saliva, CSF, nuchal skin biopsy, and corneal scrapings can be used for diagnosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 29-year-old goes on a month-long trek across the Himalayas. Which of the following physiological adaptations would you expect to see in him at high altitudes following acclimatization? 1. Erythropoietin secretion increases 2. Tissue myoglobin decreases 3. Tissue content of cytochrome oxidase increases 4. pH of blood increases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3, 4

At high altitude, decreased atmospheric oxygen causes hypoxia, leading to several acclimatization responses to improve oxygen delivery and utilization.

Key adaptations:

• ↑ Erythropoietin (EPO) secretion → increased RBC production → improved oxygen-carrying capacity.
• ↑ Mitochondrial oxidative enzymes such as cytochrome oxidase, enhancing tissue oxygen utilization.
• Respiratory alkalosis occurs due to hyperventilation, causing an increase in blood pH initially.

Incorrect statement:

• Tissue myoglobin actually increases, not decreases, to improve oxygen storage in muscle.
questions.learning: 1, 3, 4 At high altitude, decreased atmospheric oxygen causes hypoxia, leading to several acclimatization responses to improve oxygen delivery and utilization.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl presents with severe headache, photophobia, high-grade fever, papilledema, and positive Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows low glucose, elevated protein, and neutrophil- predominant pleocytosis. Gram staining of the CSF demonstrates Gram-negative diplococci. Which organism is the most likely cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical signs of meningitis (fever, nuchal rigidity, Kernig's/Brudzinski's signs) combined with the "neutrophil-predominant" CSF profile are diagnostic of acute bacterial meningitis. The specific microbiological clue—"Gram-negative diplococci"—is pathognomonic for Neisseria meningitidis. Haemophilus influenzae (Option A) is a Gram-negative "coccobacillus," not a diplococcus. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option B) is the most common cause overall but would appear as "Gram-positive" diplococci. Listeria monocytogenes (Option D) is a Gram-positive bacillus, usually seen in neonates or the elderly. Meningococcal meningitis is a medical emergency because it can progress rapidly to septicemia and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. Immediate treatment with intravenous third-generation cephalosporins (like Ceftriaxone) is mandatory. Prophylaxis for close contacts is also required using rifampicin or ciprofloxacin. Identifying the morphology and Gram-stain reaction of the causative agent is the most critical early step in diagnosing bacterial meningitis
questions.learning: The clinical signs of meningitis (fever, nuchal rigidity, Kernig's/Brudzinski's signs) combined with the "neutrophil-predominant" CSF profile are diagnostic of acute bacterial meningitis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All of the following management plans are correct except:
options: Pregnant woman with history of three second-trimester abortions → Cervical cerclage + progesterone
Pregnant woman with history of two second-trimester abortions and cervical length ≤2.5 cm on TVS → Cervical cerclage + progesterone
Pregnant woman with history of one PTL/second-trimester abortion and cervical length ≤2.5 cm → Only progesterone
Pregnant woman with no history of abortion but cervical length <2.5 cm → Only progesterone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pregnant woman with history of one PTL/second-trimester abortion and cervical length ≤2.5 cm → Only progesterone

Prevention of recurrent preterm birth (PTL) and cervical insufficiency is based on a combination of obstetric history and transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) cervical length.

| Clinical Scenario | Management

| ----------------- | ----------

| ≥3 previous second-trimester losses/preterm births | History-indicated cerclage + progesterone

| ≥2 second-trimester losses with cervical length ≤2.5 cm | Cerclage + progesterone

| Previous PTL/second-trimester loss with cervical length ≤2.5 cm | Cerclage + progesterone

| No prior PTL/loss but cervical length <2.5 cm | Progesterone alone

A woman with:

• Previous preterm labor or second-trimester loss, and
• Short cervix (≤2.5 cm)

is at high risk for recurrent preterm birth and generally requires both cervical cerclage and progesterone, not progesterone alone.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following are features of Korsakoff syndrome? A. Confabulation B. Amnesia C. Peripheral neuropathy D. Ophthalmoplegia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3

Korsakoff syndrome presents with amnesia, confabulation, and peripheral neuropathy. Ophthalmoplegia is part of Wernicke’s encephalopathy, not Korsakoff.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 Korsakoff syndrome presents with amnesia, confabulation, and peripheral neuropathy. Ophthalmoplegia is part of Wernicke’s encephalopathy, not Korsakoff.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: For a 40-year-old patient undergoing a minor surgical procedure, which type of intravenous fluid is considered most appropriate for use during the surgery?
questions.explanation: For a standard or minor surgical intervention in a healthy adult, Crystalloids (such as Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate) are the most appropriate and commonly used intraoperative fluids. Crystalloids are effective for replacing insensible losses and maintaining hemodynamic stability during the procedure. They are safe, inexpensive, and readily available. Colloids (Option B), such as albumin or starch solutions, are reserved for cases with significant blood loss or severe capillary leak, as they remain in the intravascular space longer but carry risks of allergic reactions and renal issues. Isolyte P (Option A) is a maintenance fluid typically used in pediatric populations due to its lower sodium content; using it in an adult could lead to hyponatremia. Option D is a medical condition, not a fluid. Standard surgical management focuses on "goal-directed" fluid therapy to avoid both dehydration and fluid overload, both of which can impair postoperative recovery and wound healing. Crystalloids remain the foundational choice for routine volume maintenance
questions.learning: For a standard or minor surgical intervention in a healthy adult, Crystalloids (such as Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate) are the most appropriate and commonly used intraoperative fluids.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During the menstrual cycle, in which phase is vacuolation a characteristic histological finding?
questions.explanation: The endometrium undergoes predictable histological changes under the influence of hormones. The secretory phase (Option A), which occurs after ovulation under the dominance of progesterone, is definitively characterized by the presence of subnuclear vacuoles in the glandular epithelial cells. This "vacuolation" typically appears around day 17 of a standard 28-day cycle and is the earliest histological sign that ovulation has occurred. In contrast, the proliferative phase (Option B) is characterized by mitoses and tubular glands under the influence of estrogen, with no vacuoles present. The menstrual phase (Option C) involves the breakdown and shedding of the functional layer with associated hemorrhage. Therefore, because vacuolation represents the onset of the progestational effect on the glands to prepare for potential embryo implantation, it is a pathognomonic feature specific only to the secretory phase of the menstrual cycle

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
Match the following:

1. Eonism
a. Sexual gratification by having intercourse with animals

2. Algolagnia
b. Sexual pleasure by wearing clothes of the opposite sex

3. Frotteurism
c. Sexual gratification in inflicting pain

4. Necrophilia
d. Sexual gratification by rubbing private parts against another person

e. Sexual gratification by intercourse with dead bodies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-b, 2-c, 3-d, 4-e

The correct answer is option A: 1-b, 2-c, 3-d, 4-e

1. Eonism
b. Sexual pleasure by wearing clothes of the opposite sex

2. Algolagnia
c. Sexual gratification in inflicting pain

3. Frotteurism
d. Sexual gratification by rubbing private parts against another person

4. Necrophilia
e. Sexual gratification by intercourse with dead bodies

Paraphilias or perversions are sexual stimuli or acts that are deviations from normal sexual behaviors but are necessary for some people to experience arousal and orgasm.

1. Eonism (also known as transvestism) is a sexual perversion, where a person's whole personality is dominated by a desire to be identified as a member of the opposite sex. This is usually seen in males who obtain sexual pleasure by wearing female clothes. There is no hormonal/genital abnormality.

2. Algolagnia is sexual pleasure derived from inflicting pain (active algolagnia) or enduring pain (passive algolagnia).

Active algolagnia also called Sadism, is the sexual gratification obtained from acts of physical cruelty or infliction of pain upon one's partner. It is seen more commonly in men. To obtain sexual gratification the sadist may bite, beat, cut, burn, or otherwise mistreat or abuse his sexual partner.

3. Frotteurism refers to the sexual gratification achieved by touching or rubbing against a non-consenting person. This behavior often occurs in busy and crowded places. It is predominantly described in men.

4. Necrophilia is an obsession with obtaining sexual gratification from dead bodies.

Bestiality is an act of using a lower animal for sexual gratification. It is an unnatural sexual offence and is punishable in India.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During a laryngeal surgical procedure, a patient develops loss of sensation above the vocal cords. Which nerve primarily supplies sensory innervation to this area?
questions.explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is the primary structure providing sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa situated above the level of the vocal folds (vocal cords). This nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane alongside the superior laryngeal artery to supply the vestibule of the larynx. In contrast, the recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option B) is responsible for sensory innervation below the level of the vocal cords and motor supply to all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. The glossopharyngeal nerve (Option C) provides sensory supply to the oropharynx and the posterior third of the tongue, but not the internal larynx. The external laryngeal nerve (Option D) is a purely motor nerve that innervates the cricothyroid muscle. Injury to the internal laryngeal nerve typically results in a loss of the protective cough reflex, significantly increasing the risk of aspiration. Therefore, the specific anatomical boundary mentioned—above the vocal cords—definitively identifies the superior laryngeal nerve as the responsible sensory mediator
questions.learning: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is the primary structure providing sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa situated above the level of the vocal folds (vocal cords).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is gametocidal to all the species causing malaria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primaquine

Primaquine is gametocidal to all species causing malaria. It inhibits transmission of malaria.

The drugs with clinically important gametocidal activity (against all species) are:

• High activity:

• Artemisinins
• Primaquine

• Low to moderate activity:

• Chloroquine
• Quinine
• Atovaquone/proguanil

• No activity:

• Mefloquine
• Pyrimethamine
• Sulfadoxine
• Tetracycline
questions.learning: Primaquine Primaquine is gametocidal to all species causing malaria. It inhibits transmission of malaria.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The best time to identify the type of twin pregnancy on ultrasound is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 11-14 weeks

The best time to identify the type of twin pregnancy on ultrasound is 11-14 weeks.

Twin pregnancies should ideally be dated when the crown–rump length (CRL) measurement is between 45 and 84 mm (i.e. 11 + 0 to 13 + 6 weeks of gestation).

Chorionicity should be ideally determined between 11 + 0 and 13 + 6 weeks of gestation (the earliest time to identify chorionicity is 7 weeks). This is done using the membrane thickness at the site of insertion of the amniotic membrane into the placenta. The T‐sign (in monochorionic twins) or lambda sign (in dichorionic twins) can be seen here. As the determination of chorionicity is most accurate when the amnion and chorion have not yet been fused, the first‐trimester scan in twin pregnancy is highly important.

Markers of dichorionicity include 4 layers of membranes between the twins, membrane thickness >2mm, different sex of twins, 2 different placentas, and positive twin peak sign.

Women with an uncomplicated dichorionic twin pregnancy should have a first‐trimester scan, a detailed second‐trimester scan, and scans every 4 weeks thereafter.

Women with uncomplicated monochorionic twins should have a first‐trimester scan and then scans every 2 weeks from 16 weeks onwards. This is done in order to detect TTTS and TAPS in a timely manner.
