questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
An unimmunized 2-year old child presented with coryza, conjunctivitis, and bluish-white spots in his buccal mucosa near the lower molar teeth. A day later, he developed a maculopapular rash on the face and neck. What is the nature of the causative virus?

ss - Single stranded
ds - Double-stranded
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Enveloped ss RNA

Fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash and Koplik spots are suggestive of measles. Measles virus is an enveloped, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) virus.

Koplik spots are small, bluish-white ulcerations on the inner aspect of the cheek at the level of premolars. These are pathognomic for measles. The measles virus, a paramyxovirus, has an incubation period of 7-18 days. After this, the prodrome phase begins with mild fever, conjunctivitis, upper respiratory tract infection, and pathognomic Koplik spots. This is followed by the eruptive stage, characterised by the appearance of maculopapular rash on the 4th day of fever. The rash begins on the face and spreads to the torso and extremities. Lymphadenopathy may be present.

These are multinucleated giant cells formed by the fusion of infected cells. The images below show the characteristic rashes and the Koplik spots seen in measles.

The most common complication of measles is acute otitis media. Sinusitis and mastoiditis are also seen. The most common cause of death in measles is pneumonia, which may be giant cell pneumonia. It is caused by the virus directly or can be due to superadded bacterial infection. Black measles or hemorrhagic measles is a fatal complication characterized by hemorrhagic skin eruptions. It is rarely seen nowadays.

Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a rare but fatal complication characterized by cognitive decline, spasticity of limbs, and seizures. It is insidious in onset and clinical manifestations usually begin 7-10 years after primary measles infection. It is caused due to persistent infection with a genetically altered variant of the measles virus within the central nervous system. Other complications include croup, tracheitis, bronchiolitis, diarrhea and vomiting, febrile seizures, and encephalitis.

The diagnosis of measles infection is mainly clinical but may be confirmed by serological demonstration of IgM antibodies. IgM antibodies appear 1-2 days after the rash and are detectable for 1 month. The management is mainly supportive. There is no role for antivirals. Low serum retinol levels in children with measles are associated with higher morbidity and mortality and hence vitamin A therapy is indicated for all patients with measles.

Live attenuated vaccine for measles is safe and effective with no evidence of person-to-person transfer of vaccine strains. It is a freeze-dried product requiring reconstitution. 0.5ml is administered subcutaneously in the right upper arm in 2 doses- at the 9th month and between the 16th - 24th month.
questions.learning: Enveloped ss RNA Fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash and Koplik spots are suggestive of measles. Measles virus is an enveloped, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) virus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which demographic indicator is used to compare life expectancy between two different countries?
questions.explanation: The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite statistical tool used to rank countries by level of human development, serving as a key indicator for comparing life expectancy across different nations. It encompasses three major dimensions: a long and healthy life (measured by life expectancy at birth), knowledge (mean and expected years of schooling), and a decent standard of living (GNI per capita). In contrast, Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALY) (Option A) measures the value of health outcomes by combining quantity and quality of life. Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALY) (Option B) quantifies the overall burden of disease, representing years lost due to ill-health or early death. The Human Poverty Index (HPI) (Option D) focuses specifically on deprivations rather than general development or expectancy. Therefore, HDI is the standard demographic measure used internationally to benchmark and compare the longevity and life expectancy of populations between distinct countries
questions.learning: The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite statistical tool used to rank countries by level of human development, serving as a key indicator for comparing life expectancy across different nations.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Absolute refractory period is due to:
options: Closure of active gates of sodium channel
Closure of inactive gates of sodium channel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Closure of inactive gates of sodium channel

Absolute refractory period is due to closure of inactive gates of sodium channel.

Voltage-gated sodium channels have 3 states that you can find them in. They can either be closed, open, or inactive.

When the stimulus causes activation of the open gates, sodium rushes into the cell causing the membrane potential to become more positive. After 0.5 to 1 millisecond, the inactive gate automatically closes and no stimulus, no matter how strong, can excite the nerve. This is called the absolute refractory period.
questions.learning: Closure of inactive gates of sodium channel Absolute refractory period is due to closure of inactive gates of sodium channel. Voltage-gated sodium channels have 3 states that you can find them in.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient came to the emergency with pain in the epigastrium radiating to the back and recurrent vomiting. On examination, guarding was present in the upper epigastrium. The erect chest X-ray was normal. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Serum lipase

The clinical scenario of the patient presenting with abdominal pain, recurrent vomiting, and upper epigastric guarding in a chronic alcoholic is highly suggestive of acute pancreatitis. The normal erect chest X-ray indicates that there is no pneumoperitoneum (effectively ruling out perforation). The next step is to send blood samples for serum lipase levels.

While contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the abdomen (option D) is the best investigation to rule out a case of acute pancreatitis, it is not the next step after an abdominal X-ray.

Acute pancreatitis is often caused by gallstones (70%) or alcoholism (25%). The cardinal symptom is acute-onset severe pain in the upper quadrant of the abdomen. The patient usually presents in shock (hypotension and tachycardia) and tachypnoea. Some may also present with signs of bleeding into the fascial planes leading to discoloration of the sites involved:

1. Cullen’s sign: Around the umbilicus
2. Grey Turner’s sign: Flanks
3. Fox sign: Inguinal region
4. Bryant’s sign: Scrotum

The diagnosis is often clinical with a laboratory diagnosis of serum lipase preferred over serum amylase. The severity of the acute pancreatitis is assessed using the Ranson and Glasgow scoring system ( ≥3 at 48h of onset of pain ). APACHE, SOFA, SAPS, and MODS can also be used to assess the severity of pancreatitis in intensive care (ICU) settings.

Pancreatitis is managed conservatively with initial nasogastric drainage followed by intravenous fluids, analgesia, and frequent monitoring of vital signs, urine output, and blood gases.

Other options:

Option A: Upper gastrointestinal intestinal (GI) endoscopy is performed by passing a flexible endoscope and is the best method for examining the upper gastrointestinal mucosa. It doesn't help us diagnose pancreatitis.

Option B: The alcohol breath test is used as a screening test to measure the concentration of alcohol in a person's breath, but doesn't help us diagnose pancreatitis.
questions.learning: Serum lipase — The clinical scenario of the patient presenting with abdominal pain, recurrent vomiting, and upper epigastric guarding in a chronic alcoholic is highly suggestive of acute pancreatitis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An adult patient presents with tall stature, pigeon chest deformity, long arm span, lens dislocation, and cardiac defects. This patient is likely to have a defect in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fibrillin

The clinical features—tall stature, long arm span, pectus deformity (pigeon chest), lens dislocation, and cardiac abnormalities (aortic root dilation)—are classic for Marfan syndrome.

• Mutation in fibrillin-1 (FBN1 gene)
• Fibrillin is a key component of microfibrils in connective tissue

Clinical features explained:

• Skeletal: Tall, long limbs (arachnodactyly), pectus deformity
• Ocular: Lens dislocation (typically upward)
• Cardiac: Aortic root dilation → risk of aortic aneurysm/dissection

Why other options are incorrect:

• Elastase: Enzyme, not structural protein defect
• Collagen: Seen in Ehlers-Danlos or osteogenesis imperfecta
• Laminin: Basement membrane component

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A young man who has just returned from the USA develops fever, cough, and breathlessness. A chest radiograph shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Culture on Sabouraud Dextrose Agar (SDA) reveals white to light brown puffy colonies. Lactophenol blue staining shows the findings as depicted in the image. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Histoplasmosis

The image shows the tuberculate macroconidia, with finger-like projections which, along with the history, is a characteristic feature of Histoplasma.

Histoplasmosis (Darling’s disease) is a granulomatous disease caused by a dimorphic fungus, Histoplasma capsulatum. It is endemic in the USA, in the states bordering the Ohio River valley and the lower Mississippi River. In India, it is reported from the region of West Bengal, along the Ganga River. The fungus inhabits humid and acidic soil that contains a large amount of bird or bat droppings.

H. capsulatum is transmitted by inhalation of spores (i.e. microconidia) which usually circulate in the air after the contaminated soil is disturbed. After the spores enter into the lungs, they are engulfed inside the alveolar macrophages and then transform into yeast forms.

Clinically, the classical histoplasmosis ranges from asymptomatic infection (in immunocompetent people) to life-threatening illness seen in people with low CMI. The various clinical types include:

• Pulmonary histoplasmosis - Acute form presents with mild flu-like illness, pulmonary infiltrates in the chest X-ray with hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Chronic cavitary histoplasmosis may be seen in smokers with underlying structural lung disease.
• Mucocutaneous histoplasmosis - Skin and oral mucosal lesions may develop secondary to pulmonary infection. Oral lesions are particularly seen in Indian patients.
• Disseminated histoplasmosis - It develops if CMI is very low (e.g. untreated HIV-infected people or following organ transplantation). The common sites affected are bone marrow, spleen, liver, eyes, and adrenal glands.

Diagnosis :

Direct microscopy - Histopathological staining of the specimens reveals tiny oval yeast cells (2–4 μm size) with narrow-based budding within the macrophages with an underlying granulomatous response.

Culture - It is the gold standard method of diagnosis. Specimens should be inoculated onto media such as SDA, blood agar, and BHI agar in duplicate and incubated simultaneously at 25°C and 37°C.

At 25°C it forms a mycelial phase and produces white to buff brown colonies that consist of two types of conidia or spores - tuberculate macroconidia (with typical thick walls and finger-like projections which is a characteristic feature) and microconidia( smaller, thin, and smooth-walled).
At 37°C it gets converted into yeast form (creamy white colonies), which is best developed in special media like Kelley’s media.
Treatment :

Liposomal amphotericin B is the antifungal agent of choice in acute pulmonary and disseminated histoplasmosis. Itraconazole is recommended for chronic cavitary pulmonary histoplasmosis.

Other options :

Option A - Cryptococcosis: Cryptococcus neoformans typically presents as a lung infection or meningitis in immunocompromised individuals. On SDA, Cryptococcus forms mucoid colonies, and Lactophenol blue would show encapsulated yeast, which differs from the presentation in this case.

Option C - Blastomyces causes North American Blastomycosis/ Chicago disease. Pulmonary involvement is the most common form followed by skin. Histopathological staining shows thick-walled yeast, with single broad-based budding (figure 8 appearance).

Option D: Mucormycosis typically affects immunocompromised patients and presents with invasive disease, often causing necrotizing infections in the sinuses or lungs. The fungal hyphae seen on Lactophenol blue are broad, non-septate, and ribbon-like, which does not match the culture description here.
questions.learning: Histoplasmosis — The image shows the tuberculate macroconidia, with finger-like projections which, along with the history, is a characteristic feature of Histoplasma.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
A 10-year-old child weighing 30 kg presents with a history of loose stools for 2 days. On examination, there is severe dehydration. Laboratory investigations are as follows. What is the initial management as per ISPAD guidelines?

RBS
550 mg/dL

pH
7.01

Na+
158 mEq/L

Urine glucose
3+
options: Manage ABC, NS 20 mL/kg and start insulin after 1 hour
Manage ABC, NS 20 mL/kg along with insulin 0.1 IU/kg/hr
Manage ABC, NS 10 mL/kg along with insulin 0.1 IU/kg/hr
Manage ABC, NS 10 mL/kg and start insulin after 1 hour
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Manage ABC, NS 20 mL/kg and start insulin after 1 hour

The given clinical scenario with severe dehydration, hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and metabolic acidosis is suggestive of diabetic ketoacidosis. Based on the ISPAD guidelines, the initial management includes management of the airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC) and fluid replacement with an IV bolus of 20 mL/kg NS (Normal saline). This is followed by an IV insulin infusion of 0.05 - 0.1 U/kg/hr, at least 1 hour after starting fluid replacement therapy.

The International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD) guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for the management of DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis) in children and adolescents.

Diabetic ketoacidosis is the most serious complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus. Clinical manifestations of diabetic ketoacidosis include:

• Dehydration, tachypnea with deep, sighing respiration (Kussmaul breathing)
• Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain that may mimic an acute abdominal condition
• Confusion, drowsiness, and coma in severe cases.

The diagnosis of DKA is based on the triad of hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. All three biochemical criteria are required to diagnose DKA

• Hyperglycemia (blood glucose >200 mg/dl)
• Venous pH < 7.3 or serum bicarbonate <18 mmol/L
• Ketonemia or ketonuria

Initial management includes management of the airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC) according to Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) guidelines. Following that emergency assessment is done, which includes:

• Immediate measurement of blood glucose, blood or urine ketones, serum electrolytes and blood gases
• Assessment of level of consciousness.
• Two peripheral intravenous (IV) lines should be inserted.

The goal of therapy is to correct dehydration, correct acidosis, reverse ketosis, and gradually blood glucose concentration to near normal. Monitor for acute complications, and identify and treat any precipitating event.

Fluid replacement should always begin before starting insulin therapy. One or more boluses of 0.9% saline at 20 mL/kg are given to restore peripheral circulation. Insulin therapy with 0.05–0.1 U/kg/hr must begin at least 1 hour after starting fluid replacement therapy. Insulin of 0.05 U/kg/hr can be considered if pH is > 7.15.

Potassium replacement is given only when potassium is <5.5 mmol/L. In rare cases of hypokalemia with potassium <3.0 mmol/L, defer insulin treatment.

Bicarbonate administration is not recommended except for treatment of severe acidosis (pH < 6.9) or in cases of life-threatening hyperkalemia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the name of the procedure shown in the image that was performed on the patient?
questions.explanation: The clinical photograph shows a surgical opening in the anterior neck with a specialized tube (tracheostomy tube) held in place by neck ties. This is a tracheostomy (Option C), a procedure where an opening is created in the trachea, typically between the second and third tracheal rings, to bypass an upper airway obstruction or provide long-term mechanical ventilation. Endotracheal intubation (Option A) involves passing a tube through the mouth or nose into the trachea and would not be visible on the external surface of the neck. Needle cricothyroidotomy (Option B) is an emergency procedure involving a small needle through the cricothyroid membrane, used only for temporary oxygenation. An oropharyngeal airway (Option D) is a simple plastic device placed in the mouth to keep the tongue from blocking the throat. The permanent-looking surgical stoma and tube placement clearly identify the procedure as a tracheostomy

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A body fluid sample is being studied and has Na: 10 mEq/L, K: 140 mEq/L, CI: 4 mEq/L. Identify the compartment from which the sample has been obtained.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intracellular fluid

The sample obtained is from the intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment. The ICF contains large quantities of potassium (K+) ions - 140 mEq/L . The ICF also has lesser amounts of sodium (Na+) and Chloride (Cl-) ions.

The extracellular fluid (ECF) compartment includes interstitial fluids and plasma. In contrast to the ICF, the ECF has an abundance of sodium, chloride, calcium and bicarbonate ions, and lesser amounts of potassium, phosphate and magnesium ions.

The image below depicts the proportion of the important anions and cations present in the intracellular and extracellular fluids.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which among the following is associated with Cryoglobulinemia?
questions.explanation: Cryoglobulinemia refers to the presence of abnormal proteins in the blood that thicken and clump together in cold temperatures. It is most strongly associated with chronic Hepatitis C infection, which accounts for approximately 80-90% of cases of mixed cryoglobulinemia. The virus triggers a chronic immune response leading to the production of monoclonal or polyclonal immunoglobulins that form immune complexes. These complexes can cause vasculitis, leading to symptoms such as purpura, arthralgia, and weakness (Meltzer's triad). While certain hematological malignancies like B-cell Leukemia (Option D) or lymphoma can cause Type I cryoglobulinemia, Hepatitis C is the classic and most frequent association in clinical exams. Ovarian cancer (Option B) and Diabetes (Option C) are not standard associations for this condition. Treatment primarily focuses on managing the underlying viral infection, often with direct-acting antivirals, to reduce the stimulus for cryoglobulin production

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the duration of short term memory?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 30-300 seconds

Short-term memory lasts for seconds to minutes, hence of the given 4 options, 30-300 seconds is the most appropriate answer.

Memory is usually divided into two forms: Explicit or declarative memory which is associated with consciousness or awareness. Implicit or nondeclarative memory does not involve awareness and its retention does not usually involve processing in the hippocampus.

Explicit and many forms of implicit memory involve

• Short-term memory and
• Long-term memory.

Short-term memory:

It lasts seconds to minutes; the encoding process for short-term explicit memory involves the hippocampus. It lasts only till the person continues to think about the number or facts.

Working memory is a form of short-term memory that keeps information available, usually for very short periods of time, until the individual plans action based on it.

Long-term memory:

It stores memories that can be recollected after years or even for a lifetime. These memories are stored in various parts of the neocortex. The various parts of the memories such as, visual, auditory, olfactory, etc., are localised to the cortical regions concerned with these functions. All these parts of the memories are brought together by long-term changes in the strength of transmission at relevant synaptic junctions so that all the components are brought to consciousness when that particular memory is recalled.

Neural basis of memory:

The basis of memory is the alteration in the strength of the selected synaptic connections. Second messenger systems contribute to the changes in the neural circuits which are required for learning and memory. Alterations in the cellular membrane channels also contribute to it.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A mother brought her one-year-old child to a pediatric surgeon after noticing a groin swelling that appears during micturition or crying and moves medially. What is the most likely cause of this swelling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Indirect inguinal hernia

In children, the most common type of inguinal hernia is an indirect inguinal hernia, caused by failure of obliteration of the processus vaginalis (a congenital defect). The swelling:

• Appears during crying, coughing, or straining (increased intra-abdominal pressure)
• Is often intermittent and reducible
• Passes through the deep inguinal ring, traverses the inguinal canal, and may extend into the scrotum.
• On examination, it is felt medial to the examiner’s finger during invagination of the scrotum (a classical clinical finding for an indirect hernia).

Why not the other options?

• A. Direct inguinal hernia: Rare in children; acquired due to weakness of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal and occurs medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
• C. Femoral hernia: Rare in children and presents below the inguinal ligament.
• D. Undescended testis: Presents as an absent testis from the scrotum, not an intermittent groin swelling.

questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: An 18-year-old woman presents with a rapidly progressive purpuric rash over both lower limbs. Two days earlier, she developed mild pain in her knees and ankles. The lesions initially appeared around one knee and subsequently spread symmetrically over both legs. She has no fever, constitutional symptoms, gastrointestinal complaints, or recent sore throat. Laboratory investigations show: • Hemoglobin: 14 g/dL • Platelet count: 260,000/mm³ • Leukocyte count: 9,000/mm³ Which of the following histopathologic findings is most likely in a biopsy of the skin lesion?
options: Extensive intravascular fibrin deposition without inflammatory infiltrate
Obliterative endarteritis with lymphocytes and plasma cells
Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with eosinophils around vessels
Small-vessel wall damage with perivascular neutrophilic infiltration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Small-vessel wall damage with perivascular neutrophilic infiltration

This patient most likely has cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis, presenting with:

• Palpable purpura over dependent areas, especially the lower limbs
• Arthralgia
• Normal platelet count
• Absence of systemic toxicity

The characteristic histology is small-vessel vasculitis with neutrophilic infiltration, vessel-wall necrosis, and fragmented neutrophil nuclei known as leukocytoclasia.

Typical biopsy findings include:

• Perivascular neutrophils
• Fibrinoid necrosis of small vessels
• Nuclear debris from fragmented neutrophils
• Extravasation of red blood cells

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Extensive intravascular fibrin deposition without inflammatory infiltrate: More consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation.
• B. Obliterative endarteritis with lymphocytes and plasma cells: Classically seen in syphilis.
• C. Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with eosinophils around vessels: Suggests eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, usually associated with asthma and eosinophilia.

High-yield pearl:

• Leukocytoclastic vasculitis = palpable purpura + normal platelets + neutrophilic small-vessel inflammation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: During a police investigation, skeletal remains are recovered from a crime scene. For forensic evaluation, it becomes necessary to determine whether the bones are of human origin or belong to a dog. Which of the following tests would be most helpful in differentiating human bones from canine bones?
questions.explanation: As discussed in Question 77, the Precipitin test is the standard serological method used to determine the species of origin for biological remains, including bone extracts. It involves reacting proteins extracted from the bone with anti-human sera; a positive reaction (precipitation) confirms the bones are human. Acid-phosphatase (Option B) is used to screen for semen in sexual assault cases. LDH (Option C) is an enzyme used to estimate the time since death in some contexts but does not identify species. The Teichmann test (Option D) is a confirmatory test for the presence of blood by forming hemin crystals but does not differentiate between species. While gross anatomical features often suggest whether a bone is human or animal (canine), the Precipitin test provides the definitive biochemical proof necessary for legal proceedings. Identifying the origin of bones is the crucial first step in any forensic anthropology investigation to determine if a homicide inquiry should be initiated
questions.learning: As discussed in Question 77, the Precipitin test is the standard serological method used to determine the species of origin for biological remains, including bone extracts.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to recurrent, generalized tonic-clonic seizures over the past 24 hours. He takes no medications and has no family history of epilepsy. The patient's temperature is 39.4⁰C (103⁰F), blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 112/min, and respirations are 10/min. During the examination, the patient suddenly develops sustained, generalized tonic-clonic convulsions without fully regaining consciousness between episodes. Which of the following describes the mechanism of action of the most appropriate initial therapy for his seizures?
options: Blockade of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
Blockade of presynaptic voltage-gated sodium channels
Inhibition of vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enhanced postsynaptic chloride influx

This child has status epilepticus (continuous seizures without regaining consciousness). The initial treatment is a benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam/diazepam or IM midazolam).

Mechanism of action of benzodiazepines:

• Bind to GABA-A receptors
• Increase frequency of chloride channel opening
• Cause enhanced postsynaptic Cl⁻ influx → neuronal hyperpolarization → rapid seizure termination

Stepwise management of status epilepticus:

1. First-line: Benzodiazepines → enhance GABA-mediated Cl⁻ influx
2. Second-line: Phenytoin/fosphenytoin, valproate, levetiracetam
3. Refractory: Phenobarbital, propofol, midazolam infusion
questions.learning: Enhanced postsynaptic chloride influx — This child has status epilepticus (continuous seizures without regaining consciousness). The initial treatment is a benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam/diazepam or IM midazolam).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A person had undergone the serology for suspected hepatitis B infection. His/her serology shows the presence of HBs antigen and also IgG anti-HBc along with the presence of anti-HBe, while HBe antigen is negative. Which one of the following diagnoses is the correct interpretation of the serology results?
options: Chronic hepatitis B infection with active viral replication
Chronic hepatitis B infection with low viral replication
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chronic hepatitis B infection with low viral replication

The serology shows:

• HBsAg positive → Current hepatitis B infection.
• IgG anti-HBc positive → Indicates previous/current natural HBV infection; it is not produced after vaccination.
• HBeAg negative → Active viral replication is not strongly indicated.
• Anti-HBe positive → Suggests seroconversion from HBeAg to anti-HBe, usually associated with reduced viral replication.

Therefore, the pattern is most consistent with chronic HBV infection with low viral replication.

Why not the other options?

• (a) Active hepatitis B infection: Too nonspecific. The presence of HBsAg confirms infection, but the HBeAg-negative/anti-HBe-positive pattern specifically suggests lower replication.
• (b) Chronic HBV with active viral replication: Typically associated with HBeAg positivity and high HBV DNA. However, HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis can occasionally have active replication due to precore/core promoter mutations, so HBV DNA is required for definitive assessment.
• (c) Chronic HBV with low viral replication — Correct: HBsAg +, IgG anti-HBc +, HBeAg −, anti-HBe + is the classic exam pattern.
• (d) Recovery/vaccination: Recovery requires HBsAg negativity and anti-HBs positivity. Vaccination produces anti-HBs only, without anti-HBc.
questions.learning: Chronic hepatitis B infection with low viral replication The serology shows: • HBsAg positive → Current hepatitis B infection. • IgG anti-HBc positive → Indicates previous/current natural HBV infection; it is not produced after vaccination. • HBeAg…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with profuse vaginal discharge associated with a characteristic fishy odor. Microscopic examination of the vaginal smear reveals the cell shown in the image. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of profuse vaginal discharge, a characteristic fishy odor (especially noticeable after adding KOH—the "whiff test"), and the microscopic visualization of Clue cells is diagnostic for Bacterial vaginosis (BV). Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells so heavily coated with bacteria (Gardnerella vaginalis) that their borders appear blurred and stippled. Herpes (Option A) presents with painful vesicles. Candida albicans (Option B) causes a thick, "curd-like" discharge and shows pseudohyphae on microscopy. Trichomonas vaginalis (Option C) involves a green, frothy discharge and motile flagellated protozoa. BV results from a dysbiosis where normal lactobacilli are replaced by anaerobic bacteria. It is the most common cause of abnormal vaginal discharge in women of childbearing age. Diagnosis is confirmed using Amsel's criteria. Management involves oral or topical metronidazole. While BV is not technically a sexually transmitted infection, it is associated with increased sexual activity and can increase the risk of acquiring other STIs, including HIV
questions.learning: The clinical triad of profuse vaginal discharge, a characteristic fishy odor (especially noticeable after adding KOH—the "whiff test"), and the microscopic visualization of Clue cells is diagnostic for Bacterial vaginosis (BV).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The parents of a 9-year-old girl have noticed their often staring blankly which is at times, associated with chewing movements. There were also complaints of daydreaming and a decline in school performance. During the episodes, she did not have a problem with maintaining her posture, and there were no generalised tonic and clonic movements. The EEG of the child is given below. Which of the following is a first-line agent to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sodium valproate

The EEG shows generalized symmetric 3 Hz spike and wave pattern, which is diagnostic of absence seizures. Of the given antiepileptic drugs, sodium valproate is the first-line agent to treat this condition. Ethosuximide and Valproic acid are the only 2 FDA approved first-line antiepileptic drugs for absence seizures.

Typical absence seizures are characterized by sudden, brief lapses of consciousness without loss of postural control. There is no postictal confusion. The following subtle motor signs may accompany the episodes

* Rapid blinking of the eyelids

* Chewing movements

* Small-amplitude clonic movements of the hands

Hyperventilation has a tendency to provoke the absence seizures.

NOTE: Ethosuxamide and Valproate are effective for the treatment of absence seizures. However, between these 2 drugs, Ethosuxamide would be a better first-line treatment choice for uncomplicated typical absence seizures followed by Valproate. Atypical absence seizures respond well to valproate.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The graphical representation for flow cytometry analysis is done by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Histogram, dot plot

Flow cytometry results are typically presented by two-dimensional dot plots or one-dimensional histograms.

Histograms compare only a single parameter. A large number of events detected at one particular intensity will be displayed as a spike on the histogram. They are fast to read and easy to understand.

Dot plots can compare 2 or more parameters simultaneously on a 2D scatterplot. Each distinct event is represented as a single dot and events with similar intensities will cluster together in the same region on the scatter plot. They are a more complex, illustrative representation of data.

Pie charts and bar diagrams are used for representing qualitative data. A line diagram is used to show the trend of events or changes over passage of time.
questions.learning: Histogram, dot plot Flow cytometry results are typically presented by two-dimensional dot plots or one-dimensional histograms. Histograms compare only a single parameter.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In Pringle Manoeuvre, clamping includes which of the following? 1. Common bile duct 2. Hepatic artery 3. Portal vein 4. Inferior vena cava Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The Pringle manoeuvre is a temporary vascular control technique used during liver surgery or hepatic trauma to reduce bleeding by clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament, thereby occluding the portal triad.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Common bile duct ✔️: Part of the portal triad.
• 2. Hepatic artery ✔️: Part of the portal triad.
• 3. Portal vein ✔️: Part of the portal triad.
• 4. Inferior vena cava ❌: Not clamped in the Pringle manoeuvre.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 The Pringle manoeuvre is a temporary vascular control technique used during liver surgery or hepatic trauma to reduce bleeding by clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament, thereby occluding the portal triad.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with renal failure develops vomiting in ICU. ABG analysis showed pH - 7.4, Na+ = 145 mEq/L, Cl- = 100 mEq/L, HCO3- = 24 mEq/L, PaCO2 = 40 mmHg. What is the likely metabolic abnormality?
options: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with metabolic alkalosis
High anion gap metabolic alkalosis with normal metabolic acidosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High anion gap metabolic acidosis with metabolic alkalosis

The likely metabolic abnormality in this patient is high anion gap metabolic acidosis with metabolic alkalosis.

Patients with renal failure may have metabolic acidosis and associated vomiting in this patient may cause metabolic alkalosis. However, the parameters of arterial blood gas analysis appear to be normal. This disparity raises the suspicion of a mixed acid-base disorder.

When metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis coexist in the same patient, pH may be in the normal range. In such cases, the presence of an elevated anion gap denotes the presence of metabolic acidosis.

The anion gap (AG) is calculated as:

AG = [Na+] – ([Cl-] + [HCO3-])

= 145-(100+24)

= 21

AG is high, which points to high AG metabolic acidosis.

In high anion gap metabolic acidosis, excess H+ ions are buffered by bicarbonate and the bicarbonate level falls. The fall in HCO3- is expected to be equal to the rise in anion gap. The difference between the rise in anion gap and the fall in HCO3- (delta gap) is zero in simple HAGMA.

Delta gap = (Actual anion gap - Normal anion gap) - (Normal bicarbonate - Actual bicarbonate)

Associated vomiting in this patient results in loss of acid and hence the fall of bicarbonate level is less compared to the rise in the anion gap. A delta gap of more than +6 indicates the presence of additional metabolic alkalosis.

In this case, the delta gap is 10, which points to metabolic alkalosis in addition to high AG metabolic acidosis.
questions.learning: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with metabolic alkalosis The likely metabolic abnormality in this patient is high anion gap metabolic acidosis with metabolic alkalosis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 45-year-old female presents with a mass in the neck. Her T4 levels are high with decreased TSH. She undergoes thyroid ablation therapy using I-131. What is the most likely adverse effect associated with I-131 treatment in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypothyroidism

I-131 is a beta-emitter that is taken up by thyroid tissue as well as differentiated thyroid cancers and is used for treatment of thyroid cancer. The most likely adverse effect is hypothyroidism.

I131 emits both beta and gamma rays. It is used both for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes for thyroid disorders.

I-131 therapy is commonly used to ablate any remaining thyroid tissue after a total thyroidectomy, particularly in cases of thyroid cancer or hyperthyroidism. The goal is to destroy these remaining cells, and while effective, this process almost invariably leads to hypothyroidism. This is an expected and often desired outcome, as the patient will then be managed with levothyroxine replacement therapy to maintain normal thyroid hormone levels.

Other options:

Options A and C: Thyroid storm is a state of severe hyperthyroidism, I-131 destroys thyroid tissue, making hyperthyroidism or thyroid storm unlikely.

Option D: Osteoporosis is not a known side effect of I-131 therapy.
questions.learning: Hypothyroidism I-131 is a beta-emitter that is taken up by thyroid tissue as well as differentiated thyroid cancers and is used for treatment of thyroid cancer.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of increased consumption of bajra (pearl millet) roti now presents with complaints of drowsiness and giddiness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ergotism

The clinical scenario of a patient presenting with drowsiness and giddiness following increased consumption of bajra is highly indicative of ergotism.

Ergot or Claviceps purpurae is a field fungus. Food grains like bajra, rye, sorghum, and wheat have a tendency to get contaminated with this ergot fungus. It grows as a blackish mass and the seeds become black and irregular(refer to image below). These get harvested along with the food grains and consumption of this ergot-infested grain leads to ergotism.

Acute cases present with nausea, vomiting, giddiness, and drowsiness for a period of up to 24 to 48 hours after the ingestion of ergot grain. In cases of chronic consumption, they present with painful cramps in limbs, and peripheral gangrene due to vasoconstriction of capillaries.

Ergot-infested grains can be removed easily by floating them in 20 percent saltwater. Floatation and handpicking can also be used for the removal.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old male with a known history of diabetes came with a wound on his foot. Identify the given condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Trophic ulcer

The given picture showing an ulcer with punched-out edges over a pressure point is most likely that of a trophic ulcer/neuropathic ulcer.

A neuropathic ulcer is one that occurs as a result of peripheral neuropathy. In peripheral neuropathy, lack of sensation over the pressure points leads to cumulative microtrauma, minor wounds, or cuts that remain unnoticed but eventually develop into ulcers.

Features of a neuropathic ulcer include

* Painless ulcer

* Punched out ulcer with regular margins

* Often located on the plantar surface of the foot

* Ulcer margins show the presence of calluses

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 52-year-old carpenter presents with the history of a persistent non-healing ulcer on his lower alveolus. He is a smoker for last 30 years and also chews tobacco. What is the next most appropriate step in the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Edge biopsy of ulcer

A persistent non-healing ulcer of the lower alveolus in a long-term smoker and tobacco chewer is highly suspicious for oral squamous cell carcinoma.

The next appropriate step is biopsy, preferably an incisional biopsy from the edge of the ulcer, including the transition between normal and abnormal tissue.

• A. X-ray mandible: May be performed later to assess bony involvement, but it does not establish the diagnosis.
• B. Edge biopsy: Correct. Provides tissue for histopathological confirmation of malignancy.
• C. Local gum paint: Inappropriate when malignancy is suspected.
• D. Systemic antibiotics: Not indicated unless there is evidence of superimposed infection.
questions.learning: Edge biopsy of ulcer — A persistent non-healing ulcer of the lower alveolus in a long-term smoker and tobacco chewer is highly suspicious for oral squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient develops profuse uterine bleeding following a lower segment cesarean section (LSCS). Despite administration of oxytocin, the bleeding persists. What should be the next immediate step in management?
questions.explanation: In cases of persistent atonic postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) where first-line uterotonics like oxytocin fail, the next recommended step is mechanical intervention. Uterine balloon tamponade (e.g., using a Bakri balloon) is the preferred first-line mechanical measure. It is a minimally invasive, fertility-preserving procedure that applies hydrostatic pressure to the uterine walls to control bleeding and allow for patient stabilization. Uterine artery embolization (Option B) is an alternative for stable patients but requires interventional radiology. Internal iliac artery ligation (Option C) is a more complex surgical procedure reserved for refractory cases. Hysterectomy (Option D) is the definitive last resort for life-threatening hemorrhage after conservative measures have failed. Thus, balloon tamponade is the appropriate immediate next step
questions.learning: In cases of persistent atonic postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) where first-line uterotonics like oxytocin fail, the next recommended step is mechanical intervention.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with gradually worsening swelling around his wrist over the past 3 months. Based on the provided X-ray image, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays an eccentric, expansile, and multi-loculated lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the distal radius, classically described as having a "soap-bubble" appearance. Most significantly, the lesion extends right up to the subchondral bone (articular surface). These are the hallmark radiological findings for Osteoclastoma, also known as a Giant Cell Tumor (GCT) (Option C). GCT is typically seen in young adults (ages 20-40) and is locally aggressive. Ewing’s sarcoma (Option A) classically shows an "onion-skin" periosteal reaction in the diaphysis. Osteosarcoma (Option B) would show a "sunburst" appearance and Codman's triangle. Osteochondroma (Option D) appears as a bony growth on a stalk (exostosis) pointing away from the joint. Because the subarticular "soap-bubble" location is so characteristic, Osteoclastoma is the definitive diagnosis. Treatment involves surgical curettage and bone grafting or cementation to prevent joint collapse
questions.learning: The X-ray displays an eccentric, expansile, and multi-loculated lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the distal radius, classically described as having a "soap-bubble" appearance.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not an example of passive immunity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Toxoid

Passive immunity involves transfer of preformed antibodies without activation of the recipient’s immune system.

| Feature | Active Immunity | Passive Immunity

| ------- | --------------- | ----------------

| Source | Self-produced | External antibodies

| Onset | Slow | Immediate

| Memory | Present | Absent

| Duration | Long-lasting | Short-lived

| Examples | Vaccines (toxoid) | IgA, antitoxin, mAbs

Antitoxins, monoclonal antibodies, and IgA in breast milk provide immediate protection and are classic examples of passive immunity.

Toxoids are inactivated toxins used as vaccines that stimulate endogenous antibody production.

Hence, toxoid induces active immunity and is not an example of passive immunity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: ‘Masson Bodies’ formed due to proliferation of immature collagen are a characteristic histopathological finding seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia

Masson bodies are the histopathological hallmark of Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP) (formerly called Bronchiolitis Obliterans Organizing Pneumonia [BOOP]). They consist of plugs of loose fibroblastic tissue composed of immature collagen and fibroblasts filling the alveolar ducts, alveoli, and bronchioles, while the underlying lung architecture is preserved.

COP represents an organizing response to lung injury rather than irreversible fibrosis and usually responds dramatically to corticosteroid therapy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Lymphocytic Interstitial Pneumonia (LIP): Characterized by diffuse interstitial lymphocytic infiltration, commonly associated with Sjögren syndrome and HIV, not Masson bodies.
• C. Desquamative Interstitial Pneumonia (DIP): Characterized by accumulation of pigmented macrophages in alveoli, strongly associated with smoking.
• D. Respiratory Bronchiolitis: Also a smoking-related disease, characterized by pigmented macrophages in respiratory bronchioles, not fibroblastic plugs.
questions.learning: Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia Masson bodies are the histopathological hallmark of Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP) (formerly called Bronchiolitis Obliterans Organizing Pneumonia [BOOP]).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient underwent a coronary bypass graft with the great saphenous vein. The patient now complains of paresthesia and sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Saphenous nerve

The given clinical vignette in a patient with paresthesia and sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot is suggestive of injury to the saphenous nerve.

Injury to the saphenous nerve is common following venous cut down for access to the great saphenous vein, in this case for coronary bypass graft.

Saphenous nerve:

It is the longest and largest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve and is the longest nerve in the body. It arises from the posterior division of the femoral nerve. It then enters the adductor canal and exits it by piercing the fascia lata between the gracilis and sartorius and supplies the skin over the patella. The saphenous nerve then descends along the medial border of the tibia along with the great saphenous vein (anterior to the vein) and supplies the skin on the medial side of the knee, leg, and foot as far as up to the first metatarsophalangeal joint.

Saphenous nerve injury:

When the great saphenous vein is being harvested for coronary bypass graft, injury to the saphenous nerve is common as it closely travels with the great saphenous vein. Sensory loss over the medial side of the knee, leg, and foot is observed in saphenous nerve injury.

Other options:

Option A: Superficial peroneal nerve injury causes sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the leg and the dorsum of the foot.

Option C: Femoral nerve gives rise to anterior cutaneous branches, the saphenous nerve, and motor supply to the quadriceps and sartorius. Anterior cutaneous branches supply the skin on the anterior thigh and knee. If the saphenous nerve was not an option in the question, the femoral nerve would have been the next best answer.

Option D: Sural nerve injury causes sensory loss over the posterior and lateral aspects of the distal third of the leg and lateral side of the foot and fifth toe. It is often used as an autologous peripheral nerve graft as it is readily identified and easy to harvest.
questions.learning: Saphenous nerve — The given clinical vignette in a patient with paresthesia and sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot is suggestive of injury to the saphenous nerve.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following are advantages of endotracheal intubation, in a child requiring pediatric advanced life support? I. Inspiratory time can be controlled II. Positive end-expiratory pressure can be provided III. Peak expiratory pressure can be controlled IV. Reduced risk of aspiration of gastric contents Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

In Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS), endotracheal intubation (ETI) provides a definitive airway for children requiring advanced airway management. It ensures effective oxygenation and ventilation, protects the airway from aspiration, and allows precise control of ventilatory parameters.

Why is B correct?

• I. Inspiratory time can be controlled. ✔

• Correct.
• Mechanical ventilation through an endotracheal tube allows precise control of inspiratory time, tidal volume, respiratory rate, and FiO₂.

• II. Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) can be provided. ✔

• Correct.
• PEEP helps prevent alveolar collapse, improves functional residual capacity, and enhances oxygenation.

• III. Peak expiratory pressure can be controlled. ✘

• Incorrect.
• Ventilators control peak inspiratory pressure (PIP), not peak expiratory pressure.

• IV. Reduced risk of aspiration of gastric contents. ✔

• Correct.

A cuffed (or appropriately fitted uncuffed in infants) endotracheal tube provides airway protection and reduces the risk of aspiration.
questions.learning: I, II and IV — In Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS), endotracheal intubation (ETI) provides a definitive airway for children requiring advanced airway management.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following genetic mutations is most commonly associated with familial cases of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)?
questions.explanation: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder that destroys motor neurons. Approximately 10% of cases are familial, and the most common genetic cause identified in these instances is a mutation in the SOD1 (superoxide dismutase 1) gene. This mutation leads to a toxic gain-of-function in the SOD1 protein, triggering motor neuron death through oxidative stress and protein aggregation. The CFTR mutation (Option A) is the cause of cystic fibrosis, affecting chloride transport in epithelial cells. The HTT mutation (Option C) involves a CAG repeat expansion causing Huntington's disease. The FMR1 mutation (Option D) results in Fragile X syndrome, the leading inherited cause of intellectual disability. Therefore, SOD1 remains the definitive genetic marker for familial ALS

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with giant cell arteritis presented with headache, jaw claudication, polymyalgia rheumatica, and mononeuritis multiplex. What should be the first-line treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Steroids

Steroids are the first-line management for giant cell arteritis.

Giant cell arteritis (GCA), also known as temporal arteritis is an inflammation of medium and large-sized vessels. It is more common in women and people aged >50 years.

The clinical features include headache associated with scalp pain and jaw claudication, fever, fatigue, malaise, and weight loss. Half of the patients have signs of superficial temporal artery inflammation, including erythema, pain on palpation, nodularity, thickening, or reduced pulsation on the affected side. Gentle pressure on the scalp may elicit focal or generalized tenderness.

GCA is very commonly associated with polymyalgia rheumatica characterized by morning stiffness and pain around the shoulders and hip. It is also associated with mononeuritis multiplex which is characterized by peripheral neuropathy in two or more separate nerve areas.

A dreaded complication is ischemic optic neuropathy, which can lead to sudden blindness. Therefore, patients with a clinical diagnosis of GCA, especially with headaches or visual symptoms should immediately be started on steroids. If treatment is delayed beyond 48 hours, there may be irreversible damage.

Lab reports reveal an elevated ESR level, hypo-/normo-chromic anemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase levels, and increased levels of IgG and complement. The diagnosis can be confirmed by a temporal artery biopsy. It may not be positive in all patients, due to patchy involvement of the vessels. Obtaining a biopsy segment of 3-5 cm with serial sectioning may yield a positive result. A color doppler ultrasound can be used as an alternative.

The mainstay of treatment in GCA is steroids. Prednisolone 40-60 mg is given for one month followed by tapering doses. The duration of treatment is approximately 2 years or more. Methylprednisolone 1000 mg for 3 days should be given for patients presenting with visual symptoms.

Aspirin reduces the occurrence of visual loss and can be given in addition to steroids. Newer drugs used in the treatment of giant cell arteritis are tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) and abatacept (CTLA4-Ig). Both these drugs are used adjunctively to steroid therapy.

Histopathology of giant cell arteritis shows panarteritis with infiltration of inflammatory mononuclear cells with giant cell formation. Intimal thickening and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina is also seen.

The image below shows internal elastic lamina fragmentation (black arrow) and giant cells (yellow arrow) in a cerebral artery.
questions.learning: Steroids Steroids are the first-line management for giant cell arteritis. Giant cell arteritis (GCA), also known as temporal arteritis is an inflammation of medium and large-sized vessels.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The image of a drug is given below. It is used in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subglottic stenosis

The given drug is Mitomycin-C. It is used topically in the management of subglottic stenosis.

Mitomycin-C is derived from the Streptomyces caespitosus bacteria. It can modify wound healing at a molecular level by inhibiting DNA synthesis by cross-linking DNA, acting like an alkylating agent (cell cycle non-specific). It has been used to inhibit post-surgical scar formation and as a chemotherapeutic agent for solid tumors.

Mitomycin-C is employed in the treatment of superficial bladder tumors, postoperative glottic and subglottic stenosis, and tracheal scarring after tracheal reconstruction surgery.

Subglottic stenosis is the narrowing of the airway in the subglottis, clinically presenting with biphasic stridor. Diagnosis is made if the subglottic diameter is <4mm in full-term infants and if the subglottic diameter is <3mm, in the case of premature infants.

Myer-Cotton grading of subglottic stenosis is as follows:

Grade
Obstruction

Grade I
≤50%

Grade II
51-70%

Grade III
71-99%

Grade IV
No detectable lumen
questions.learning: Subglottic stenosis — The given drug is Mitomycin-C. It is used topically in the management of subglottic stenosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the ideal time and method of removing hair before surgery to avoid surgical site infection?
options: On the OT table with electric hair clippers
With a razor 24 hours before surgery
With a hair removal cream on the previous day
On the OT table with a razor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. On the OT table with electric hair clippers

To avoid surgical site infection, hair should be removed on the OT table with electric hair clippers.

Measures to decrease the incidence of surgical site infections (SSIs)

Patient preparation:

1) Smoking cessation four to six weeks prior to elective surgery is recommended to decrease the incidence of pulmonary complications.

2) Bowel preparation prior to abdominal surgeries is expected to decrease the incidence of SSIs.

Infection control:

1) Timely administration of preoperative antimicrobial prophylaxis.

2) All surgical team members must practice appropriate surgical hand hygiene measures.

3) Surgeons and other team members within the premises of the operation theater should routinely wear barrier clothing such as scrubs, caps, and gowns.

4) Preoperatively, the patient must be advised to use topical mupirocin and bathe with chlorhexidine to aid in Staphylococcus aureus decolonization.

5) Shaving hair with razors at the operative site is not advised. If hair removal is absolutely necessary, it may be performed with hair clippers.

Miscellaneous perioperative measures:

1) Maintain normothermic OT

2) Ensure laminar airflow

3) Minimise red cell transfusions

4) Ensure adequate glycemic control.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following cutaneous malignancies does not metastasize through the lymphatics? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Basal cell carcinoma

• Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common cutaneous malignancy and is characterized by slow-growing, locally invasive behavior with an extremely low metastatic potential. In contrast to squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, and Kaposi sarcoma, BCC rarely spreads through lymphatic channels, making local tissue destruction rather than metastasis its major clinical concern.
• BCC typically presents as a pearly papule with rolled borders and surface telangiectasia on sun-exposed skin. Histology shows basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, reflecting its locally invasive nature.

Key Learning Point:

• Basal cell carcinoma → Locally aggressive, rarely metastasizes
• Squamous cell carcinoma → Frequently spreads via regional lymph nodes
• Melanoma → Early lymphatic and hematogenous dissemination
• Kaposi sarcoma → May involve lymph nodes and visceral organs

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In neonatal resuscitation, which of the following is the most effective indicator of successful ventilatory effort?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rise in heart rate

An increase in the heart rate is the most effective indicator of successful ventilatory effort. The response to neonatal resuscitation at various steps is assessed based on the heart rate.

As soon as a baby is born, the tone, cry, breathing efforts, and respiratory efforts are assessed. If the tone is poor, or if the baby is not breathing, the following measures are done immediately - warming to maintain the normal temperature, proper positioning of the baby's airway, i.e. sniffing position with the head slightly extended, clearing of airway secretions, and tactile stimulation.

After the initial steps of neonatal resuscitation, the heart rate of the baby must be assessed. If the heart rate is < 100 beats per minute (bpm), positive pressure ventilation is provided along with SPO2 monitoring to ensure adequate ventilation.

If the heart rate remains at < 100 bpm, ventilation corrective steps and/or endotracheal intubation have to be considered. The ventilation corrective steps are as follows and can be remembered with the mnemonic MRSOPA.

1. Mask has to be reapplied
2. Reposition head
3. Suction the secretions
4. Open mouth slightly and ventilate
5. Pressure is increased slightly
6. Airway may be changed

If the heart rate is < 60 bpm, chest compressions are initiated over the lower third of the sternum at a rate of 90 compressions/min. The ratio of compressions to ventilation is 3: 1 (90 compressions: 30 breaths).

If the heart rate still remains <60 bpm, despite effective compressions and ventilation, then epinephrine (1:10,000 solution at 0.1–0.3 mL/kg intravenously or 0.5–1 mL/kg intratracheally) should be administered. The dosage can be repeated every 3–5 minutes. Persistent bradycardia may signify inadequate ventilation or severe cardiac compromise.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following ion channels in peripheral chemoreceptors is oxygen-sensitive?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. K+

Potassium channels in the peripheral chemoreceptors are oxygen-sensitive.

Type I glomus cells (carotid and aortic body) have O2-sensitive K+ channels, whose conductance is reduced in proportion to the degree of hypoxia.

This reduces the K+ efflux, depolarizing the cell and causing Ca2+ inﬂux.

Hypoxia induces vasoconstriction by inhibition of oxygen-sensitive potassium channels in pulmonary vascular smooth muscle cell membranes. This leads to depolarization of the cell membrane and activation of calcium channels causing the influx of calcium ions. The Ca2+ influx triggers action potentials and consequent excitation of the afferent nerve endings and constriction of small arteries and arterioles.

When the concentration of O2 in the alveoli decreases below normal the adjacent blood vessels constrict. This effect is opposite to the effect observed in systemic vessels, which dilate rather than constrict in response to low O2 levels.

This is because the low oxygen concentrations can :

* Stimulate the release of or increase sensitivity to vasoconstrictor substances such as endothelin or reactive oxygen species.

* Decrease the release of vasodilators such as nitric oxide from the lung.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient’s hysterosalpingogram shows fluid- filled, S-shaped structures on both sides. What is the most likely diagnosis corresponding to this finding?
questions.explanation: A hysterosalpingogram (HSG) that demonstrates dilated, fluid-filled, S-shaped structures on both sides of the pelvis is diagnostic for bilateral hydrosalpinx. Hydrosalpinx occurs when the distal end of the fallopian tube becomes blocked, often due to past pelvic inflammatory disease, causing the tube to fill with fluid and become tortuous. In a normal HSG (Option A), the contrast should be seen spilling freely into the peritoneal cavity. A bilateral cornual block (Option B) would show contrast stopping at the junction of the uterus and the tubes, with no visualization of the tubes themselves. Extravasation into the venous system (Option C) appears as a fine, reticular pattern of contrast moving away from the uterus into the pelvic veins. Bilateral hydrosalpinx is a major cause of infertility, as it prevents egg pick-up and sperm transport. Management typically requires surgical intervention, such as salpingectomy or IVF, depending on the severity of the tubal damage

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Where is the signaling sequence in a type 2 membrane protein located?
options: Inside the membrane at the N-terminal end
Inside the membrane at the C-terminal end
Outside the membrane at the N-terminal end
Outside the membrane at the C-terminal end
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inside the membrane at the N-terminal end

The signaling sequence in a type 2 membrane protein is located inside the membrane (transmembrane region).

A membrane protein can be either integral protein (spans the thickness of the cell membrane) or peripheral protein (attached to the peripheral side of the membrane).

Integral membrane proteins or transmembrane proteins are embedded in the cell membrane, spanning through the entire thickness. They are anchored by hydrophobic interactions and require the use of detergent for solubility.  Examples are ligand-binding receptors for hormones or neurotransmitters, transport proteins like Na+-K+ ATPase, pores, ion channels, cell adhesion molecules, and GTP-binding proteins (G proteins).

Peripheral proteins are attached only to one surface of the cell membrane and do not penetrate all the way through. They are often attached to integral proteins. Examples are cell surface receptors, enzymes, ankyrin.

Signaling sequences are 16 to 30 amino acid residues in length and located at the N-terminal extension of the membrane proteins. After an appropriate trigger, they are either cleaved (and bind to MHC class I of the endoplasmic reticulum) or act as a membrane anchor (transporting proteins across the membrane).

Integral proteins can be divided into:

• Type I integral proteins have a cleavable N-terminal signal sequence (towards the cytosol). Examples include histocompatibility antigens, glycophorin, and membrane immunoglobulin.
• Type II integral proteins have a non-cleavable N terminal combined signal/anchor sequence. Examples include transferrin receptors and glycosyl transferases.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: By what factor does the resistance of an artery increase if its diameter is reduced to one-third of its original value?
questions.explanation: According to Poiseuille’s law, the resistance to fluid flow through a vessel is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius or diameter . This mathematical relationship is expressed as . If the diameter of an artery is reduced to one-third of its original size, the new resistance can be calculated by substituting the change into the proportionality formula. Since the diameter becomes , the resistance increases by a factor of . Calculating results in 81. Therefore, a three-fold reduction in diameter leads to an 81-fold increase in vascular resistance. Options A (9 times), C (27 times), and D (18 times) do not follow the inverse fourth-power relationship defined by vascular physiology. This principle explains why even small changes in vessel caliber, such as in atherosclerosis or vasospasm, can significantly impact blood pressure and organ perfusion
questions.learning: According to Poiseuille’s law, the resistance to fluid flow through a vessel is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius or diameter .

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An infant is brought to the clinic by the parents with the history of a swelling in the neck since birth. On examination, the swelling is found to be soft, partially compressible and brilliantly trans-illuminant. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cystic hygroma

A cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation) is the most likely diagnosis because it typically presents as:

• Present since birth
• Soft and compressible
• Brilliantly transilluminant
• Usually located in the posterior triangle of the neck
• May infiltrate surrounding tissues and can enlarge with respiratory infections

Why not the other options?

• (a) Sternomastoid tumour: Usually presents as a firm mass within the sternocleidomastoid muscle in early infancy; does not brilliantly transilluminate.
• (b) Branchial cyst: Usually presents later in childhood or young adulthood as a lateral neck swelling; generally does not transilluminate brilliantly.
• (c) Thyroglossal cyst: Usually a midline neck swelling that moves with swallowing or tongue protrusion.

questions.text: The life cycle of which of the following is depicted in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nipah virus

The given image depicts the life cycle of the Nipah virus.

Nipah virus is an RNA virus that belongs to the family Paramyxoviridae, genus Henipavirus. It is a zoonotic virus that shows both animal-to-human (bats, pigs) and human-to-human transmission. The natural hosts are fruit bats of the Pteropodidae family.

The clinical manifestations include asymptomatic subclinical infection, acute respiratory infection, and fatal encephalitis. There is no treatment or vaccine available for either people or animals. The primary treatment for humans is supportive care.

Nipah virus is on the WHO list of Blueprint priority diseases.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What characteristic clinical sign is usually seen following an injury to the hypoglossal nerve?
options: Tongue deviation to the contralateral side
Tongue deviation to the same side
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) provides motor innervation to all intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue, including the genioglossus. The genioglossus muscle is primarily responsible for protruding the tongue. In a healthy individual, the simultaneous action of both genioglossus muscles results in a straight, midline protrusion. When one hypoglossal nerve is injured, the genioglossus muscle on the affected side becomes paralyzed. Consequently, when the patient attempts to protrude their tongue, the unopposed action of the healthy genioglossus muscle on the intact side pushes the tongue toward the side of the lesion. Deviation to the contralateral side (Option A) is not seen in lower motor neuron hypoglossal injuries. Falling of the tongue (Option C) and total inability in protrusion (Option D) would require bilateral nerve damage. Therefore, ipsilateral tongue deviation is the classic clinical sign of a unilateral hypoglossal nerve injury
questions.learning: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) provides motor innervation to all intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue, including the genioglossus. The genioglossus muscle is primarily responsible for protruding the tongue.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of these drug transport systems do not require ATP?

1. Simple diffusion
2. Paracellular
3. Facilitated diffusion
4. Antiport (Na/K ATPase)
5. Symport
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1,2,3

Paracellular transport, Simple Diffusion and Facilitated diffusion do not require ATP as they are all passive transport mechanisms.

1: Simple diffusion : Simple diffusion is a passive transport mechanism where molecules (water, carbon dioxide, nitrogen) move from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration and is not carrier mediated.

2: Paracellular : Paracellular transport involves movement of molecules through tight junctions between cells without the need for energy (ATP).

3: Facilitated diffusion : This also occurs along a concentration gradient, but involves carrier proteins to help move the drug across the membrane. No ATP is used because the process is still passive (driven by the concentration gradient).

4: Antiport (Na/K ATPase): Antiport transport system actively moves ions (Na+, K+) against their concentration gradient using ATP in the opposite direction. It is a form of primary active transport.

5: Symport : Two substances are transported in the same direction across a membrane. ATP is required to move substances against their gradients, often via a secondary active transport mechanism.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old female comes with a sudden onset of pain in the right eye. It is associated with colored halos, decreased visual acuity and a steamy cornea is seen, the pupil is mid-dilated and fixed. IOP is 60 mmHg. What is the diagnosis?
options: Secondary angle closure glaucoma by uveitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute angle closure glaucoma

Acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) is an ophthalmic emergency caused by sudden closure of the anterior chamber angle, leading to a rapid rise in intraocular pressure.

Classical clinical features:

• Sudden severe eye pain
• Colored halos around lights (corneal edema)
• Decreased vision
• Steamy/hazy cornea
• Mid-dilated, fixed pupil
• Markedly raised IOP (often >50–60 mmHg)

Pupillary block → iris bows forward → trabecular meshwork obstruction → acute rise in IOP

Why not others:

• A. Neovascular glaucoma:

• Gradual onset, associated with diabetes/CRVO
• Iris neovascularization, not acute mid-dilated pupil

• C. Secondary angle closure glaucoma (uveitis):

• Associated with inflammation signs (cells, flare, posterior synechiae)
• Usually not such abrupt presentation with classic halos

• D. Phacomorphic glaucoma:

• Lens-induced angle closure (intumescent cataract)
• Typically with visible lens swelling and shallow anterior chamber, less classic mid-dilated fixed pupil picture
questions.learning: Acute angle closure glaucoma Acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) is an ophthalmic emergency caused by sudden closure of the anterior chamber angle, leading to a rapid rise in intraocular pressure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which anatomical structure is indicated at the site marked within the anatomical snuff box?.
questions.explanation: The anatomical snuff box is a triangular depression on the lateral aspect of the wrist. Its lateral (anterior) boundary is formed by the tendons of the Abductor pollicis longus and the Extensor pollicis brevis. The medial (posterior) boundary is formed by the tendon of the Extensor pollicis longus. The image points to the lateral boundary, making Extensor pollicis brevis the correct identification. Adductor pollicis (Option A) is a deep muscle of the hand and not a boundary of this space. Flexor pollicis longus (Option C) is located on the volar aspect of the wrist. While the Cephalic vein (Option D) and the superficial branch of the radial nerve cross over the snuff box, they are not the tendon structure highlighted. The floor of the snuff box contains the radial artery and the scaphoid bone, making it a critical site for palpating the pulse and assessing scaphoid fractures

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
A 6-month-old child presented with leucocoria (cat's eye reflex) in the right eye. A cranial pathology was detected. The lesion is positive for synaptophysin, NSE, and chromgranin, and shows a palisade in a spoke-and-wheel arrangement, surrounding a central core. Identify the condition.

NSE-Neuron specific enolase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinoblastoma

The clinical history along with histology showing palisade in a spoke-and-wheel arrangement, surrounding a central core(Flexner Wintersteiner rosettes) and the lesion being positive for synaptophysin, NSE, and chromogranin is suggestive of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma is a malignant proliferation of immature retinal neural cells and is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. It is associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14. It is a tumor of a group called small round blue cell tumors because the immature retinal neural cells are seen as small round cells with large nuclei.

White pupillary reflex or leukocoria is the most common presenting feature, followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision.

Image showing leukocoria of left eye.

Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features of a well-differentiated tumor include Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen.

The histopathological image of retinoblastoma is shown below.

Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy. The commonly used three-drug regimen is the CVE regimen consisting of vincristine, carboplatin, and etoposide. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy. Enucleation is done when:

• the tumor involves more than half of the retina
• the optic nerve is involved
• glaucoma is present and the anterior chamber is involved

In the stage of extraocular extension, the globe bursts through the sclera, usually near the limbus or the optic disc. This is followed by rapid fungation and involvement of extraocular tissues resulting in marked proptosis. Distant metastasis occurs through the lymphatic spread and the direct extension by continuity to the optic nerve and brain.

Other options:

Option B: Medulloblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumor of childhood that occurs exclusively in the cerebellum. Patients usually present with headaches, ataxia, and signs of brainstem involvement.

Histologically, the tumor is very densely cellular. Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and elongated or crescent-shaped hyperchromatic nuclei. Tumor cells form Homer Wright rosettes. They express neuronal markers such as synaptophysin.

Option C: Pineoblastomas are tumours in the pineal region that are best described as small, round, blue-cell tumours. They closely resemble medulloblastomas and retinoblastomas. They are regarded as WHO grade 4 tumours and are the most aggressive and high-grade tumour among pineal parenchymal tumours. The below image shows tightly packed small round blue cells (high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio).

Option D: Epidermoid carcinoma arises from ectodermal cells misplaced during the closure of the neural tube in the process of embryogenesis. There is an accumulation of keratin and cholesterol which gives the tumours their pearly or milky white appearance. A substantial region of keratin is encased in a thin layer of epithelial cells on the outside of an epidermoid tumour. Fatty acids and keratin are found inside the tumour, while stratified squamous epithelium, or normal skin cells, make up the outside of the growth.
