questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following peaks marked in the image below is responsible for ovulation ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

The label marked 2 represents the LH surge ,which is responsible for ovulation.

Phases of the menstrual cycle :

Follicular phase (days 0–14)

* A primordial follicle develops to the Graafian stage, with atresia of neighboring follicles.

* LH and FSH receptors are up-regulated in theca and granulosa cells.

* Estradiol levels increase and cause proliferation of the uterus.

* FSH and LH levels are suppressed by the negative feedback effect of estradiol on the anterior pituitary.

* Progesterone levels are low.

Ovulation (day 14)

* Occurs 14 days before menses, regardless of cycle length. Thus, in a 28-day cycle, ovulation occurs on day 14; in a 35-day cycle, ovulation occurs on day 22.

* A burst of estradiol synthesis at the end of the follicular phase has a positive feedback effect on the secretion of FSH and LH (LH surge).

* Ovulation occurs as a result of the estrogen-induced LH surge.

* Estrogen levels decrease just after ovulation (but rise again during the luteal phase).

* Cervical mucus increases in quantity; it becomes less viscous and more penetrable by sperm.

Luteal phase (days 14–28)

* Progesterone levels are high.

* The corpus luteum begins to develop, and it synthesizes estrogen and progesterone. Vascularity and secretory activity of the endometrium increase to prepare for receipt of a fertilized egg.

* Basal body temperature increases because of the effect of progesterone on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center.

* If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses at the end of the luteal phase. As a result, estradiol and progesterone levels decrease abruptly.

Menses (days 0–4)

* The endometrium is sloughed because of the abrupt withdrawal of estradiol and progesterone.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The finding seen in the image is?
questions.explanation: Herbert's pits are small, shallow, oval depressions located at the limbal conjunctiva. They are formed during the healing of limbal follicles and are considered pathognomonic evidence of a previous infection with Chlamydia trachomatis (trachoma). In the WHO grading system, they are typically seen during the scarring stage (TS). Horner-Trantas spots (Option A) are chalky white dots seen in vernal keratoconjunctivitis. Pannus (Option C) refers to superficial vascularization of the cornea. Arlt's line (Option D) is a linear scar on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, not the limbus. While both Arlt's line and Herbert's pits are associated with chronic trachoma, their anatomical locations differ significantly. The visual evidence of limbal pitting confirms the diagnosis of Herbert's pits
questions.learning: Herbert's pits are small, shallow, oval depressions located at the limbal conjunctiva. They are formed during the healing of limbal follicles and are considered pathognomonic evidence of a previous infection with Chlamydia trachomatis (trachoma).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient presented with neck swelling which moves with deglutition as shown below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyroglossal cyst

A thyroglossal cyst is the only midline neck swelling that moves with deglutition. This is because the thyroid gland is fixed to the hyoid.

Thyroglossal duct cyst:

It is a congenital midline neck swelling that typically presents during childhood often noticed after an upper respiratory infection. It represents the persistence of the track of the thyroid gland and can be found adjacent to the midline. The thyroid gland descends early in fetal life from the base of the tongue towards its position in the lower neck. At the time of descent, the hyoid bone has not been formed and the track of the thyroid gland is variable, passing in front, through, or behind the eventual position of the hyoid body.

Clinical features of thyroglossal cyst:

• Classically the cyst moves upwards on swallowing and on tongue protrusion. This indicates attachment to the hyoid bone.
• Swelling is smooth, soft, fluctuant (cystic), nontender, mobile, often transilluminant.
• Thyroid fossa is empty, if there is no thyroid in the normal location.

Complications of thyroglossal cyst:

• The most common complication is infection.
• Thyroglossal fistula is an acquired condition that either follows infection of the cyst which bursts open or due to inadequate removal of the cyst.
• 1% of thyroglossal duct cysts are found to be malignant of which the most common type of cancer is papillary (85%).

Neck swellings that move with deglutition are:

• Thyroid swellings
• Subhyoid bursitis
• Dermoid cysts attached to the hyoid bone

However, only the thyroglossal cyst moves with tongue protrusion. This is because the duct extends from the foramen caecum of the tongue to the isthmus of the gland.

Sistrunk’s operation is performed to excise the cyst and prevent a recurrence. It involves the excision of the whole thyroglossal tract, involving removal of the body of the hyoid bone, and suprahyoid tract through the tongue base to the vallecula at the site of the primitive foramen caecum along with the core of tissue on either side.
questions.learning: Thyroglossal cyst — A thyroglossal cyst is the only midline neck swelling that moves with deglutition. This is because the thyroid gland is fixed to the hyoid.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Dronabinol are true? 1. It is used in AIDS-related weight loss 2. It acts on the CB1 receptor 3. It is used in chronic pain management 4. It is excreted unchanged in faeces
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 2

• Target: CB1 receptors (primarily CNS)
• Action: Inhibits neurotransmitter release (via ↓ cAMP, ↓ Ca²⁺ influx)
• Modulates:

• Appetite
• Nausea
• Pain perception (limited clinical role)

Dronabinol is a synthetic THC used for AIDS-related anorexia/cachexia and chemotherapy-induced nausea. It acts mainly via central CB1 cannabinoid receptors to stimulate appetite. It is not a standard drug for chronic pain management. The drug undergoes hepatic metabolism rather than being excreted unchanged in feces.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presents with persistent tearing, ocular discharge, and swelling at the inner corner of her eye, and is diagnosed with chronic dacryocystitis. What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation: Chronic dacryocystitis in an adult is primarily caused by an irreversible obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct, leading to the accumulation of tears and subsequent infection within the lacrimal sac. The definitive treatment of choice is Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR). This surgical procedure creates a new, permanent bypass track between the lacrimal sac and the middle meatus of the nasal cavity, effectively restoring tear drainage. Lacrimal sac massage (Option A) and Probing (Option D) are first-line treatments for congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction in infants, but they have a very high failure rate in adults with established chronic inflammation. Syringing (Option C) is a diagnostic tool used to confirm the site of obstruction but is not a curative treatment. DCR can be performed via an external approach (with a skin incision) or endoscopically through the nose. Preoperative evaluation includes syringing and sometimes dacryocystography. Successful DCR provides immediate and long-term relief from epiphora and recurrent bouts of painful infection
questions.learning: Chronic dacryocystitis in an adult is primarily caused by an irreversible obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct, leading to the accumulation of tears and subsequent infection within the lacrimal sac.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the most likely stage of TB hip in a female with left leg shortening?
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis of the hip progresses through well-defined stages based on the extent of joint involvement. In Stage 1 (synovitis), there is pain, limp, and muscle spasm, but no deformity or limb shortening. In Stage 2 (early arthritis), joint involvement begins with some destruction of cartilage and bone, yet true shortening is still not a prominent feature. Stage 3 (advanced arthritis) is characterized by extensive joint destruction, including erosion of the femoral head and acetabulum. This leads to subluxation or dislocation of the hip joint, resulting in true limb shortening, deformity (often flexion, adduction, and internal rotation), and marked restriction of movement. The presence of left leg shortening in the patient is a key indicator of this advanced stage. In Stage 4 (healing stage), the disease becomes inactive, leading to fibrosis or ankylosis, and deformities may persist but are residual. Thus, limb shortening is a hallmark of Stage 3 TB hip, making it the most appropriate answer
questions.learning: Tuberculosis of the hip progresses through well-defined stages based on the extent of joint involvement. In Stage 1 (synovitis), there is pain, limp, and muscle spasm, but no deformity or limb shortening.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An infant is brought to the pediatrics outpatient department with abdominal distension and jaundice. The mother reports increased appetite in recent months, and examination reveals hepatomegaly. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: The presentation of hepatomegaly and a distended abdomen in an infant, particularly when associated with "increased appetite" (frequent feedings to compensate for hypoglycemia), is suggestive of von Gierke's disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I). This condition is caused by a deficiency in Glucose-6-phosphatase. This enzyme is critical for the final step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; its absence prevents the liver from releasing glucose into the blood, leading to severe fasting hypoglycemia and massive glycogen accumulation in the liver. Glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Option B) is McArdle's (muscle) or Hers (liver) disease, which is generally milder than von Gierke's. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency (Option C) is galactosemia, which causes jaundice and hepatomegaly but typically presents with feeding intolerance rather than increased appetite. Glycogen synthase deficiency (Option D) would lead to a small liver and fasting hypoglycemia but not hepatomegaly. Von Gierke's also features doll-like facies and hyperlipidemia
questions.learning: The presentation of hepatomegaly and a distended abdomen in an infant, particularly when associated with "increased appetite" (frequent feedings to compensate for hypoglycemia), is suggestive of von Gierke's disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During walking, the hip bone on the side of the suspended leg is raised by the action of which muscle present in the supporting leg?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gluteus Medius

Gluteus Medius of the supporting leg is responsible for raising the hip bone on the side of the suspended leg.

Actions of Gluteus Medius:

•  Hip abduction
•  Stabilizes the pelvis during gait.
•  Assists the internal rotation of the thigh.

Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus act as the abductors of the hip joint. Stabilizing the pelvis on the femur during walking is done by these muscles. It is demonstrated by asking the subject to stand on one limb.

Trendelenburg Sign:
Trendelenburg sign is a clinical sign used to assess the function of the gluteus medius.
It is positive when the pelvis drops on the opposite side of the stance leg, indicating weakness or dysfunction of the gluteus medius on the supporting leg.
In a healthy individual, the gluteus medius contracts to prevent the pelvis from tilting when one leg is lifted. If the gluteus medius is weak or paralyzed, the pelvis tilts toward the side of the suspended leg.

Option B: Gluteus Maximus: Extends and externally rotates the hip; key for climbing stairs and rising from sitting. Weakness causes difficulty in hip extension, affecting activities like standing up or climbing.

Option C: Obturator Internus: Externally rotates and stabilizes the hip joint; abducts the thigh when the hip is flexed. Dysfunction can impair hip rotation, commonly affected in pelvic injuries.

Option D: Quadratus Femoris: Externally rotates and adducts the hip. Injury or entrapment of the nerve to quadratus femoris can cause deep hip pain and weakness in rotation.
questions.learning: Gluteus Medius Gluteus Medius of the supporting leg is responsible for raising the hip bone on the side of the suspended leg. Actions of Gluteus Medius: • Hip abduction • Stabilizes the pelvis during gait. • Assists the internal rotation of the thigh.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Crypta magna is the remnant of:
questions.explanation: The embryological development of the pharyngeal apparatus is critical for forming structures of the head and neck. The second pharyngeal pouch is specifically responsible for the formation of the palatine tonsils. As the pouch endoderm proliferates into the surrounding mesenchyme, it forms the tonsillar crypts. The crypta magna (or intratonsillar cleft) is the largest and most prominent of these crypts and represents the original lumen or remnant of the second pharyngeal pouch itself. The first pouch (Option A) forms the Eustachian tube and middle ear. The third pouch (Option C) forms the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands. The fourth pouch (Option D) contributes to the superior parathyroid glands and the ultimobranchial body. Therefore, because the palatine tonsils are the direct derivative of the second pouch, the crypta magna is its definitive anatomical remnant
questions.learning: The embryological development of the pharyngeal apparatus is critical for forming structures of the head and neck. The second pharyngeal pouch is specifically responsible for the formation of the palatine tonsils.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The middle radioulnar joint is an example of a:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fibrous joint

The middle radioulnar joint is an example of a fibrous joint (syndesmosis).

The radius and ulna are united with each other by three joints:

• Proximal (superior) radioulnar joint
• Middle radioulnar joint
• Distal (inferior) radioulnar joint

Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are uniaxial pivot joints (synovial) and are involved in pronation and supination movements of the forearm.

The middle radioulnar joint is a fibrous joint (syndesmosis). The radius and ulna, in the middle, are connected by two syndesmoses namely:

• The oblique cord - extends from the lateral side of the ulnar tuberosity to the radius, distal to the radial tuberosity.
• Interosseous membrane - a broad, thin collagenous structure, which runs perpendicular to the oblique cord. It extends distomedially between the interosseous borders of the radius and ulna.

Based on the structure, joints are classified into three types:

• Fibrous joints

• Sutures
• Syndesmosis
• Gomphosis

• Cartilaginous joints

• Primary cartilaginous joints or synchondrosis
• Secondary cartilaginous joints or symphysis

• Synovial joints

• Ball-and-socket or spheroidal joints
• Sellar or saddle joints
• Condylar or bicondylar joints
• Ellipsoid joints
• Hinge joints
• Pivot or trochoid joints
• Plane joints

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which among the following is the most common parotid gland tumor?
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma, also known as a benign mixed tumor, is the most common overall salivary gland tumor and specifically the most common tumor of the parotid gland. It characteristically presents as a slow-growing, painless, firm mass, often located in the superficial lobe of the parotid. Warthin's tumor (Option B), or cystadenolymphoma, is the second most common benign parotid tumor, typically occurring in older male smokers and often presenting bilaterally. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (Option D) is the most common malignant salivary gland tumor, but its overall incidence is lower than that of pleomorphic adenoma. Adenoid cystic carcinoma (Option C) is another malignancy known for its "Swiss cheese" appearance on histology and its tendency for perineural invasion, but it is less common in the parotid than in the minor salivary glands. Understanding this hierarchy is essential for clinicians when evaluating a facial mass to determine the likely biological behavior and plan appropriate surgical intervention
questions.learning: Pleomorphic adenoma, also known as a benign mixed tumor, is the most common overall salivary gland tumor and specifically the most common tumor of the parotid gland.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about lupus nephritis in pregnancy?
options: Immunosuppression can be continued during pregnancy
Pregnancy to be planned once the disease has been quiescent for at least 6 months and there is no evidence of renal dysfunction
High dose corticosteroids for lupus flare in pregnancy is safe
Ecospirin, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, corticosteroids, azathioprine are safe in pregnancy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ecospirin, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, corticosteroids, azathioprine are safe in pregnancy

Option D is not true about lupus nephritis in pregnancy. Methotrexate and cyclophosphamide are teratogenic and hence they are not safe during pregnancy.

Systemic lupus erythematosus(SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disorder involving the multisystem. It affects young women of childbearing age. The renal involvement of the disease can manifest in the form of active lupus nephritis or flare-ups during pregnancy.

Clinical features include fever, weight loss, migratory joint pain, and myalgias. It can lead to preterm births, preeclampsia, and pregnancy loss while the infant can suffer from neonatal lupus and heart block.

Antinuclear antibodies are useful for screening the disease. Double-stranded DNA (ds DNA) is highly specific in diagnosing. Other antibodies such as lupus anticoagulant, antiphospholipid antibodies, anti-Ro, and anti-La antibodies are useful in diagnosis.

Management is as follows

• Preconceptional planning plays an important role. Conception during a period of quiescence for at least 6 months determines a successful outcome. Stable remission of renal disease for at least 6 months before conception is recommended.
• Corticosteroids are useful during episodes of lupus flare and can be used safely in pregnancy. For patients on chronic corticosteroid therapy, intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg, three doses are given 8 hourly during labor or at the time of cesarean delivery.
• Immunosuppressants such as azathioprine can be continued during pregnancy. It may be used in case of severe SLE
• Hydroxychloroquine is found to be the best for maintenance and is safe in pregnancy. It can prevent the need for prolonged corticosteroid therapy.
questions.learning: Ecospirin, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, corticosteroids, azathioprine are safe in pregnancy Option D is not true about lupus nephritis in pregnancy.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 20-year-old patient presents with painful swelling in the middle finger around the proximal phalanx. An X-ray was done and it is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Enchondroma

The above clinical vignette and X-ray findings point toward the diagnosis of enchondroma.

Enchondromas are benign tumors consisting of a lobulated mass of cartilage encapsulated by fibrous tissue. It is more commonly seen in 20 to 30 years of age. Small bones of hands and feet are commonly involved followed by the femur and humerus.

The patient usually presents with long-standing swelling from one or more phalanges or metacarpals, without much pain. Diagnosis can be done by X-ray, which can show expanding lytic lesions, occasionally, a biopsy will be required if the diagnosis is unclear. Enchondromas of long bones may undergo malignant transformation into chondrosarcoma.

Treatment is removal by curettage and it is indicated if there is pain or pathological fracture.

Other options:

Option A: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignancy of bone that produces osteoid matrix or mineralized bone.  X-ray shows periosteal reaction and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunburst (sunray) appearance as shown below.

Option B: Ewing's sarcoma is the second most common primary malignancy of bone after osteosarcoma. Onion-peel appearance due to deposition of periosteal reaction in layers is seen on radiology (as shown below) and Homer-Wright rosettes, which are round groupings of cells with a central fibrillary core may be seen histologically.

Option C: Osteoclastoma is also called a giant cell tumour because multinucleated osteoclast-type giant cells are present on histology. The image below shows an X-ray of a giant cell tumor showing an eccentrically located solitary lytic lesion in the epiphysis and the typical soap bubble appearance

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The heart of the activated sludge process is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aeration tank

The activated sludge process is a part of the secondary sewage treatment and the heart of this process is the aeration tanks.

Pearl PF1009: Modern Sewage Treatment

Primary treatment

* Screening

* A large metal screen is used to intercept large floating objects like dead animals, wood, rags, etc., so as to prevent clogging

* Grit chamber

* It is also called detritus chamber

* It allows for the settlement of heavier solids like gravel or sand and permits the organic matter to flow through

* The grit that is collected at the bottom is then disposed of.

* Primary sedimentation

* In a primary sedimentation tank, sewage is allowed to flow slowly so that suspended matter is sediments to form sludge which is then removed without disturbing the rest of the operation.

* Biological action takes place here and breaks down complex organic solids

* Scum in the form of grease and fat collect on top of the tank

* Sometimes, chemicals like lime are added to the effluent to enhance precipitation

Secondary treatment

* Trickling filter method

* The trickling or percolating filter is a bed of crushed stones or clinker

*  Effluent from the primary sedimentation tank is spread over the filter bed and as it percolates through it, it gets oxidized by bacterial flora. There is no actual filtration that occurs.

* The oxidized sewage forms a light green material called humus and it is then led into secondary sedimentation tanks.

* Activated sludge process

* This is done in place of the trickling filter method. Both are not done together

* The heart of the activated sludge process is the aeration tank

* In these tanks, the effluent from primary sedimentation is mixed with activated or return sludge (sludge from the final settling tank) and is then exposed to aeration for 6 to 8 hours.

* During aeration, organic matter is oxidized into carbon dioxide, nitrates and water with the help of aerobic bacteria in the activated sludge.

* Secondary sedimentation

* From the trickling filters or aeration tanks, the oxidized sewage is allowed into a secondary sedimentation tank where it is held for 2 – 3 hours.

* Here, aerated sludge or activated sludge is formed, part of which is pumped back into an aeration tank

* Sludge digestion

* Sludge digestion can be done by incubating it under favorable conditions to allow anaerobic auto-digestion. This is done in sludge digestion tanks.

* Disposal of sludge is also done by sea disposal

* Sludge can also be disposed of by composting with solid refuse

* Disposal of effluent

* Disposal of effluent can be done by dilution in water bodies which has to then be chlorinated

* Disposal on land is possible if the effluent can be used for irrigation purposes

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the term used to denote the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births?
questions.explanation: It is a common error to use the terms "rate" and "ratio" interchangeably in maternal health. The Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) specifically measures the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. This measure reflects the obstetric risk associated with pregnancy. The Maternal Mortality Rate (Option A), in contrast, measures deaths per 1,000 women of reproductive age, reflecting the risk of death in the general female population. The Infant Mortality Rate (Option C) measures deaths of infants under 1 year per 1,000 live births. The Perinatal Mortality Rate (Option D) includes late fetal deaths and early neonatal deaths. Because the denominator "live births" is used to define the obstetric risk, the "ratio" is the correct statistical term. Understanding this distinction is vital for accurate public health reporting and international comparisons
questions.learning: It is a common error to use the terms "rate" and "ratio" interchangeably in maternal health. The Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) specifically measures the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A teenage patient presented with a history of dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain. On ultrasonography, a transverse vaginal septum was seen. Which of the following is she likely to have? (NEET PG 2021)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endometriosis

A transverse vaginal septum can obstruct menstrual outflow, leading to cryptomenorrhea and retrograde menstruation.

Clinical features:

• Dysmenorrhea
• Chronic pelvic pain
• Hematocolpos or hematometra
• Cyclical pain after menarche

Retrograde menstruation allows endometrial tissue to reflux through the fallopian tubes into the pelvic cavity, increasing the risk of endometriosis.

Why other options are incorrect:

• B. Tubo-ovarian abscess is usually related to pelvic inflammatory disease
• C. Dermoid cyst is a benign ovarian germ cell tumor
• D. Theca lutein cysts are associated with high β-hCG states

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient presented with left facial weakness. Routine lab workup was normal. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Corticosteroids

A patient with acute onset unilateral facial weakness and normal investigations is most likely having Bell’s palsy (idiopathic facial nerve palsy).

First-line management:

·         Corticosteroids (within 72 hours) → reduce nerve inflammation and edema

·         Significantly improve recovery outcomes

·         Inflammation of facial nerve (CN VII) within facial canal

·         Leads to compression → demyelination → weakness of facial muscles

Clinical features:

·         Unilateral facial paralysis

·         Inability to close eye (lagophthalmos)

·         Loss of forehead wrinkling (LMN lesion)

Why other options are incorrect:

·         Acyclovir: May be added in severe cases, but not first-line alone

·         Antibiotics: No role (non-bacterial)

·         Physiotherapy: Adjunct, not initial primary treatment
questions.learning: Corticosteroids — A patient with acute onset unilateral facial weakness and normal investigations is most likely having Bell’s palsy (idiopathic facial nerve palsy).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with headache and visual disturbances. MRI brain reveals a cerebellar hemangioblastoma. On further evaluation, abdominal imaging shows a solid renal mass suggestive of clear cell renal carcinoma. Family history reveals that his father and paternal aunt had similar CNS and renal tumors at a young age. Which of the following genetic mutations is most likely responsible for this condition?
options: Loss of function of TSC1/TSC2 gene
Mutation in VHL tumor suppressor gene
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mutation in VHL tumor suppressor gene

Familial occurrence of renal tumors with CNS tumors suggests von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease.

VHL gene mutations predispose to renal cell carcinoma, hemangioblastomas of the brain and retina, and pheochromocytoma.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The instrument shown in the image is not used for which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Upper airway examination

The image shows a tracheostomy tube. It is not used for upper airway examination.

Tracheostomy involves making an opening and placing a stoma in the anterior wall of the trachea.

Functions:

1. Provides an alternative pathway for breathing by bypassing the obstruction.
2. Improves alveolar ventilation by reducing dead space by 30-50% and reducing airway resistance
3. Uses a cuff to protect the airways from secretions and blood
4. Allows suction of secretions in the setting of the impaired cough reflex.
5. Allows positive pressure respiration
6. Allows administration of anesthesia

Indications:

1. Respiratory obstruction due to

1. Infections (laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis, epiglottitis, diphtheria)
2. Trauma due to external injury, mandibular or maxillofacial fractures
3. Neoplasms
4. Foreign bodies or edema
5. Bilateral abductor paralysis
6. Congenital anomalies

2. Retained secretions

1. Inability to cough due to coma, spasm, or paralysis of respiratory muscles
2. Aspiration of pharyngeal secretions
3. Painful cough

3. Respiratory insufficiency due to emphysema, chronic bronchitis
questions.learning: Upper airway examination — The image shows a tracheostomy tube. It is not used for upper airway examination.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is typically seen in diabetic retinopathy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tractional retinal detachment

Diabetic retinopathy, especially in its advanced stage (proliferative diabetic retinopathy, PDR), is characterized by neovascularization and fibrovascular proliferation, which can lead to tractional retinal detachment (TRD).

• Chronic hyperglycemia → retinal ischemia
• ↑ VEGF → new fragile vessels form
• Associated fibrous tissue contracts → pulls retina away → TRD

Why not others:

• Myopic refractive error: Related to axial elongation, not diabetes
• Posterior staphyloma: Seen in pathological myopia
• Retinoschisis: Splitting of retinal layers, unrelated to diabetic changes

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the recommended concentration or dose of oxygen to be used during resuscitation of a full-term newborn with respiratory distress?
questions.explanation: According to the current Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) guidelines, resuscitation of full-term infants should be initiated with room air, which contains 21% oxygen. Research has shown that room air is as effective as 100% oxygen (Option D) for resuscitation and is significantly safer, as it reduces oxidative stress and potential injury to the brain and lungs. Intermediate doses like 50% (Option B) or 70% (Option C) are not used for initial resuscitation in term babies. If the infant’s oxygen saturation (SpO2), measured via pulse oximetry, does not meet specific target levels according to the post-birth timeline, the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) can then be gradually titrated upwards using a blender. For preterm infants ( weeks), resuscitation may start at slightly higher levels (21%–30%), but for the full-term neonate described in the question, room air (21%) is the definitive standard starting point
questions.learning: According to the current Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) guidelines, resuscitation of full-term infants should be initiated with room air, which contains 21% oxygen.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A mother brings her 9-month-old infant for evaluation, concerned that no BCG scar has developed despite the child having received the BCG vaccine at birth. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Do the Mantoux test & wait for the result
Refer the baby for a chest X-ray & further evaluation
questions.explanation: Following BCG vaccination, approximately 10% of children may not develop a visible scar; however, the absence of a scar is not an indicator of lack of immunity. National and WHO immunization guidelines state that if a child has a documented history of receiving the vaccine at birth and is otherwise healthy, no further action or revaccination is necessary. Therefore, the doctor should simply reassure the mother. Giving the vaccine again (Option B) is not recommended. Performing a Mantoux test (Option C) is unnecessary in an asymptomatic, previously vaccinated child. A chest X-ray (Option D) is only indicated if the child exhibits clinical symptoms suggestive of tuberculosis infection. The BCG vaccine is a live-attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis intended to protect infants from severe forms of TB like miliary TB and meningitis
questions.learning: Following BCG vaccination, approximately 10% of children may not develop a visible scar; however, the absence of a scar is not an indicator of lack of immunity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A child presents with the findings shown in the image below. Which structure is most likely involved in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cranial nerve 7

The given clinical findings are suggestive of Bell's palsy which is a paralysis of the facial nerve.

Facial nerve paralysis can be central or peripheral. Peripheral is more common and is usually idiopathic.

Bell's palsy is an acute onset idiopathic, peripheral facial paralysis. It is a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve and involves the ipsilateral side of the upper and lower halves of the face.

It presents an inability to close the eye, and if the patient attempts to close it, it turns up and out. This is known as the Bell's phenomenon. Other features include drooling of saliva and facial asymmetry. There may be noise intolerance and a loss of taste sensation.

Bell's palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion. Investigations should rule out all other possible causes of facial paralysis.

Treatment of Bell's palsy involves prednisone 60-80 mg daily during the first 5 days and then tapered over the next 5 days. Tape to depress the upper eyelid during sleep and artificial tears can be used to prevent corneal drying. Most patients recover within a few weeks or months.

Other options:

Option B: In oculomotor nerve (CN 3) palsy, there is ptosis, a dilated pupil, and the eye appears to be down and out due to the unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique action.

Option C: Orbicularis oculi palsy refers to weakness or paralysis of the muscle responsible for closing the eyelids. This condition can lead to incomplete eyelid closure, resulting in exposure keratitis and difficulty blinking.

Option D: Erb's palsy is a paralysis of the arm caused by injury to the upper brachial plexus (C5-C6 nerves), often during birth. It results in weakness or loss of movement in the shoulder and arm, commonly presenting as a "waiter's tip" deformity as shown in the image below.
questions.learning: Cranial nerve 7 — The given clinical findings are suggestive of Bell's palsy which is a paralysis of the facial nerve. Facial nerve paralysis can be central or peripheral.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a High-risk group for HIV?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Long distance truck drivers (LDTD)

High-risk groups for HIV are those with direct high-risk sexual or parenteral exposure, such as IDU, MSM, and CSW, due to needle sharing or unprotected sex.

Long-distance truck drivers are classified as a bridge population, not a core high-risk group, as they facilitate transmission between high-risk groups and the general population.
questions.learning: Long distance truck drivers (LDTD) High-risk groups for HIV are those with direct high-risk sexual or parenteral exposure, such as IDU, MSM, and CSW, due to needle sharing or unprotected sex.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents with prolonged labor in emergency. She is being taken for Cesarean section. Which of the following is the correct position in which the nurse should keep the patient on the OT table?
options: Supine with wedge under right hip
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Supine with wedge under right hip

The position of the patient in the Cesarean section is supine, with a wedge under the right hip.

The wedge beneath the right hip creates a left lateral tilt to aid venous return and avoid hypotension.
questions.learning: Supine with wedge under right hip — The position of the patient in the Cesarean section is supine, with a wedge under the right hip. The wedge beneath the right hip creates a left lateral tilt to aid venous return and avoid hypotension.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which statement refers best to the criteria for starting an urban community health center?
options: Caters to a population of 1-1.5 lakh
Referral centre for 2- 3 primary health centers
No sub-district and district hospitals present in the area
Should have a 100-bed facility in metro cities
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Should have a 100-bed facility in metro cities

An urban community health center (U-CHC) has a 100-bed facility in metro cities.

U-CHC acts as a referral center for 4–5 urban primary health centers (U-PHC). It is usually a 30–50 bedded facility that caters to a population of 2,50,000.

When it comes to metro cities, it caters to a population of 5,00,000 with a 100-bed facility. These hospitals will have surgeons, gynecologists, physicians, and pediatricians, along with x-ray and laboratory facilities.

The specialists at the community health center can refer a patient to the state-level hospital or the nearest medical college hospital directly. The subdistrict and district hospitals operate in addition to CHC to cater to the population.

Services of CHC:

• Care of routine and emergency cases in medicine and surgery
• Maternal, newborn, and child health
• Family planning
• All the national health program functions
• Physical medicine and rehabilitation services
questions.learning: Should have a 100-bed facility in metro cities — An urban community health center (U-CHC) has a 100-bed facility in metro cities. U-CHC acts as a referral center for 4–5 urban primary health centers (U-PHC).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Photostress test is used to differentiate between:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Macula and optic nerve disease

Photostress test is used to differentiate between the disease involving the macula and optic nerve.

This test is of particular use in early macular diseases such as central serous retinopathy.

In this test, one eye is covered and the patient is asked to read the smallest line on the near chart. A bright light is then shone into the eye for 15 seconds, and the patient is asked to read the line again, and the time taken to recover is noted. The test is repeated with the other eye.

In normal people and in patients with optic nerve disease, the recovery time is not affected. Whereas, in patients with macular disease the recovery time is prolonged and is usually more than one-third of the normal recovery time. This is because, in macular disease, the photoreceptors are damaged, and there is a delay in the visual pigment regeneration process.
questions.learning: Macula and optic nerve disease Photostress test is used to differentiate between the disease involving the macula and optic nerve. This test is of particular use in early macular diseases such as central serous retinopathy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements about Hodgkin's Lymphoma is not true?

RS - Reed Sternberg cells
options: Waldeyer's ring is the most common site to be involved
RS cells are immunopositive for CD30 and PAX5
RS Cells are of B cell origin
Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype and presents as a mediastinal mass
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Waldeyer's ring is the most common site to be involved

The statement that Waldeyer's ring is the most common site involved in Hodgkin's Lymphoma is incorrect; the most commonly affected sites are the cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes.

The slide below shows the classic appearance of the RS cells showing the owl's eye appearance.

WHO classifies Hodgkin's lymphoma into 5 subtypes:

• Nodular sclerosis: Frequent lacunar cells
• Mixed cellularity
• Lymphocyte-rich
• Lymphocyte depletion
• Nodular lymphocyte predominance

The first 4 subtypes are considered classical Hodgkin's lymphoma. The RS cells are CD15+, PAX5 and CD30+. The lymphocyte predominant type is considered non-classical Hodgkin's lymphoma with CD15-, CD30-, CD20+, and EB -.

Other options:

Option B: RS cells are immunopositive for CD30 and PAX5: Reed-Sternberg cells typically express CD30 and PAX5, among other markers. These immunohistochemical markers help in confirming the diagnosis of Hodgkin's Lymphoma.

Option C: RS Cells are of B cell origin: Despite their atypical appearance, RS cells are derived from B lymphocytes, specifically from germinal center B cells.

Option D: Nodular sclerosis is the most commonly present as a mediastinal mass: Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype of Hodgkin's lymphoma and often presents with a mediastinal mass, particularly in younger patients.
questions.learning: Waldeyer's ring is the most common site to be involved The statement that Waldeyer's ring is the most common site involved in Hodgkin's Lymphoma is incorrect; the most commonly affected sites are the cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with abdominal pain, hypotension, and a CT scan showing no abnormalities. On physical examination, there is blackish discoloration of the perineal skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of severe abdominal pain, systemic hypotension (shock), and blackish discoloration of the perineal skin (specifically known as Turner's sign) is highly suggestive of severe, necrotizing Acute Pancreatitis. Turner's sign results from the retroperitoneal tracking of blood from the inflamed pancreas into the subcutaneous tissues of the flanks or perineum. While Necrotizing fasciitis (Option A) also presents with skin discoloration and shock, the primary symptom is typically excruciating local pain rather than general abdominal pain with a normal abdominal CT. Pancreatitis-related skin signs include Cullen's sign (periumbilical) and Turner's sign (flank). A "normal" CT scan very early in the disease course does not rule out pancreatitis, as radiographic signs of necrosis can take 48-72 hours to develop. Management involves intensive fluid resuscitation, analgesia, and monitoring for organ failure. These skin signs are ominous indicators of a poor prognosis and severe internal hemorrhage
questions.learning: The combination of severe abdominal pain, systemic hypotension (shock), and blackish discoloration of the perineal skin (specifically known as Turner's sign) is highly suggestive of severe, necrotizing Acute Pancreatitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In the management of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis, especially in immunocompromised patients like those with AIDS, which drug is considered the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis is a major opportunistic infection and a leading cause of blindness in patients with advanced AIDS (typically when CD4 count is ). The drug of choice for both initial induction and long-term maintenance therapy is Ganciclovir. It can be administered intravenously, orally (as valganciclovir), or as an intravitreal injection. Ganciclovir works by inhibiting the viral DNA polymerase. Cotrimoxazole (Option A) is used for the prophylaxis and treatment of Pneumocystis pneumonia. Valacyclovir (Option B) is highly effective against HSV and VZV but has poor activity against CMV. Tenofovir (Option C) is a foundational drug in antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV itself, not an anti-CMV agent. CMV retinitis characteristically presents with a "pizza-pie" appearance (hemorrhage and necrosis) on the retina. Management must also focus on immune reconstitution through ART, as the retinitis will inevitably relapse if the CD4 count remains profoundly low despite antiviral therapy
questions.learning: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis is a major opportunistic infection and a leading cause of blindness in patients with advanced AIDS (typically when CD4 count is ).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the options below does not serve as an indication for performing a cesarean section?
questions.explanation: Previous history of macrosomia. A Cesarean section is indicated when a vaginal delivery would pose a significant risk to the mother or infant. Absolute cephalopelvic disproportion (Option A) means the fetal head cannot physically pass through the maternal pelvis, necessitating surgery. Central placenta previa (Option C) is a life-threatening condition where the placenta completely covers the internal os, making vaginal birth impossible due to hemorrhage risk. Advanced carcinoma of the cervix (Option D) is an indication because the tumor tissue is friable and obstructive, making vaginal delivery dangerous. A previous history of macrosomia (delivering a large baby, Option B) is NOT a direct indication for a C-section in a current pregnancy. Each pregnancy is assessed independently; unless the current fetus is suspected of being macrosomic in a way that suggests disproportion, a trial of labor is usually encouraged. Therefore, a past history of macrosomia alone does not mandate surgical delivery.
questions.learning: A Cesarean section is indicated when a vaginal delivery would pose a significant risk to the mother or infant. Absolute cephalopelvic disproportion (Option A) means the fetal head cannot physically pass through the maternal pelvis, necessitating surgery.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy presents with dark-colored urine, reduced urine output, hypertension, and facial edema. His history includes a sore throat approximately two weeks earlier. Urinalysis shows albuminuria, and renal biopsy reveals enlarged, pale glomeruli with epithelial humps. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of "cola-colored" (dark) urine, edema, and hypertension in an 8-year-old following a throat infection (pharyngitis) is pathognomonic for Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN). PSGN typically occurs 1-3 weeks after a Group A Beta-hemolytic Streptococcus infection. The definitive diagnostic hallmark on electron microscopy is the presence of subepithelial humps (immune complex deposits). Nephrotic syndrome (Option C) would present with massive edema but typically lacks hypertension and hematuria. IgA nephropathy (Option D) usually presents within days of an infection ("synpharyngeal") rather than after a two-week latent period. Post-staphylococcal GN (Option A) is more common in adults with other infections. Because the history, age, and pathognomonic "humps" on biopsy all align with the classic post-infectious sequel of Streptococcus, PSGN is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of "cola-colored" (dark) urine, edema, and hypertension in an 8-year-old following a throat infection (pharyngitis) is pathognomonic for Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which type of blood can be safely transfused to a patient with the Bombay (Oh) blood group?
questions.explanation: A patient with the Bombay blood group (Oh phenotype) lacks the H antigen, which is present in all other blood groups (A, B, AB, and O). They also have anti-A, anti-B, and anti-H antibodies. Therefore, scientifically, such patients can receive only Bombay blood, because even O negative blood contains H antigen and can trigger a severe hemolytic reaction. However, in some exam contexts or emergency situations, O negative blood is considered the best available option, especially when Bombay blood is not readily available. Hence, exam keys may mark O negative as the answer. Why other options are incorrect: (A) A blood: Contains A and H antigens → reacts with anti-A and anti-H antibodies. (B) B blood: Contains B and H antigens → reacts with anti-B and anti-H antibodies. (C) AB blood: Contains A, B, and H antigens → highly incompatible. Thus, while Bombay blood is ideal, the exam-oriented answer is O negative
questions.learning: A patient with the Bombay blood group (Oh phenotype) lacks the H antigen, which is present in all other blood groups (A, B, AB, and O). They also have anti-A, anti-B, and anti-H antibodies.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the context of a national public health program targeting anemia, which initiative implements the “6×6×6 strategy”?
questions.explanation: The Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, launched in 2018, aims to reduce the prevalence of anemia across the life cycle. It is famously defined by its comprehensive "6x6x6 strategy". This refers to: 1. Target Beneficiaries: Including children (6-59 months, 5-9 years), adolescents, women of reproductive age, pregnant women, and lactating mothers. 2. Interventions: Such as prophylactic iron-folic acid supplementation, deworming, and counseling. 3. Institutional Mechanisms: Like intra-ministerial coordination and a national digital portal. Poshan Abhiyan (Option B) is a broader overarching mission for holistic nutrition but is not synonymous with this specific 6x6x6 framework. Kishori Shakti Yojana (Option C) targets adolescent girls specifically rather than this multi-tiered approach. AMB aims for a 3% annual reduction in anemia prevalence, a more ambitious target than previous programs. Its success relies on strengthening the supply chain and community mobilization through frontline workers. Anemia Mukt Bharat represents a significant shift toward data-driven, life-cycle-based public health interventions in India
questions.learning: The Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, launched in 2018, aims to reduce the prevalence of anemia across the life cycle. It is famously defined by its comprehensive "6x6x6 strategy".

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding depersonalization disorder?
options: More common after life threatening trauma
Seen in seizure and migraine patients
Mean age at onset is 25 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. More common after life threatening trauma

Depersonalization is common after a life-threatening trauma.

The DSM-V defines depersonalisation as experiences of unreality, detachment, or being an outside observer with respect to one’s thoughts, feelings, sensations, body, or actions (e.g., perceptual alterations, distorted sense of time, unreal or absent self, emotional and/ or physical numbing).

Another term called derealization refers to the experiences of unreality or detachment with respect to the surroundings.

The DSM-V diagnostic criteria for depersonalization/derealization disorder is as follows:

1. The presence of persistent or recurrent experiences of depersonalization, derealization, or both.
2. Intact reality testing, during the episodes.
3. The symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
4. The disturbance is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance(e.g., a drug of abuse, medication) or another medical condition(e.g., seizures). (option b)
5. The disturbance is not better explained by another mental disorder, such as schizophrenia, panic disorder, major depressive disorder, acute stress disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder, or another dissociative disorder.

Characteristic features of depersonalization/derealization disorder:

• The condition commonly occurs after a life-threatening trauma.
• There is no gender preponderance. Male:Female ratio is 1:1 (option c).
• Mean age at onset is 16 years (option d).
• The condition is commonly associated with symptoms such as an altered sense of time, difficulty in remembering past memories, anxiety and depression.
questions.learning: More common after life threatening trauma Depersonalization is common after a life-threatening trauma. The DSM-V defines depersonalisation as experiences of unreality, detachment, or being an outside observer with respect to one’s thoughts, feelings,…

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: On a chest X-ray, obliteration of the right cardiac border is observed. Which of the following structures is likely involved in this pathology?
questions.explanation: The "silhouette sign" is a fundamental concept in chest radiology where the loss of a normal anatomical interface indicates pathology in the adjacent lung tissue. The right cardiac border is anatomically adjacent to the "right middle lobe" (RML). Therefore, a consolidation or mass that "obliterates the right cardiac border" is located in the right middle lobe (Option C). Pathology in the right lower lobe (Option A) would obliterate the right diaphragmatic border but leave the cardiac silhouette sharp. The right ventricle (Option B) is not usually the border-forming structure on a PA chest X-ray, and the right atrium (Option D) is the border-forming structure, but its obliteration is caused by lung pathology sitting next to it. Understanding these relationships allows radiologists to localize lobar pneumonia or atelectasis on a single frontal projection. The RML is a common site for infection and its involvement is best confirmed on a lateral view showing an opacity between the major and minor fissures
questions.learning: The "silhouette sign" is a fundamental concept in chest radiology where the loss of a normal anatomical interface indicates pathology in the adjacent lung tissue.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: When measuring the barrel of a rifled firearm, the caliber of the weapon depends on?
options: No of lead balls prepared from one pound of lead metal
Ratio between length of cartilage & bullet
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Distance between 2 opposite lands

Caliber is measured as the distance between two diametrically opposite lands.

It is the internal dimension of the barrel and is measured in millimetres or inches.

Note: For a smooth barrel weapon, it is measured as the distance between two diametrically opposite points on the inner circumference.
questions.learning: Distance between 2 opposite lands Caliber is measured as the distance between two diametrically opposite lands. It is the internal dimension of the barrel and is measured in millimetres or inches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which structure is formed by the structure indicated by the arrow?
questions.explanation: The arrow identifies the notochord, an embryonic midline structure derived from mesoderm that serves as the primitive axial skeleton. While it mostly disappears during development, its remnant persists as the nucleus pulposus, the gelatinous core of the adult intervertebral disc. The annulus fibrosus (Option A) is the tough outer ring of the intervertebral disc, but it originates from the sclerotome portion of the mesoderm rather than the notochord itself. The neural tube (Option C) is formed from ectoderm; although its formation is induced by signals from the notochord, it is not a direct derivative. The septum transversum (Option D) is another mesoderm-derived structure that contributes to the formation of the diaphragm and is unrelated to the notochordal pathway. Therefore, the notochord's specific adult anatomical legacy is the creation of the nucleus pulposus, which functions to absorb spinal compression
questions.learning: The arrow identifies the notochord, an embryonic midline structure derived from mesoderm that serves as the primitive axial skeleton. While it mostly disappears during development, its remnant persists as the nucleus pulposus, the gelatinous core of the…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 2-year-old was brought to the emergency department with difficulty swallowing for the last few hours. The X-ray is given below. Which is the next best step to manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Esophagoscopy

The clinical picture of the child presenting with difficulty in swallowing and the given x-rays are suggestive of a foreign body lodged in the esophagus, most likely a coin/disc battery.

The given x-rays are anteroposterior and lateral views of the chest and neck. Coins, disk batteries, and small toy items are commonly ingested by children.

The flat surface of a coin in the esophagus is seen on the anteroposterior view (AP view) i.e; they are oriented in the coronal plane. The edge is seen on the lateral view. While coins in the trachea lie in the sagittal plane, those in the oesophagus typically lie in the coronal plane.

Presenting symptoms are choking, gagging, and coughing followed by excessive salivation, dysphagia, food refusal, vomiting, or pain in the neck and throat. Respiratory distress is seen if the esophageal foreign body impinges on the larynx or tracheal wall.

Imaging with PA and lateral views of the chest and abdomen should be done.

Treatment includes the removal of the foreign body by esophagoscopy.

Pearl PF0104: Acute stridor/ Noisy breathing

Stridor indicates an upper airway problem. Look for a history of foreign body aspiration and signs of toxicity.

Important differentials:

Condition
Findings

Croup

Non-toxic, viral prodrome, barking cough

X-ray neck shows steeple sign

Epiglottitis

Toxic child, drooling saliva

Lateral X-ray neck shows thumb sign

Diphtheria
Cervical lymph nodes (bull neck), dirty grey/ white membrane, and un-immunized

Foreign body aspiration
Choking, decreased air entry, unilateral hyperinflation
questions.learning: Esophagoscopy — The clinical picture of the child presenting with difficulty in swallowing and the given x-rays are suggestive of a foreign body lodged in the esophagus, most likely a coin/disc battery.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented after a road traffic accident (RTA) with a head injury. CT head is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Depressed skull fracture

The clinical history and the CT image are suggestive of a depressed skull fracture of the left frontal bone.

A depressed skull fracture occurs when a portion of the skull is pushed inward due to trauma, creating a depression in the bone. This type of fracture can occur as a result of a direct impact to the head, such as in a road traffic accident.

The management of depressed skull fractures:

* The first step is to order a CT scan to know the degree of depression and to exclude the presence of an intracranial hematoma or contusion.

* The depressed fracture is elevated and managed as an open fracture (surgery) if:

* The degree of depression is greater than the thickness of the adjacent skull

* The wound is are open and grossly contaminated

* There are focal neurological deficits

* Less severe depressed fractures are managed by the closure of the overlying scalp laceration, if present.

Other options:

Option A: Concussion refers to a temporary disturbance in brain function following head trauma and typically does not show up on CT scans.

Option B: Epidural hematoma often appears as a lens-shaped collection of blood on CT scans.

Option D: Subarachnoid hemorrhage may appear as diffuse or localized blood on imaging.

Pearl PF0368: Types of skull vault fracture

Diastatic fracture - Separation of sutures due to blow with blunt weapon or from cerebral edema. It is also called sutural fracture.

Fissured fracture/Linear fracture:

* Linear skull fractures are breaks in the bone that traverse the full thickness of the skull from the outer to inner table.

* They are usually fairly straight with no bone displacement.

* The common cause of injury is blunt force trauma where the impact energy transferred over a wide area of the skull.

Pond fracture - Occurs in children due to elasticity of bones. It is also known as indented fracture.

Depressed fracture - Caused by a heavy weapon with a small striking surface. Its shape indicates the type of weapon which is produced. So it is also called 'signature fracture'.

Comminuted fracture - It is also called spider web fracture and has a stellate appearance where there is no displacement of fracture.
questions.learning: Depressed skull fracture — The clinical history and the CT image are suggestive of a depressed skull fracture of the left frontal bone. A depressed skull fracture occurs when a portion of the skull is pushed inward due to trauma, creating a depression in…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient presents with an endometrial thickness of 14mm with an adnexal mass. She has a history of complex endometrial hyperplasia with the presence of atypical cells. Which of the following is likely the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Metastasis endometrial cancer to ovary

This patient with endometrial hyperplasia and an adnexal mass likely has endometrial cancer with metastasis to the ovaries.

For those who undergo TVUS (transvaginal USG) and have an EEC (endometrial echo complex) >4 mm, localized thickening, or an indistinct or nonvisible EEC, endometrial sampling is a reasonable next step.

Investigations for endometrial carcinoma include:

* Endometrial aspiration biopsy is the first investigation for abnormal uterine bleeding, especially in females >35 years.

* Dilatation and fractional curettage was the best diagnosis method, but now it is not used.

* Hysteroscopy and biopsy: The investigation of choice for endometrial cancer.

* Transvaginal USG is used as an adjunct to endometrial biopsy.

* A Pap smear is not reliable to diagnose endometrial carcinoma. It is more useful as a screening tool rather than a diagnostic tool.

If symptoms of postmenopausal bleeding persist, imaging of the endometrial cavity should be performed with one or a combination of the following: TVUS, contrast sonography, or hysteroscopy.

Note: Surgical staging is the gold standard investigation for staging endometrial carcinoma.

Other options:

Option A: Struma ovarii is a type of highly specialized teratoma that contains only thyroid tissue. If it is functioning, it may lead to hyperthyroidism.

Option C: Polycystic ovarian disease is a disease characterized by menstrual abnormalities and hyperandrogenism in women of reproductive age. This condition has been linked to risk factors such as obesity and insulin resistance. Clinically these patients present with infertility and features of hyperandrogenism such as hirsutism and acne. On ultrasound, these patients have larger ovaries with an increased number of follicles. Multiple follicles that are peripherally located in the ovary can be seen on ultrasound. This is also called the string of pearls sign.

Option D: Immature teratomas such as solid teratomas of the ovary are solid and trabeculated. They also contain cartilage, bone, hair, and sebaceous material. There is no structural order. They are generally malignant. Grossly, they have a smooth external surface and are solid on sectioning. There may be areas of necrosis or hemorrhage.
questions.learning: Metastasis endometrial cancer to ovary — This patient with endometrial hyperplasia and an adnexal mass likely has endometrial cancer with metastasis to the ovaries.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is not a contraindication to the use of morphine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acute myocardial infarction

Acute myocardial infarction is not a contraindication for morphine use.

Morphine is the opioid of choice for myocardial infarction as it relieves anxiety, chest pain, and myocardial oxygen demand.

Contraindications to the use of Morphine:

• Bronchial asthma: Histamine release can cause bronchoconstriction and precipitate attacks of asthma.
• Renal failure: Morphine-6-glucuronide (metabolite) can accumulate and lead to prolonged respiratory depression.
• Emphysema: Respiratory depression and decreased response to hypoxia can cause hypercapnia in patients with COPD
• Head injury: Hypercapnia due to respiratory depression can increase ICP. Miosis, vomiting, and effect on wakefulness make interpreting the signs of head injury difficult.
• Biliary colic: Constriction of sphincter of Oddi can worsen biliary spasm
• Hypotension and shock
questions.learning: Acute myocardial infarction Acute myocardial infarction is not a contraindication for morphine use. Morphine is the opioid of choice for myocardial infarction as it relieves anxiety, chest pain, and myocardial oxygen demand.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Galactokinesis is governed by:
questions.explanation: Galactokinesis, which refers to the ejection of milk from the mammary glands, is primarily governed by the hormone oxytocin. This occurs through the "milk-ejection reflex" or "let-down reflex." When an infant suckles, sensory signals are sent to the hypothalamus, triggering the posterior pituitary to release oxytocin into the bloodstream. Oxytocin then causes the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli, forcing milk into the ducts. Prolactin (Option A) is responsible for lactogenesis (milk production) and galactopoiesis (maintenance of secretion) but not the actual ejection. Estrogen (Option B) and Progesterone (Option D) are involved in mamogenesis (development of the breast tissue) during pregnancy but actually inhibit the stimulatory effects of prolactin until their levels drop after delivery. Understanding these specific roles is critical for managing lactation issues; oxytocin's role in ejection means that emotional stress or pain can inhibit the let-down reflex by interfering with oxytocin release

questions.text: A 30-year-old patient presents with fever, cough, and tenacious white sputum. Which of the following should be used for treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Syrup Bromhexine

Respiratory infection

↑ Viscosity (thick, sticky sputum)

Impaired ciliary clearance

Persistent cough

Need:

→ Mucolytic (break mucus)

→ NOT antitussive (suppression)

The patient has a productive cough with thick, tenacious sputum, indicating retained secretions.

Bromhexine is a mucolytic that reduces sputum viscosity and facilitates expectoration.

Antitussives like codeine or dextromethorphan suppress cough and are contraindicated in productive cough.

| C. Dextromethorphan | Non-opioid antitussive | Central cough suppression | Dry cough | ❌ Productive cough present → contraindicated | No analgesia, unlike codeine

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the yoke muscle of the right lateral rectus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left medial rectus

The right lateral rectus and left medial rectus represent a pair of yoke muscles.

Yoke muscles are also known as contralateral synergists. They are pair of muscles, one from each eye, which contracts simultaneously during version movements. Version movements also known as conjugate movements are synchronous (simultaneous) symmetric movements of both eyes in the same direction.

Examples:

* Right MR and Left LR

* Right LR and Left MR

* Right SO and Left IR

* Right IO and Left SR

* Right SR and Left IO

* Right IR and Left SO

(MR: Medial rectus; LR: Lateral rectus; SO: Superior oblique; IO: Inferior oblique; SR: Superior rectus; IR: Inferior rectus.)

These pairs of contralateral synergists receive equal and simultaneous innervation during version movements according to Herring’s Law of Equal Innervation.

Pearl PF1399: Laws governing ocular movements

Sherrington’s Law of Reciprocal Innervation

During ocular motility, an increased flow of innervation to the contracting muscle is accompanied by the decreased flow of innervation to the relaxing antagonist muscle.

Example:

During dextroversion, an increased innervation flow to the right lateral rectus (LR) and left medial rectus (MR) is accompanied by decreased flow to the right MR and left LR.

Herring’s Law of Equal Innervation

According to this law, equal and simultaneous innervation flows from the brain to the contralateral synergists and contralateral antagonists.

Example:

* During convergence: Both medial recti get equal innervation

* During dextroversion: Right LR and left MR get equal innervation

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the lesion in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Viral keratitis

The above image shows a dendritic ulcer caused by herpes simplex virus.

Herpes simplex causes epithelial keratitis and in severe forms, dendritic ulcers develop. Most of the patients present with redness, photophobia, watering, and blurred vision. On examination, visual acuity and corneal sensation are reduced. Follicular conjunctivitis and blepharitis may develop but are usually mild. Clinical reactivation occurs due to multiple stress factors and causes recurrent infections.

The fluorescein-stained image under slit-lamp examination shows dendritic ulcers, a pathognomic feature of epithelial keratitis. They are mostly treated with acyclovir 3% ointment or ganciclovir 0.15% gel.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During an appendectomy in a 2-year-old child, the surgeon incidentally discovers a 2-inch long structure located approximately 2 feet proximal to the ileocecal valve. What is the most likely diagnosis of this finding?
questions.explanation: The "Rule of 2s" is the classic aid for identifying Meckel's diverticulum (Option C): it is found in 2% of the population, is approximately 2 inches long, is located 2 feet (60 cm) proximal to the ileocecal valve, and often presents by 2 years of age. This incidental finding during abdominal surgery matches these exact dimensions. Meckel's is a remnant of the vitelline duct. Sarcoma (Option A) is a malignant tumor and would not present as a uniform diverticular structure. Appendicitis (Option B) refers to the inflammation of the appendix itself, not an additional small bowel structure. Zenker's diverticulum (Option D) is a pharyngeal pouch found in the neck, not the abdomen. Meckel's can contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue, leading to painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding or intestinal obstruction. Therefore, based on the specific anatomical location and the "rule of 2s," it is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which lymphoma is strongly associated with overexpression of BCL2?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Follicular lymphoma

Follicular lymphoma is associated with overexpression of BCL2.

Follicular lymphoma

• Arises from germinal center B cells
• Usually, presents in the middle age.
• (14;18) translocation
• BCL-2 is the inhibitor of apoptosis and causes promotion of the follicular lymphoma cell.

Clinical features

• It presents as painless generalized lymphadenopathy with less commonly the involvement of CNS, GIT, or testes.
• Median survival is for 7-9 years
• In almost 50% of patients, this cancer gets transformed to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Lymph node biopsy

• Closely packed follicles
• Centrocytes (small cell with the cleaved nucleus and scant cytoplasm) and centroblasts (large cell with open nuclear chromatin and multiple nucleoli).

Bone marrow

• Para-trabecular lymphoid aggregates

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 52-year-old female presents with metastatic breast cancer. She has previously undergone treatment with surgery, radiation, and multiple lines of chemotherapy, but her disease has progressed. Genetic testing reveals a BRCA1 mutation, indicating an impaired DNA repair mechanism. Her cancer is classified as HER2-negative and hormone receptor-positive. Given the genetic findings, her oncologist considers using a therapy that targets the PARP enzyme to exploit the DNA repair vulnerability of her cancer cells. Which of the following drugs would be appropriate to prescribe as a PARP inhibitor in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rucaparib

BRCA mutation = defective DNA repair system

Normal cells repair DNA via 2 major pathways:

• BRCA (Homologous recombination) → repairs double-strand breaks
• PARP pathway → repairs single-strand breaks

BRCA-mutated tumors have defective homologous recombination repair and are sensitive to PARP inhibition via synthetic lethality. Rucaparib is a PARP inhibitor that blocks DNA repair, causing tumor cell death. Palbociclib is a CDK4/6 inhibitor, vorinostat is an HDAC inhibitor, and ustekinumab is an immunologic agent. Targeting PARP exploits the DNA repair defect in BRCA cancers.

| Drug | Target | Use

| ---- | ------ | ---

| Rucaparib | PARP | BRCA cancers

| Palbociclib | CDK4/6 | Breast cancer

| Trastuzumab | HER2 | HER2+ cancer

| Imatinib | BCR-ABL | CML

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A case of gestational trophoblastic neoplasm is detected to have metastasis in the lungs. It is considered as stage _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. III

Metastases in the lungs are considered stage III GTN (gestational trophoblastic neoplasia) in FIGO classification.

International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) staging for GTN is as follows:

Stage
Description

I
GTN confined to the uterus

II

GTN extends outside of the uterus but is limited to the genital structures

(adnexa, vagina, broad ligament)

III
GTN extends to the lungs, with or without known genital tract involvement

IV
All other metastatic sites i.e. kidney, liver, brain, bowel, etc.

The chest X-ray below shows lung metastasis - stage III GTN.

Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) refers to the aggressive invasion of the endometrium and myometrium by trophoblast cells. It includes invasive mole, gestational choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumors, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumors. GTN is diagnosed based on elevated β-hCG levels. FIGO criteria for diagnosis of GTN:

• Persistence of β-hCG level plateau in 4 measurements for 3 weeks or longer
• Rise in β-hCG levels in 3 or more consecutive measurements done weekly, over a period of 2 weeks or longer
• Elevated β-hCG level for 6 months or more
• Histologic diagnosis of choriocarcinoma

Treatment for low-risk disease is chemotherapy with methotrexate, while those with high-risk disease are treated with etoposide, methotrexate, and dactinomycin alternating with cyclophosphamide and vincristine (EMA/CO) chemotherapy.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Following complete ileal and partial jejunal resection, the patient is most likely to have
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin B12 deficiency

After complete ileal and partial jejunal resection, the patient is likely to have vitamin B12 deficiency.

Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum. B12 binds to intrinsic factor, a protein secreted by the parietal cells of the stomach, and the complex is absorbed across the ileal mucosa. Hence after ileal resection, there is impaired absorption of vitamin B12.

Clinical features of megaloblastic anemia (cyanocobalamin and folate deficiency):

Clinical features

Gastrointestinal

Weight loss

Diarrhea

Constipation

Hematological

Leucopenia

Ineffective erythropoiesis and unconjugated jaundice

Cardiovascular

Atherosclerosis leading to PVD, CAD (due to elevated homocysteine)

Neurological (only B12)

Peripheral neuropathy

Subacute combined degeneration (degeneration of the posterior and pyramidal tracts of the spinal cord)

Pregnancy (only folate)

Recurrent fetal loss

Neural tube defects

Others

Peripheral smear findings:

* Macro-ovalocytes are seen.

* Most macrocytes lack the central pallor of normal red cells and even appear hyperchromic, but the MCHC is not elevated.

* Reticulocyte count is low.

* Nucleated red cell progenitors occasionally appear in the circulating blood when anemia is severe.

* Neutrophils are also larger than normal (macro polymorphonuclear) and show nuclear hypersegmentation, with five or more nuclear lobules.

Bone marrow findings:

* Markedly hypercellular as a result of increased hematopoietic precursors

* Sieve-like pattern of chromatin of immature precursors (Megaloblasts)

* Granulocytic precursors display dysmaturation in the form of giant metamyelocytes and band forms

* Megakaryocytes abnormally large and have bizarre, multilobate nuclei

* Derangement in DNA synthesis causes most precursors to undergo apoptosis in the marrow (ineffective hematopoiesis) and leads to pancytopenia

* Duodenum + upper jejunum: Iron

* Jejunum: Folate

* Terminal Ileum: Vitamin B12
