questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A 30-year-old female patient, on treatment for infertility, came with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and mild vaginal bleeding. Her beta hCG level was 2800 mIU/mL. On ultrasound, a 3cm mass was seen in the left adnexa. It contained a gestational sac with no fetal cardiac activity. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?

hCG- Human chorionic gonadotropin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Single dose methotrexate

A patient on infertility treatment, with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding with beta hCG levels of 2800 mIU/mL, and a gestational sac in the left adnexa points to the diagnosis of unruptured ectopic pregnancy and the most appropriate management is single-dose methotrexate.

A pregnancy is considered ectopic if implantation occurs at a site outside the uterine cavity. The majority of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube, the ampulla being the most common site.

Management of ectopic pregnancy:

Expectant management: Ectopic pregnancies measuring <3 cm and with declining beta hCG levels initially <1500 mIU/mL may resolve without intervention and can be managed expectantly.

Medical management with single or multiple-dose methotrexate is preferred if:

• Hemodynamic stability
• Serum beta-hCG ≥1500 mIU/ml and ≤5000 mIU/mL
• Mean sac diameter <3.5cm with no fetal cardiac activity detected on transvaginal ultrasound.
• Patients are willing and able to comply with post-treatment follow-up and have access to emergency medical services within a reasonable time frame in case of a deterioration in the clinical status.

Methotrexate(MTX) can be given as a single IM dose of 50 mg/m2 or as a multiple-dose regimen of 1mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5, and 7.

Surgical management with salpingectomy or salpingostomy is done when:

• Criteria for expectant and medical management are not met
• Gestational sac >3.5 cm
• Fetal cardiac activity present
• Beta hCG > 5000 mIU/mL
• Significant pain and hemoperitoneum
• Failure of expectant or medical management
• Clinical status of patient warrants urgent intervention
• Doubtful compliance with medical management

Milking of the tube through the fimbriae carries a high risk of bleeding, damage to the tube, the persistence of trophoblastic tissue, and recurrence of ectopic pregnancy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with hepatosplenomegaly and hypoglycemia. After a meal, glucagon administration increases blood glucose levels. However, after an overnight fast, glucagon administration does not improve blood glucose levels. Liver biopsy reveals increased abnormal glycogen accumulation. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Debranching enzyme

Debranching enzyme deficiency (Glycogen Storage Disease type III – Cori disease) leads to accumulation of abnormally structured glycogen with short outer branches (limit dextrin) in the liver.

Key Clinical Features

• Hepatomegaly and hypoglycemia
• Abnormal glycogen accumulation in liver
• Partial ability to mobilize glycogen

Key Diagnostic Clue

• After a meal: glucagon increases glucose because some glycogen breakdown is still possible.
• After prolonged fasting: glucagon cannot increase glucose, as the remaining glycogen cannot be further degraded due to lack of debranching enzyme.

| Disease | Enzyme Defect | Key Feature

| ------- | ------------- | -----------

| Von Gierke (Type I) | Glucose-6-phosphatase | Severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis

| Cori disease (Type III) | Debranching enzyme | Limit dextrin accumulation, hepatomegaly

| McArdle disease (Type V) | Muscle phosphorylase | Exercise intolerance, myoglobinuria
questions.learning: Debranching enzyme Debranching enzyme deficiency (Glycogen Storage Disease type III – Cori disease) leads to accumulation of abnormally structured glycogen with short outer branches (limit dextrin) in the liver.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with urethral discharge. A gram stain smear is made from the discharge sample and the following microscopic image is seen. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neisseria gonorrheae

The above image shows gram‐negative intracellular diplococci within phagocytes in a stained smear from the urethral discharge sample, which is seen in infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

According to CDC recommendations 2021, the first line of treatment in uncomplicated gonococcal infections is a single dose of ceftriaxone 500 mg IM.

Note: BASHH (British Association for Sexual Health and HIV) in the United Kingdom also recommends higher doses of ceftriaxone of about 500 mg along with azithromycin because it would result in fewer failures.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with a fever and altered sensorium. The peripheral smear shows multiple rings in the RBC. A diagnosis of chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum was made. What is the most likely course of treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Artesunate

Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria is diagnosed, and the recommended treatment is artesunate.

Major manifestations of severe falciparum malaria include more than two convulsions in 24 hours, unarousable coma/cerebral malaria (failure to localise or respond appropriately to stimuli or coma persisting for >30 min after generalised convulsion), acidosis, severe normocytic normochromic anaemia, renal failure, pulmonary oedema, hypoglycaemia, shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Other manifestations include haemoglobinuria, hyperparasitaemia, jaundice, and extreme weakness.

The treatment of choice is artesunate given at a dose of 2.4 mg/kg stat IV, followed by 2.4 mg/kg at 12 and 24 hours, and then daily if necessary. If artesunate is unavailable, artemether is given at a dose of 3.2 mg/kg stat IM, followed by 1.6 mg/kg QD, or quinine dihydrochloride is given at a dose of 20 mg of salt/kg infused over 4 hours, followed by 10 mg of salt/kg infused over 2–8 hours.

Plasmodium falciparum causes malignant tertian malaria. This means that the fever has a periodicity of 48 hours, corresponding to one cycle of erythrocytic schizogony. Malignant because it is a more severe and fatal type of malaria.

Falciparum malaria shows a very high percentage of RBCs containing ring forms. This high-level parasitemia is more often seen in Plasmodium falciparum infections than in infections by other plasmodia. After the ring forms in the peripheral blood, the rest of the erythrocytic cycle occurs in the capillaries of the brain and internal organs. So, only ring forms can be seen in the peripheral blood and not the late trophozoites and schizonts. The gametocytes of P. falciparum are crescent-shaped or “banana-shaped” (as shown below), whereas those of the other plasmodia are spherical.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following marked structure is damaged in respiratory distress syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

Type II pneumocytes, which are marked as 2 in the above image, are damaged in respiratory distress syndrome.

The cells forming the lining epithelium of alveoli (also called pneumocytes) are mainly of the following types:

• Type I pneumocytes - large flattened cells which present a very thin diffusion barrier for gases. These cells have large cytoplasmic extensions and form the primary lining cells of the alveoli. They are connected to each other by tight junctions.
• Type II pneumocytes (granular pneumocytes) - These are rounded secretory cells bearing microvilli on their free surfaces. These cells secrete the surfactant which decreases the surface tension between the thin alveolar walls and thus prevents alveoli from collapsing during respiration. Type II cells are important in alveolar repair as well.

The below image shows the pneumocytes lining the alveoli:

The alveoli are surrounded by pulmonary capillaries. The alveoli also contain other specialized cells, including pulmonary alveolar macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells, neuroendocrine cells, and mast cells.

Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) is seen in premature infants, due to the decreased production and secretion of the lung surfactant. The surfactant reduces the alveolar surface tension. This phospholipid is synthesized in type II pneumocytes (also called granular pneumocytes) in the endoplasmic reticulum.

The surfactant appears in the amniotic fluid between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation. Mature levels of the pulmonary surfactant are present usually after 35 weeks of gestation. In a premature infant, there is a decrease in both the quantity and quality of surfactant resulting in respiratory distress syndrome.

Administration of antenatal glucocorticoids to mothers who deliver at 24 to 34 weeks can increase surfactant production and reduce the risk of RDS. It includes either giving 2 doses of betamethasone 12mg/dose with 24 hours between each dose, or 4 doses of dexamethasone 6mg/dose, with 12 hours between each dose.

Mild to moderate RDS can be managed with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). CPAP is a noninvasive modality of support where a continuous distending pressure (5-7 cm H20) is applied at the nostril level to keep the alveoli open in a spontaneously breathing baby. Severe cases will require mechanical ventilation.

Surfactant administration is reserved for severe cases and moderate cases not improving even with fiO2> 40% in CPAP.

With treatment, it rarely leads to respiratory failure and has a good prognosis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of these is not an essential feature for the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder?
options: Restrictive patterns of behaviour and interests
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cognitive impairment

Cognitive impairment does not form part of the diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder.

The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder are as follows:

• Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, currently or by history
• Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities, currently or by history
• Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life).
• Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning.
• These disturbances are not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay. Intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder frequently co-occur; to make comorbid diagnoses of autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability, social communication should be below that expected for the general developmental level.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the medical term used to describe a clavicular fracture that occurs during childbirth?
questions.explanation: Cleidotomy is the medical term for the intentional surgical division or fracture of one or both fetal clavicles. This rare and extreme procedure is performed during difficult deliveries, specifically in cases of severe shoulder dystocia where other maneuvers have failed, or in destructive operations for a dead fetus. By fracturing the clavicle, the shoulder girdle diameter is reduced, allowing the body to pass through the birth canal. Craniotomy (Option A) involves reducing the size of the fetal head. Symphysiotomy (Option B) is a surgical procedure to widen the maternal pelvis by dividing the pubic symphysis. The Zavanelli maneuver (Option C) involves pushing the fetal head back into the uterus to perform an emergency cesarean section. Cleidotomy is generally considered a procedure of last resort due to the potential for neonatal injury, but it can be life-saving for the mother when vaginal delivery is obstructed. Thus, the specific term for fetal clavicle fracture in this context is cleidotomy

Correct answer: A. Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 1% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 0.1

In the given scenario, absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 1% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 0.1.

Let us reconstruct the design table in the following way:

Health hazard (-)
Total

New drug

15225 (a+b)

Relative risk (RR) is given as a/(a+b) ÷ c/(c+d).

RR = 1603/15225 ÷ 1804/15225 = 0.106/0.118 = 0.89 ≈ 0.90.

Relative risk reduction (RRR) = 1 – Relative risk. In this scenario, RRR = 1 – 0.9 = 0.1 or 10%.

Incidence of a disease is the absolute risk of contracting it.

Absolute risk rate of the group using new drug = a/(a+b) = 1603/15225 = 0.106 or 10.6% ≈ 11%.

Absolute risk rate of the group using placebo = c/(c+d) = 1804/15225 = 0.118 or 11.8% ≈ 12%.

Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is the difference in the absolute risk rates between the placebo and the drug. In this scenario, ARR = 12% - 11% = 1%.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old male, a known case of COPD was admitted to the ICU and was on oxygen therapy with 2 Liters of oxygen. He was found to be hypo-ventilating and an arterial blood gas analysis done showed pH:7.33 and pCO2 as 64 mmHg. Which of the following is the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Non-Invasive PPV should be given

Since the patient is having an acute exacerbation of COPD and his ABG shows PaCO2 >45 mmHg and pH<7.35, he is having acidosis and respiratory failure. This is an indication for Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation and is the next step in the management of this patient.

Indications of NIPPV:

* Apnea: Central and Obstructive

* Hypoventilation syndrome: Central and Obesity hypoventilation syndromes

* Neuromuscular and chest wall disorders

* Respiratory failure: PaCO2 >45 mmHg

Initial management of acute exacerbation of COPD includes:

* Bronchodilators: Inhaled beta-agonists and muscarinic antagonists

* Antibiotics

* Supplemental oxygen

* Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation

If initial NIPPV fails, then, invasive PPV may be provided. However, during the invasive PPV, the tidal volume is reduced to prevent damage to the alveolar structures. This decrease in minute ventilation causes progressive hypercapnia. This is however permitted to a certain extent for the benefit of the patient (commonly known as permissive hypercapnia).

Contraindications of NIPPV:

* Cardiovascular instability

* Impaired mental status or inability to cooperate

* Copious secretions or the inability to clear secretions

* Craniofacial abnormalities

* Trauma precluding effective fitting of the mask

* Extreme obesity

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Gall stone chemistry most commonly seen amongst the following is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Crystalline cholesterol monohydrate

The most common gallstone chemistry seen is crystalline cholesterol monohydrate.

Types of gallstones:

1. Cholesterol stones (75% of gallstones) have >70% cholesterol by weight and are composed of crystalline cholesterol monohydrate. The majority of cholesterol stones have a mixed composition with bile pigments and calcium, in addition to the cholesterol. They are the most common type of gall stones worldwide and in India.
2. Pigment stones have <20% cholesterol and are dark due to the presence of calcium bilirubinate as the major constituent.

1. Black pigment stones (20% of gallstones) - are formed due to supersaturation of unconjugated bilirubin (seen in hereditary hemolytic anemia (like sickle cell and hereditary spherocytosis)
2. Brown pigment stones (5% of gallstones) - formed secondary to infections (like E. coli, and Ascaris lumbricoides)

Note: Pure cholesterol stones are uncommon and account for <10% of all stones.
questions.learning: Crystalline cholesterol monohydrate — The most common gallstone chemistry seen is crystalline cholesterol monohydrate. Cholesterol stones (75% of gallstones) have >70% cholesterol by weight and are composed of crystalline cholesterol monohydrate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: This instrument is not used in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute anal fissure

The instrument given in the above image is a proctoscope and proctoscopy is contraindicated in acute anal fissures.

Due to pain, digital rectal examination and anoscopy are not performed immediately in acute anal fissures. Acute anal fissures are examined under anaesthesia in operating room when needed.

Anal fissure:

Clinical features

* Severe pain associated with defecation resolves spontaneously and reappears during the next evacuation

* It may even be associated with the passage of fresh blood noticed on tissue after wiping

* Most of the fissures are located in the posterior midline, with the rest being located in the anterior midline. Fissures located laterally can be possible due to other diseases like HIV, TB, syphilis, Crohn's disease, or carcinoma.

Treatment of Anal fissure

* The focus is to normalise bowel habits. Bowel softeners, dietary fibres, and adequate water should be recommended

* Medical therapy involves the topical application of glyceryl trinitrate. It releases nitric oxide and relaxes the internal anal sphincter. This reduces spasms and pain and improves vasculature to promote healing

* Surgical therapy is recommended for chronic fissures that have failed medical therapy. Lateral internal sphincterotomy is the procedure of choice. The aim of this procedure is to decrease the spasms of the internal sphincter by dividing a portion of the muscle.
questions.learning: Acute anal fissure — The instrument given in the above image is a proctoscope and proctoscopy is contraindicated in acute anal fissures. Due to pain, digital rectal examination and anoscopy are not performed immediately in acute anal fissures.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following abnormalities in a woman with preeclampsia: 1. Platelet count less than 1 lakh/cumm 2. Serum creatinine > 1.1 mg/dL 3. Pulmonary edema 4. Proteinuria > 1 g per day Which of the above describe severe features of preeclampsia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Preeclampsia is considered to have severe features when there is evidence of significant maternal end-organ dysfunction.

1. Platelet count <1 lakh/cumm — Correct

• Thrombocytopenia below 100,000/µL is a severe feature.

2. Serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL — Correct

• Renal impairment with serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubling of the baseline value is a severe feature.

3. Pulmonary edema — Correct

• Pulmonary edema indicates significant end-organ involvement and is a severe feature.

4. Proteinuria >1 g/day — Incorrect

• The quantity of proteinuria does not determine the severity of preeclampsia.
• Once proteinuria is ≥300 mg/24 h (or equivalent), increasing amounts do not classify the disease as severe.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following about the enteric nervous regulation system is false? 1. Interstitial cells of Cajal are pacemakers 2. It can function independently of the brain and spinal cord 3. All the afferents are from the vagus nerve 4. Myenteric plexus is in the Lamina propria
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3, 4

The Enteric Nervous System (ENS) is like a quiet maestro conducting digestion:

• Coordinates motility, secretion, and blood flow
• Works independently of CNS (but can be modulated by it)

Can function independently of CNS input. Interstitial cells of Cajal act as pacemakers generating slow waves. Afferents are not exclusively vagal; significant intrinsic and spinal afferents exist.

| Function | Motility | Secretion, blood flow

Clinical correlations

| Disease | Defect

| ------- | ------

| Hirschsprung disease | Absence of ganglion cells

| Achalasia | Loss of inhibitory neurons

| IBS | Dysregulated ENS

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following culture media can be used for the growth of Rhinosporidium seeberi?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Non-cultivable

Rhinosporidium seeberi is the causative agent of rhinosporidiosis, a chronic granulomatous disease characterized by friable, polypoidal masses involving the nose, nasopharynx, and conjunctiva. Despite extensive research, R. seeberi has not been successfully cultured on artificial media and is therefore considered non-cultivable. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination, which demonstrates large thick-walled sporangia containing numerous endospores.

Why not the other options?

• A. Blood agar: Used for many bacteria; Rhinosporidium does not grow on it.
• B. Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA): Used for most fungi, but Rhinosporidium seeberi is non-cultivable.
• C. Lowenstein–Jensen medium: Used for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
questions.learning: Non-cultivable Rhinosporidium seeberi is the causative agent of rhinosporidiosis, a chronic granulomatous disease characterized by friable, polypoidal masses involving the nose, nasopharynx, and conjunctiva.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a painless ulcer in the eye. On examination, a long branching ulcer with desquamated epithelium is seen on the cornea. What could be the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dendritic ulcer

A long branching corneal ulcer with desquamated epithelium is typical of a dendritic ulcer seen in herpes simplex keratitis. As shown in the image below:

Herpes viral keratitis, also known as herpetic keratoconjunctivitis, is a form of keratitis caused by recurrent herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection in the cornea. The virus, which lies dormant in the trigeminal ganglion after an initial infection, periodically reactivates and replicates. These reactivations result in unilateral symptoms of epithelial or stromal keratitis.

Patients with epithelial keratitis complain of foreign-body sensation, light sensitivity, redness, and blurred vision associated with focal or diffuse reduction in corneal sensation. Stromal keratitis manifests as a disc-shaped area of corneal edema. In patients who are immunocompromised due to pre-existing disease or using corticosteroids, the ulcer may become large; in such cases, the lesion is called a geographic ulcer.

Treatment:

Topical antivirals are the first-line treatment.

* Trifluorothymidine 1% drops four times a day for 5 days, acyclovir 3% ointment five times a day for 21 days, or 3% vidarabine ointment five times a day for 2 weeks

* Systemic antivirals in cases of increased severity or recurrence

* Topical antibiotics to prevent secondary bacterial infection

Other options:

Option A: Fungal ulcer is typically painful, with grayish-white infiltrates, feathery margins, hypopyon and satellite lesions.An immune ring, also known as a Wesseley ring, can form around the ulcer, caused by the deposition of immune complexes.

Option C: Acanthamoeba keratitis usually occurs in contact lens users or after exposure to contaminated water and is very painful, often out of proportion to the clinical signs due to perineural invasion with a characteristic ring-shaped stromal infiltrate.

Option D: A bacterial ulcer is typically painful, with redness, watering, and a localized corneal infiltrate that may lead to hypopyon in severe cases. It does not usually present as a long, branching, or dendritic pattern.

* Coarse epithelial punctate keratitis

* Conjunctiva: acute follicular conjunctivitis

* Punctate epithelial keratitis

* Dendritic ulcer

* Geographical ulcer

* Stromal keratitis

* Disciform keratitis

* Diffuse stromal necrotic keratitis

* Trophic keratitis (meta-herpetic)

questions.text: All of the following parameters have a Bishop’s Score of 3 except: (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Soft consistency

The Bishop score is used to assess cervical favorability before induction of labor. Components of the Bishop score:

• Cervical dilatation
• Effacement
• Cervical consistency
• Cervical position
• Fetal station

Parameters scoring 3 points include:

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the first-line management for a patient presenting with a pelvic fracture associated with a confirmed rupture of the membranous urethra?
options: Insertion of a suprapubic catheter as soon as possible.
questions.explanation: Rupture of the membranous urethra is a classic complication of severe pelvic fractures. In the acute setting, the primary goal is to provide urinary diversion to prevent urine extravasation and infection while allowing the pelvic hematoma to stabilize. The standard initial management is the insertion of a suprapubic catheter (SPC) (Option A). This avoids further trauma to the injured urethra that could be caused by blind attempts at Foley catheterization. An intravenous pyelogram (IVP) (Option B) assesses the upper urinary tract and is not the priority for a urethral injury. Immediate urethroplasty (Option C) is generally avoided as the tissues are friable and the risk of impotence or incontinence is high. An MCU (Option D) is a diagnostic test performed later to evaluate the extent of the stricture once the acute injury has healed. Therefore, SPC is the essential first-aid urological intervention
questions.learning: Rupture of the membranous urethra is a classic complication of severe pelvic fractures. In the acute setting, the primary goal is to provide urinary diversion to prevent urine extravasation and infection while allowing the pelvic hematoma to stabilize.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents to the outpatient department with a 3 cm breast lump located in the upper medial quadrant. The mass has an irregular, bosselated surface with mild ulceration of the overlying skin. Histopathological examination shows the provided features. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The histological finding of hypercellular stroma arranged in "leaf-like" projections into epithelial-lined clefts is diagnostic of a Phyllodes tumor. These tumors typically present as large, rapidly growing masses with an uneven, bosselated (lobulated) surface. Ulceration of the overlying skin can occur in aggressive or malignant variants. A galactocele (Option B) is a cystic, milk-filled mass seen in lactating women, which is smooth and non-ulcerated. Fibroadenoma (Option C) is benign and well-defined but lacks the stromal hypercellularity and leaf-like growth pattern. Paget's disease (Option D) involves the nipple-areolar complex with eczematous changes and is associated with underlying ductal carcinoma. Management for Phyllodes tumors requires wide local excision with a margin of healthy tissue or mastectomy, as they have a high tendency for local recurrence

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Identify the correctly matched pair of substances with their renal clearance from the graph given below.

PAH - Para-aminohippurate
options: A - Glucose, B - PAH, C - Bicarbonate and D - Inulin
A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH
A - PAH, B - Inulin, C - Glucose and D - Bicarbonate
A - Inulin, B - Glucose, C - Bicarbonate and D - PAH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH

The correctly matched pair of substances and their renal clearance is A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH.

The concentration of the substance changes as it passes through the tubules. The tubular cells may remove the substance from the filtrate (tubular reabsorption) or add more of the substance to the filtrate (tubular secretion) or both. The amount of the substance finally excreted equals the amount filtered plus the net amount transferred out by the tubules.

PAH is filtered by the glomeruli and secreted by the tubular cells. Its concentration increases on moving through the length of the nephron due to secretion into tubules. It is represented by curve D.

Inulin is freely filtered by glomeruli and does not undergo any reabsorption or secretion. Hence, its concentration does not change throughout the length of the nephron and its excretion is constant and equal to the glomerular filtration rate. It is represented by curve C.

The majority of bicarbonate reabsorption occurs in the proximal tubule and a small amount of it flows into the distal tubules and collecting ducts. Its reabsorption occurs in all parts of the tubules, except the descending and ascending thin limbs of the loop of Henle. It is represented by curve B.

Substances like amino acids or glucose are reabsorbed along with sodium in the early portion of the proximal tubule. They have a graph that is sloping down as shown in curve A.
questions.learning: A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH The correctly matched pair of substances and their renal clearance is A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with an unruptured ectopic pregnancy confirmed on ultrasound. Medical management with methotrexate is being considered. Which of the following is a contraindication to methotrexate therapy in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cardiac activity +

Methotrexate is the preferred medical treatment for a hemodynamically stable, unruptured ectopic pregnancy. However, the presence of fetal cardiac activity is a relative contraindication because it is associated with a significantly lower success rate of medical management.

Ideal Candidates for Methotrexate

• Hemodynamically stable
• Unruptured ectopic pregnancy
• No fetal cardiac activity
• Adnexal mass <3.5–4 cm
• β-hCG <5,000 IU/L (best success with lower levels)
• Reliable for follow-up

Why not the other options?

• A. β-hCG 2200 IU/L: Suitable for methotrexate; success rates are high at this level.
• C. Sac size of 3 cm: Within the acceptable size for medical management.
• D. Primigravida: Not a contraindication to methotrexate.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with developmental delay, recurrent seizures, and history of thromboembolic episodes. On examination, he has marfanoid habitus, osteoporosis, and downward dislocation of the lens. Which of the following vitamin supplementation is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B6

The clinical picture describes homocystinuria (most commonly due to cystathionine β-synthase deficiency), an amino acid metabolism disorder.

• Intellectual disability (mental retardation)
• Seizures
• Thromboembolic tendency
• Osteoporosis / marfanoid habitus
• Ectopia lentis (downward displacement of lens)

Biochemical basis:

• Defect in conversion of homocysteine → cystathionine
• Leads to ↑ homocysteine and ↑ methionine

Treatment:

• Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is a cofactor for cystathionine β-synthase
• Some patients are B6-responsive, leading to ↓ homocysteine levels

Why not others:

• Vitamin B12: Involved in remethylation of homocysteine → methionine (different pathway)
• Thiamine (B1): Carbohydrate metabolism
• Vitamin B2: FAD-dependent reactions

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with loss of consciousness. A CT scan shows multiple small, spotty hemorrhages with preserved (full) basal cisterns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In the setting of a high-speed road traffic accident followed by immediate coma, Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) is a leading diagnosis (Option B). DAI is caused by shear forces that tear axons throughout the brain. The hallmark CT findings are multiple spotty (petechial) hemorrhages, typically located at the grey-white matter junction, in the corpus callosum, or in the brainstem. Brain contusions (Option A) are "bruises" typically found at the impact site (coup) or opposite site (contre-coup). A subdural hematoma (Option C) would appear as a crescent-shaped blood collection. Multiple infarcts (Option D) involve ischemic strokes and would not be the primary result of acute trauma. While CT may appear relatively "normal" compared to the patient's severe clinical state, the presence of these spotty hemorrhages in a comatose patient is highly diagnostic. Therefore, DAI represents the severe widespread traumatic injury described by these specific radiological cues
questions.learning: In the setting of a high-speed road traffic accident followed by immediate coma, Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) is a leading diagnosis (Option B). DAI is caused by shear forces that tear axons throughout the brain.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following half-lives and radioisotopes are correctly matched, except: (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Technetium-99m - 6 days

Technetium-99m has a half-life of 6 hours, not 6 days as incorrectly stated in option D. Tc-99m is a metastable nuclear isomer that loses roughly half of its radioactivity in that 6-hour timeframe. This short half-life makes it particularly useful for diagnostic nuclear medicine procedures since it decays quickly after imaging is complete, minimizing radiation exposure to patients.

The trapezius is a broad, flat and triangular muscle

• considering left or right side - triangular shape

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which amino acid plays a key role in the buffering capacity of blood at physiological pH?
questions.explanation: Histidine is the primary amino acid responsible for the buffering capacity of proteins at physiological pH (around 7.4). This unique property is due to its imidazole side chain, which has a pKa of approximately 6.0. Since this pKa is relatively close to physiological pH, the side chain can easily accept or donate protons, allowing histidine-rich proteins like hemoglobin to stabilize blood pH effectively. Methionine (Option A) is a sulfur-containing amino acid primarily involved in methylation. Alanine (Option B) is a key participant in glucose-alanine cycling between muscle and liver. Arginine (Option C) is highly basic (pKa ~12) and is involved in the urea cycle and nitric oxide production. The buffering action of histidine in hemoglobin is particularly important for the Bohr effect, where the protein picks up protons released during production in the tissues, helping to regulate oxygen release and maintain acid-base balance. This makes histidine a critical component for maintaining systemic pH homeostasis
questions.learning: Histidine is the primary amino acid responsible for the buffering capacity of proteins at physiological pH (around 7.4). This unique property is due to its imidazole side chain, which has a pKa of approximately 6.0.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the organism in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucor

Microscopy showing broad, aseptate, ribbon-like hyphae with irregular branching is suggestive of mucor.

Mucormycosis/ Zygomycosis is an opportunistic infection caused principally by species of rhizopus (most prevalent), mucor, and absidia. The common clinical form is rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis in which there is an invasion of the blood vessels in the nasal cavity, eyes, and brain causing thrombosis, infarction, and necrosis. The blackish discoloration is due to arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene.

Diagnosis can be made by staining them with 10% potassium hydroxide and culture. On Sabouraud agar at 30-37°C, they appear as grey-white colonies with a thick cottony, fluffy surface. Under the microscope, they appear as irregularly branched broad hyphae with aerial sporangiophores which end in a sac containing spores called sporangium.

Other options:

Options A and C: Aspergillus and Talaromyces (previously known as Penicillium) both demonstrate septate hyphae with conidiophores.

Option D: Blastomyces is a dimorphic fungus that exists in the yeast form in body tissues and cultures maintained at 37°C and in the filamentous mold form in cultures at room temperature (25°C). In the yeast form, it shows thick-walled round yeast cells with single broad-based budding, giving a figure of 8 appearance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with brief episodes of lancinating unilateral facial pain involving the buccal distribution. Pain is triggered by washing the face with cold water. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Trigeminal neuralgia

Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) is characterized by recurrent episodes of sudden, severe, electric shock-like or lancinating unilateral facial pain occurring in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve (CN V). The pain is typically triggered by innocuous stimuli, such as washing the face, brushing teeth, shaving, chewing, talking, or exposure to cold air or water.

The maxillary (V2) division is the most commonly affected, followed by the mandibular (V3) division.

Why not the other options?

• A. Migraine: Causes prolonged throbbing headache lasting 4–72 hours with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia, not brief facial pain.
• B. Medication overuse headache: Chronic daily headache due to excessive use of analgesics, not paroxysmal facial pain.
• C. Chronic paroxysmal hemicrania: Causes short unilateral headaches with autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, conjunctival injection), responds dramatically to indomethacin, and does not follow the trigeminal nerve distribution.
questions.learning: Trigeminal neuralgia Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) is characterized by recurrent episodes of sudden, severe, electric shock-like or lancinating unilateral facial pain occurring in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male patient came to the outpatient department with complaints of hematuria. A 2x2 cm bladder mass is seen which is a low-grade transitional cell carcinoma. Which among the following is the ideal management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transurethral resection of the tumour

This patient with low-grade 2x2 cm bladder cancer is likely to have non-muscle invasive bladder carcinoma (NMIBC) should undergo transurethral resection of the bladder tumor (TURBT) for accurate staging purposes.

Bladder cancer is graded (G1/2/3) based on level of differentiation. NMIBC includes stages Tis (in-situ), Ta (non-invasive papillary carcinoma), and T1 (invades lamina propria) while muscle invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) includes stages T2 (invades muscularis propria), T3 (invades perivesicular soft tissue), and T4 (invades adfjacent organs). NMIBC accounts for almost 70% of cases at presentation.

Treatment:

• NMIBC - The initial management of bladder tumors consists of transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) for accurate staging, which aids in determining the subsequent treatment plan. Intravesical therapy, involving chemotherapy (with mitomycin, doxorubicin, or epirubicin) or immunotherapy (BCG), is administered after TURBT to eradicate any remaining cancer cells. This therapy primarily targets the bladder lining and is not effective for cancers that have invaded deeper layers.
• MIBC - The standard treatment for muscle-invasive tumors is radical cystectomy and pelvic lymphadenectomy with urinary diversion (ileal conduit) (option B). Systemic adjuvant and neoadjuvant chemotherapy with M-VAC (Methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin, and cisplatin) has shown to be beneficial (option D).

Option C: Partial cystectomy can be attempted in patients with focal bladder cancer, but the risk of recurrence remains high.
questions.learning: Transurethral resection of the tumour — This patient with low-grade 2x2 cm bladder cancer is likely to have non-muscle invasive bladder carcinoma (NMIBC) should undergo transurethral resection of the bladder tumor (TURBT) for accurate staging purposes.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with hypertriglyceridemia. Which of the following drugs is most effective for lowering triglyceride levels?
questions.explanation: While statins are the best for reducing LDL, Fibrates (such as gemfibrozil or fenofibrate) are the most effective medications for reducing serum triglycerides (TG). They work by activating the Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor-alpha (PPAR-), which increases the expression of lipoprotein lipase and enhances the breakdown of TG-rich particles like VLDL. Fibrates can reduce TG levels by to . Niacin (Option B) also reduces TG but is generally less effective and less well-tolerated than fibrates. Statins (Option C) have only a modest effect on TG. Bile acid resins (Option D) can actually increase TG levels and should be avoided in patients with hypertriglyceridemia. Treating severe hypertriglyceridemia (typically ) is critical because extreme levels significantly increase the risk of acute pancreatitis. Patients on combined statin and fibrate therapy require careful monitoring due to an increased risk of muscle toxicity (myopathy)
questions.learning: While statins are the best for reducing LDL, Fibrates (such as gemfibrozil or fenofibrate) are the most effective medications for reducing serum triglycerides (TG).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was undertaken to estimate the effect of a drug ‘D’ in three different groups – Plants, Animals, and Human beings. Samples were chosen randomly out of the three groups individually. This is a type of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stratified random sampling

Stratified random sampling involves dividing the population into distinct subgroups (strata) based on a specific characteristic and then selecting samples randomly from each stratum.

Here, plants, animals, and humans form separate strata, and random samples are taken independently from each group.

This method ensures adequate representation of all subgroups and improves the precision of comparisons across strata.
questions.learning: Stratified random sampling Stratified random sampling involves dividing the population into distinct subgroups (strata) based on a specific characteristic and then selecting samples randomly from each stratum.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Contralateral hemiplegia

The structure marked in the image is the pyramid containing the pyramidal tracts. A lesion here leads to contralateral hemiplegia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Anaplasia refers to:
options: Variation in cell size and shape
Replacement of one type of cell by other
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lack of differentiation

Anaplasia refers to a lack of differentiation.

The term anaplasia means to form backward implying a reversal of differentiation to a more primitive level. The extent to which neoplastic cells resemble normal cells, both morphologically and functionally, is called differentiation.

Anaplasia is an important morphological feature of malignant transformation.

The morphological features of malignancy include:

• Anaplasia
• Pleomorphism - variation in the size and shape of cells
• Increased N: C ratio (nucleus: cytoplasmic ratio) - around 1:4 in normal cells, increases to 1:1 in malignant cells
• Hyperchromasia - coarsely clumped and darkly stained chromatin within irregular nuclei
• Increased mitosis - atypical, bizarre mitotic figures
• Loss of polarity - sheets or large masses of tumor cells grow in an anarchic, disorganized fashion
questions.learning: Lack of differentiation Anaplasia refers to a lack of differentiation. The term anaplasia means to form backward implying a reversal of differentiation to a more primitive level.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 21-year-old chronic alcoholic is brought to the emergency with confustion and tremors.On examination there is ataxia and ophthalmoplegia. Deficiency of which of the following is responsible for the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin B1

This patients clinical features are suggestive of Wernicke's encephalopathy. It is seen due to the deficiency of Thiamine/Vitamin B1. Thiamine is a cofactor for several important enzymes and also involved in the conduction of the axon potential and synaptic transmission.

Wernicke's encephalopathy/alcoholic encephalopathy is an acute neurological disorder. Glucose infusions may precipitate Wernicke’s disease in a previously unaffected patient or cause a rapid worsening of an early form of the disease (as in this patient). For this reason, thiamine should be administered to all alcoholic patients requiring parenteral glucose.

The triad is (GOA):

* Global Confusion

* Ophthalmoplegia (first symptom to improve with thiamine +dextrose infusion)

* Ataxia

Alcohol abuse leads to thiamine deficiency by the following mechanisms:

* Poor nutritional habits

* Folate deficiency which reduces thiamine absorption from the gastrointestinal tract

* Direct damage of the intestinal mucosa

Treatment:

It is a medical emergency and requires immediate administration of thiamine 100 mg IV or IM for 3 days followed by two to three times a day orally for 1 to 2 weeks.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents with headaches, visual disturbances, and hypertension. A cerebellar lesion is visible on MRI, and abdominal imaging reveals multiple cysts in the kidneys as well as a solid renal mass, which is suggestive of renal cell carcinoma. His father had similar findings and died of a brain tumour in his 40s. Which of the following chromosomal abnormalities is most likely to cause his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Deletion on chromosome 3p

The given clinical scenario of multiple renal cysts, cerebellar lesion, visual disturbances, and hypertension with a family history is most likely to be von Hippel-Lindau disease, which is characterized by deletion on chromosome 3p.

The tumor-suppressor gene VHL, which is linked to von Hippel-Lindau disease, is found on chromosome 3p. It produces a protein called VHL, which is a part of a ubiquitin ligase complex that inhibits hypoxia-induced factor 1 (HIF-1).

It is an autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by the development of highly vascularized tumors in multiple organs. These include:

* Hemangioblastomas of the retina and central nervous system

* Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors

* Pheochromocytoma

* Renal cysts develop into clear renal cell cancer

* Pancreatic cysts

* Ovary cystadenoma

* Epididymal cystadenoma

Those with VHL syndrome inherit an autosomal dominant germline mutation of the VHL gene on chromosome 3p. A "second hit" can lead to manifestations

The lesions most frequently linked to VHL disease are hemangioblastomas, which occur predominantly in the retina, cerebellum, or spinal cord.

Other options:
Option A: Deletion on chromosome 13q is associated with retinoblastoma.
Option C: Deletion on chromosome 17p is associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
Option D: Trisomy of chromosome 12 is seen in chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: With regard to Helicobacter pylori eradication in peptic ulcer disease, consider the following statements: 1. Proton-pump inhibitor is taken with two antibiotics. 2. Treatment is prescribed for at least 7 days. 3. Treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection leads to vitamin B12 deficiency. 4. Patients requiring long-term NSAIDs should undergo Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy to reduce ulcer risk. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy is recommended for patients with H. pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease to promote ulcer healing, prevent recurrence, and reduce the risk of complications.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Proton-pump inhibitor is taken with two antibiotics: Correct. Standard eradication therapy consists of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) combined with two antibiotics (e.g., clarithromycin with amoxicillin or metronidazole) or bismuth-based quadruple therapy.
• Statement 2. Treatment is prescribed for at least 7 days: Correct. Treatment is prescribed for at least 7 days, although 10–14 days (preferably 14 days) is currently recommended because of higher eradication rates.
• Statement 3. Treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection leads to vitamin B12 deficiency: Incorrect. H. pylori eradication does not cause vitamin B₁₂ deficiency. In fact, chronic H. pylori infection can lead to atrophic gastritis and impaired vitamin B₁₂ absorption, and eradication may improve B₁₂ status.
• Statement 4. Patients requiring long-term NSAIDs should undergo Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy to reduce ulcer risk: Correct. Patients who require long-term NSAID therapy should be tested for and treated for H. pylori infection, as eradication reduces the risk of NSAID-associated peptic ulcers.

Current first-line regimens:

• Bismuth quadruple therapy (preferred in many regions): PPI + Bismuth + Tetracycline + Metronidazole
• Concomitant therapy: PPI + Amoxicillin + Clarithromycin + Metronidazole
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy is recommended for patients with H. pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease to promote ulcer healing, prevent recurrence, and reduce the risk of complications.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless testicular swelling. Following orchidectomy, histopathological examination of the tumor demonstrates the presence of Reinke crystals within the tumor cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A Leydig cell tumor is a non-germ cell tumor of the testis. The pathognomonic histological finding is the presence of Reinke crystals—rod-shaped, eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic inclusions. These tumors are often hormonally active, secreting androgens or estrogens, which can lead to symptoms like precocious puberty in children or gynecomastia in adults. Sertoli cell tumors (Option A) typically show well-defined tubules but lack Reinke crystals. Seminoma (Option C) is the most common germ cell tumor, characterized by large, uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and a lymphocytic infiltrate. Yolk sac tumors (Option D) are common in infants and show characteristic Schiller-Duval bodies. Most Leydig cell tumors are benign, but approximately 10% are malignant. They typically present as a painless, firm testicular mass. Surgical orchidectomy is the standard treatment. Identifying Reinke crystals is a favorite "trigger" in medical exams for specifically naming the Leydig cell tumor, differentiating it from the more common germ cell malignancies
questions.learning: A Leydig cell tumor is a non-germ cell tumor of the testis. The pathognomonic histological finding is the presence of Reinke crystals—rod-shaped, eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic inclusions.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A full-term baby born with birth weight of 2000 g comes for well-baby visit at two months of age. Which of the following nutritional supplements would you advise?
options: Vitamin D orally 200 IU/day up to 3 months of age
Vitamin D orally 200 IU/day up to 1 year of age
Iron orally 2 mg/kg/day up to 3 months of age
Iron orally 2 mg/kg/day up to 1 year of age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Iron orally 2 mg/kg/day up to 1 year of age

Low birth weight (LBW) infants (<2500 g) are at increased risk of iron deficiency due to lower iron stores at birth. Term LBW infants should receive oral iron supplementation (2 mg/kg/day) starting at 2 months of age and continued up to 1 year of age to prevent iron deficiency anemia.

Why not the other options?

• A. Vitamin D orally 200 IU/day up to 3 months of age & B. Vitamin D orally 200 IU/day up to 1 year of age: Vitamin D supplementation is recommended at 400 IU/day, not 200 IU/day.
• C. Iron orally 2 mg/kg/day up to 3 months of age: Iron should be continued up to 1 year, not stopped at 3 months.
questions.learning: Iron orally 2 mg/kg/day up to 1 year of age Low birth weight (LBW) infants (<2500 g) are at increased risk of iron deficiency due to lower iron stores at birth.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following vaccines is not recommended after 65 years?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Human papilloma virus

Human papillomavirus vaccine is not recommended after 65 years.

In otherwise healthy elderly patients, the recommended vaccines are:

• Inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccine, 1 dose annually
• Td or Tdap booster, every 10 years
• Zoster recombinant vaccine
• Pneumococcal vaccine
• COVID-19 vaccine

The zoster recombinant vaccine is not indicated for the prevention of varicella. This vaccine is given to prevent episodes of herpes zoster and post-herpetic neuralgia. It is indicated regardless of a previous episode of Zoster.

All adults ≥65 years of age should also receive pneumococcal vaccination. This is in the form of pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) first, followed by pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) after an interval.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which trimester is the quadruple test performed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2nd trimester

Quadruple screening is a second-trimester multiple marker screening test for the detection of chromosomal anomalies like trisomy 21-Down syndrome.

Pregnancies with Down syndrome are characterized by elevated β-hCG, Inhibin and lower estriol, AFP levels.  It is performed from 15 to 21 weeks of gestation.

The triple test findings in pregnancies with fetal Down’s syndrome are characterized by:

* Low MSAFP (maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein) levels, approximately 0.7 MoM (multiples of median).

* Low unconjugated estriol levels, approximately 0.8 MoM.

* High hCG levels, approximately 2.0 MoM.

The triple test is done between 15-18 weeks for the diagnosis of Down's syndrome.

Various antenatal screening tests for aneuploidy are as follows:

Dual test (1st trimester)
Triple test (2nd trimester)
Quadruple test (2nd trimester)

Beta HCG
Beta HCG
Beta HCG

PAPPA
Unconjugated estriol
Unconjugated estriol

This can be combined with nuchal translucency by USG
MSAFP
MSAFP

Serum inhibin A

First-trimester screening with biochemical analytes (↓) PAPP-A and (↑) hCG and USG measurement of NT (↑) can improve the detection rate (87%) of Down’s syndrome. For confirmation, a prenatal genetic study (CVS, amniocentesis or cordocentesis) has to be performed.

Second-trimester screening (quad screening) at 15–18 weeks: (↓) MSAFP, (↓) uE3, (↑) inhibin A and (↑) hCG can detect trisomy 21 in 85% of cases with a false-positive rate of 0.9%. When it is combined with first-trimester screening, the detection rate is increased to 95%.
questions.learning: 2nd trimester Quadruple screening is a second-trimester multiple marker screening test for the detection of chromosomal anomalies like trisomy 21-Down syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents with generalized muscle weakness and proptosis, which worsen as the day progresses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The hallmark of Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with activity and as the day progresses, with significant improvement after rest. In a 16-year-old girl, the presentation of ptosis (which may be mistaken for eyelid protrusion or proptosis in some descriptions) and ocular muscle involvement is highly suggestive of MG. Fibromyalgia (Option B) involves widespread chronic pain and tender points but does not cause objective, fatigue-related muscle weakness or eyelid changes. Myotonic Dystrophy (Option C) is characterized by delayed muscle relaxation (myotonia) and progressive wasting, but its weakness is not typically diurnal or rapidly fluctuating with rest. Guillain-Barré Syndrome (Option D) is an acute inflammatory polyneuropathy presenting as a rapid, symmetrical ascending paralysis, usually following a viral infection, and is not a chronic fluctuating condition. Diagnosis of MG is supported by electrophysiological testing and the detection of acetylcholine receptor antibodies
questions.learning: The hallmark of Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with activity and as the day progresses, with significant improvement after rest.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which condition is characterized by a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio and FEV1 as a percentage of the predicted value, along with morning wheezing and shortness of breath?
questions.explanation: The spirometric finding of an FEV1/FVC ratio is the hallmark of an obstructive lung disease. Among the options, Asthma (Option A) is the only obstructive condition. Asthma characteristically presents with episodic shortness of breath and wheezing, which is often worse in the morning or at night. Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD) (Option B), Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) (Option C), and Silicosis (Option D) are all restrictive lung diseases. Restrictive diseases are characterized by a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio and reduced lung volumes (Total Lung Capacity). COPD also shows an obstructive ratio, but the reversible nature and morning symptoms in a potentially younger patient favor asthma. Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating bronchodilator reversibility (an increase in FEV1 by ). Identifying the "obstructive" vs. "restrictive" patterns is the first and most vital step in interpreting pulmonary function tests
questions.learning: The spirometric finding of an FEV1/FVC ratio is the hallmark of an obstructive lung disease. Among the options, Asthma (Option A) is the only obstructive condition.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the ANMOL program for auxiliary nurse midwives?
questions.explanation: ANMOL (ANM Online) is a revolutionary digital initiative by the Government of India designed to empower Auxiliary Nurse Midwives (ANMs). It is a tablet-based software application that allows ANMs to enter and update beneficiary data in real-time, even in remote areas. The primary goal is to improve the quality of data collection, tracking of pregnant women and children, and the delivery of essential maternal and child health services. By replacing manual registers with digital tablets, ANMOL reduces the administrative burden and ensures that data is readily available for monitoring and decision-making at higher levels. Options B, C, and D are not the delivery mechanisms for this specific program. The application provides alerts for upcoming immunizations or antenatal check-ups, facilitating more personalized and timely care. This transition to digital health is a cornerstone of India's efforts to reach universal health coverage and achieve Sustainable Development Goal targets for neonatal and maternal health

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All of the following are included under diagnostic criteria of severe acute malnutrition except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Height for age

Height for age is not a diagnostic criterion of severe acute malnutrition.

Criteria for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in a 6-month-old child are mid-upper arm circumference, symmetrical pedal edema , and weight for height. Height for age is not the criteria for the diagnosis of severe acute malnutrition.

The presence of any of the following confers severe acute malnutrition in children 6 to 59 months of age:

1. Weight-for-height below -3 standard deviation (<-3SD) on the WHO Growth Standard (Option B)
2. Presence of bipedal edema  (Option C)
3. Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) below 11.5 cm (Option D)

Once the child is diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition, the doctor must assess for the following complications:

1. Severe edema (+++)
2. Low appetite (failed appetite test)
3. Medical complications (severe anemia, pneumonia, diarrhea, dehydration, cerebral palsy, tuberculosis, HIV, heart disease, etc.)
One or more danger signs as per IMNCI

If any of the complications are present, the child is diagnosed with complicated SAM and is managed inpatient in the facility.

If the above-mentioned signs are absent, the child is diagnosed with uncomplicated SAM and supervised management at home is given.
questions.learning: Height for age Height for age is not a diagnostic criterion of severe acute malnutrition. Criteria for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in a 6-month-old child are mid-upper arm circumference, symmetrical pedal edema , and weight for height.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the following image:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ranula

The given scenario and the image of a cystic swelling on the floor of the mouth are suggestive of a ranula.

Ranula is a mucus extravasation cyst arising from the sublingual gland. It produces a characteristic translucent swelling that gives the appearance of a frog’s belly. A ranula usually resolves spontaneously.

A plunging ranula is a mucus retention cyst. It has mucus collecting below the gland and perforating through the mylohyoid muscle.

Treatment should include removal of the sublingual gland as this gland has multiple ducts and ranulas can recur if the gland is left behind. Incision, drainage and marsupialisation have low success rates.

Other options:

Options A: Hemangioma is the most common vascular tumor and is characterized by increased abnormal proliferation of endothelium. Hemangiomas develop in infancy and are usually not visible at birth. They appear red or maroon if superficial, and bluish if deep.

Option B: Cystic hygroma is usually seen in neonates and early childhood. They are cystic swellings filled with lymph fluid and are characteristically brilliantly translucent. They occur in the neck and can involve the parotid, submandibular, tongue, etc. The swelling is soft and partially compressible. Definitive treatment is the excision of the swelling.

Option C: The branchial cyst develops from the vestigial remnants of the second branchial cleft. Swelling in the neck beneath the anterior border of the upper third of the sternomastoid muscle. It is smooth, soft, fluctuant, and often transilluminate. The below image shows a large right-sided branchial cyst.
questions.learning: Ranula — The given scenario and the image of a cystic swelling on the floor of the mouth are suggestive of a ranula. Ranula is a mucus extravasation cyst arising from the sublingual gland.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Opening of Bartholin’s duct is in the:
options: Vestibule outside the hymen at the junction of the anterior 2/3rd and posterior 1/3rd in the groove between the hymen and labium minus
Groove between labia majora and labia minora
Superficial perineal pouch at the junction of anterior 1/3rd and posterior 1/3rd
Periurethral region in anterior 1/3rd of labia minora
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vestibule outside the hymen at the junction of the anterior 2/3rd and posterior 1/3rd in the groove between the hymen and labium minus

The Bartholin’s glands (greater vestibular glands) are paired mucus-secreting glands located in the superficial perineal pouch, posterolateral to the vaginal opening. The Bartholin’s duct opens into the vestibule, outside the hymenal ring, at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third in the groove between the hymen and the labium minus. Clinically, this corresponds approximately to the 4 o’clock and 8 o’clock positions of the vaginal introitus.

Why not the other options?

• B. Groove between labia majora and labia minora: This is not the site of the duct opening.
• C. Superficial perineal pouch at the junction of anterior 1/3rd and posterior 1/3rd: The gland lies in the superficial perineal pouch, but the duct opens into the vestibule, not the pouch.
• D. Periurethral region in anterior 1/3rd of labia minora: This describes the location of the Skene’s (paraurethral) glands, not the Bartholin’s glands.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following carries the lowest risk of developing invasive ductal carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Breast lesions are categorized by their risk of malignant transformation. Squamous metaplasia (Option D) of the lactiferous ducts is a benign, reactive change often associated with inflammation or abscesses; it carries no increased risk (lowest risk) for the development of invasive ductal carcinoma. In contrast, florid epithelial hyperplasia (Option A) and intraductal papilloma (Option B) are proliferative lesions that carry a mildly increased risk (roughly 1.5 to 2 times baseline). Atypical hyperplasia (Option C), whether ductal or lobular, is a high-risk precursor lesion carrying a significantly elevated risk (4 to 5 times baseline) of progressing to invasive cancer. Understanding this hierarchy is essential for managing patients with benign breast disease. While metaplasia sounds complex, it is essentially a structural adaptation to irritation and lacks the proliferative or atypical characteristics that drive oncogenesis. Therefore, squamous metaplasia is the correct choice for the lesion with minimal oncogenic potential

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following substances is not considered a micromineral?
questions.explanation: Minerals are divided into macrominerals and microminerals (trace elements) based on the body's daily requirement. Macrominerals are required in amounts greater than 100 mg per day. Calcium is a macromineral (Option A); it is the most abundant mineral in the body, essential for bone structure, muscle contraction, and nerve signaling. Other macrominerals include phosphorus, magnesium, sodium, and potassium. Microminerals (trace elements) are needed in minute amounts, typically less than 15-20 mg per day. Selenium (Option B), iodine (Option C), and copper (Option D) are all classified as microminerals. Iodine is crucial for thyroid hormone synthesis, while selenium and copper act as essential cofactors for various enzymes. Because the body requires significant daily intake of calcium (often 1000 mg or more), it is not a trace element. Therefore, Calcium is the correct answer to this "not" question
questions.learning: Minerals are divided into macrominerals and microminerals (trace elements) based on the body's daily requirement. Macrominerals are required in amounts greater than 100 mg per day.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old male was brought dead to the emergency after hanging. There was a dry, hard, parchment-like ligature mark 1.5 cm wide in the anterior middle third of the neck; the mark was directed posteriorly, upwards and laterally. The left eye was closed, while the right was open, and saliva drooling of saliva was present on the right side. Compression of which of the following structures explains the right eye opening?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cervical sympathetic chain

In hanging, characteristic findings include asymmetry of eye opening and salivary dribbling, which help determine the side of compression.

• Compression of the cervical sympathetic chain → loss of sympathetic supply on that side
• Leads to features of Horner’s syndrome:

• Ptosis (eye closed)
• Miosis
• Anhidrosis

Application to the case:

• Left eye closed → left sympathetic chain compressed
• Right eye open → right sympathetic chain intact
• Saliva dribbling on right side → indicates oblique ligature mark with pressure asymmetry

Why not others:

• ICA: Cerebral ischemia, not eye-opening changes
• IJV: Venous congestion, cyanosis
• Vagus nerve: Affects heart rate/voice, not eyelid position

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Excess ammonia reduces which of the following substrates of the Krebs cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Alpha ketoglutarate

Excess ammonia results in depletion of levels of alpha-ketoglutarate.

This happens because excess ammonia reacts with alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate, mainly in the CNS.
questions.learning: Alpha ketoglutarate Excess ammonia results in depletion of levels of alpha-ketoglutarate. This happens because excess ammonia reacts with alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate, mainly in the CNS.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following is not part of STEP approach by WHO?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Blood grouping

STEP approach doesn't include blood grouping.

STEP approach of WHO is a survey methodology developed to assess risk factors of non-communicable diseases(NCD). It helps the countries to establish an NCD surveillance system. The steps include the following:

* Questionnaires about behavioral risk factors like tobacco use, alcohol use, diet, and physical activity.

* Physical measurements via blood pressure (Option A), height, weight, and waist size

* Biochemical measurements via blood glucose, blood lipid profile (options C and D ), urinary sodium, and creatinine.
questions.learning: Blood grouping STEP approach doesn't include blood grouping. STEP approach of WHO is a survey methodology developed to assess risk factors of non-communicable diseases(NCD).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What do chaperones assist in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Protein folding

Chaperones assist in protein folding. They are a type of heat-shock protein weighing 70 kDa (hsp70).

Mechanism of action:

* They bind to the short sequences of hydrophobic amino acids of an extended polypeptide.

* They effectively shield the new polypeptide being synthesized from aggregating, so as to provide them an opportunity to form an appropriate secondary structure.

* In instances where a protein is thermodynamically trapped in a misfolded dead-end form, the chaperones can rescue the protein by unfolding these hydrophobic ends, providing the protein a second chance to fold productively.
questions.learning: Protein folding Chaperones assist in protein folding. They are a type of heat-shock protein weighing 70 kDa (hsp70).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organism is intrinsically resistant to the given drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Candida krusei: Fluconazole

Candida krusei is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole due to altered ergosterol pathway enzymes and reduced drug affinity. This resistance is predictable and clinically important. Other listed organisms are generally susceptible to their respective drugs. Fluconazole resistance is a classic hallmark of C. krusei.

| Drug | Mechanism

| ---- | ---------

| Fluconazole | ↓ Ergosterol synthesis

| Amphotericin B | Pore formation

| Micafungin | ↓ β-glucan (cell wall)

| Voriconazole | Ergosterol inhibition

Candida krusei = resistant to fluconazole

Candida glabrata = dose-dependent sensitivity

Voriconazole = DOC for Aspergillus

Amphotericin B = broad-spectrum
questions.learning: Candida krusei: Fluconazole Candida krusei is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole due to altered ergosterol pathway enzymes and reduced drug affinity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old destitute is brought to the emergency with a foul-smelling wound on his left foot. On examination, the wound is seen to have maggots with a lot of necrotic tissue. What is the class of this wound according to the CDC wound classification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Class 4

According to the CDC wound classification, wounds are classified into four classes:

1. Class 1 – Clean: Uninfected wound; no inflammation; respiratory, gastrointestinal, genital, or urinary tract not entered.
2. Class 2 – Clean-contaminated: Controlled entry into respiratory, gastrointestinal, genital, or urinary tract without unusual contamination.
3. Class 3 – Contaminated: Open, fresh accidental wounds, major breaks in sterile technique, or gross spillage from the GI tract.
4. Class 4 – Dirty/Infected: Old traumatic wounds with devitalized tissue or wounds with existing infection/pus/perforation.

This patient’s foul-smelling wound with maggots and extensive necrotic tissue represents a dirty/infected wound → Class 4.
questions.learning: Class 4 According to the CDC wound classification, wounds are classified into four classes: 1. Class 1 – Clean: Uninfected wound; no inflammation; respiratory, gastrointestinal, genital, or urinary tract not entered.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female came to OPD with complaints of backache. On examination, Schober test was positive and her eyes and nose were hyperpigmented. Probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ochronosis

Given X-ray shows intervertebral disc calcification and hyperpigmentation of nose and eyes are present. Both features are indicative of ochronosis as diagnosis.

• Ochronosis also known as alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder.
• It is due to deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase leading to accumulation of homogentisic acid.

• Clinical features: Triad of

• Homogentisic aciduria (urine turns dark color on standing due to oxidation or alkalinisation)
• Eumelanin like pigmentation of skin, sclera, cartilages etc.
• Degenerative chronic arthropathies especially of spine, hip, knees.

Option a: Hypoparathyroidism doesn't explain hyperpigmentation and other clinical features of hypoparathyroidism aren't mentioned.

Option b: Fluorosis - dental symptoms are not mentioned and osteoporosis will be marked in case of fluorosis. Also, hyperpigmentation is not a typical feature of fluorosis.

Option d: Ankylosing spondylitis – females are unlikely to be affected and it doesn’t explain hyperpigmentation.
