questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old primigravida with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy undergoes vaginal delivery. The first twin is delivered cephalically without complications. Ultrasound immediately after delivery confirms that the second twin is in breech presentation, fetal heart rate is reassuring, membranes are intact, and the cervix is fully dilated. What is the preferred method of delivery for the second twin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Assisted breech delivery

When the first twin is delivered cephalically, vaginal delivery is appropriate regardless of the presentation of the second twin, provided there are no contraindications. If the second twin is breech, assisted breech delivery is the preferred technique. The breech is allowed to descend spontaneously until the umbilicus is visible ("hands off the breech"), after which maneuvers such as Lovset (for the arms) and Burns–Marshall or Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit (for the after-coming head) are used.

Why not the other options?

• A. Lower segment cesarean section (LSCS ) – Not routinely required. Combined vaginal–cesarean delivery has higher maternal morbidity and is reserved for failed vaginal delivery or fetal compromise.
• B. Internal podalic version (IPV) – Indicated for a transverse or oblique lie of the second twin, not for a fetus already presenting by the breech.
• C. Breech extraction – Involves immediate traction on the fetal feet from the outset and is reserved for selected situations such as fetal distress or after internal podalic version, not for a spontaneously descending breech.

High-Yield Pearl:

Second twin breech with full cervical dilatation:

• Assisted breech delivery = Wait, then assist.
• Breech extraction = Pull from the start.
questions.learning: Assisted breech delivery When the first twin is delivered cephalically, vaginal delivery is appropriate regardless of the presentation of the second twin, provided there are no contraindications.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In evaluating occupational health hazards related to long-term asbestos exposure, which type of cancer is most strongly associated with asbestos, particularly among workers in industries such as construction, shipbuilding, and automotive repair?
questions.explanation: Mesothelioma is an aggressive and rare form of cancer that develops in the mesothelium, the thin protective lining covering most internal organs. The strongest and most well-documented risk factor for mesothelioma is exposure to asbestos fibers. When asbestos is disturbed, it releases microscopic fibers that can be inhaled or swallowed, eventually lodging in the pleura (the lining of the lungs) or peritoneum (the lining of the abdomen). These fibers cause chronic inflammation and genetic damage, leading to malignant transformation, often with a long latency period of 20 to 50 years. While asbestos also increases the risk of bronchogenic carcinoma (lung cancer), mesothelioma is the most specific and notable occupational cancer associated with it. Acute myeloid leukemia (Option B) is linked to benzene or radiation. Hepatic angiosarcoma (Option C) is classically associated with vinyl chloride exposure. Skin carcinoma (Option D) is primarily caused by UV radiation or arsenic. Thus, for workers in construction or shipbuilding, mesothelioma remains the hallmark malignancy of asbestos exposure
questions.learning: Mesothelioma is an aggressive and rare form of cancer that develops in the mesothelium, the thin protective lining covering most internal organs. The strongest and most well-documented risk factor for mesothelioma is exposure to asbestos fibers.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In the anteroposterior diameters of the pelvic inlet, the true conjugate is:
options: The distance from the midpoint of the sacral promontory to the uppermost margin of the symphysis pubis
The shortest distance between the sacral promontory and the symphysis pubis
The distance from the lowest margin of the symphysis to the sacral promontory
The distance from the posterior margin of the sacral promontory to the symphysis pubis
questions.explanation: The True Conjugate (Anatomical Conjugate) is defined as the distance between the midpoint of the sacral promontory and the uppermost margin (superior border) of the symphysis pubis. It normally measures about 11 cm. Obstetric conjugate (Option B) is the shortest distance between the sacral promontory and the posterior surface of the symphysis (approximately 10 cm); this is the most clinically important diameter for labor. Diagonal conjugate (Option C) is the distance from the lowest margin (inferior border) of the symphysis to the sacral promontory (approximately 12.5 cm); it is the only AP diameter that can be measured during a digital vaginal examination. Option D provides a description that does not match standard anatomical nomenclature for pelvic conjugates. Precise knowledge of these diameters is essential for identifying cephalopelvic disproportion. Therefore, the measurement to the superior border defines the true conjugate
questions.learning: The True Conjugate (Anatomical Conjugate) is defined as the distance between the midpoint of the sacral promontory and the uppermost margin (superior border) of the symphysis pubis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 53 year old man is found to have stage 2 hypertension without any co morbidities. Which drug will you start?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chlorthalidone

Chlorthalidone is one of the first choice drugs in the treatment of hypertension without any comorbidities.

First-choice drugs used in the treatment of hypertension in patients without any comorbidities include:

• Thiazide diuretics: Chlorthalidone is usually preferred to hydrochlorothiazide.
• Calcium channel blockers: Extended-release, long-acting dihydropyridines are preferred.
• ACE inhibitors: Captopril is preferred for the initiation of therapy. Enalapril and ramipril twice daily may also be used.

In the presence of any associated conditions or comorbidities, the first choice drugs for the treatment of hypertension would be as follows:

Conditions associated with hypertension

First choice drugs for hypertension

Diabetes

Chronic kidney disease with proteinuria

Inhibitors of renin-angiotensin system.

Angina

Beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers

Heart failure

ACE inhibitors and alpha+beta blockers such as carvedilol

Benign prostatic hyperplasia

α1 Blockers

Pregnancy

Labetalol

Atrial fibrillation

Diltiazem and verapamil

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Neuropraxia is a type of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Physiological conduction block

Neuropraxia is the mildest form of peripheral nerve injury (Seddon classification) and is characterized by a transient physiological conduction block without structural disruption of the axon or connective tissue. Recovery is complete and spontaneous, usually within days to weeks.

• Neuropraxia results in a temporary conduction block due to focal demyelination.
• The axon, endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium remain intact, allowing complete recovery.

Why not the other options?

• A. Endoneurium disruption: Seen in axonotmesis or more severe nerve injuries, not neuropraxia.
• B. Nerve trunk damage: Refers to severe nerve injury, typically neurotmesis.
• D. Axonal discontinuity: Characteristic of axonotmesis and neurotmesis, not neuropraxia.
questions.learning: Physiological conduction block Neuropraxia is the mildest form of peripheral nerve injury (Seddon classification) and is characterized by a transient physiological conduction block without structural disruption of the axon or connective tissue.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient with known hyperthyroidism who is not receiving treatment is scheduled for a total thyroidectomy. Pre-anesthetic evaluation has been inadequately performed. What is the most serious complication that is most likely to occur during surgery?
options: Hypothyroidism (C) Arrhythmia In a patient with uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, the body is in a hypermetabolic state with significantly increased sensitivity to catecholamines. Surgical stress or manipulation of the thyroid gland can precipitate a life-threatening "thyroid storm" (thyrotoxic crisis). The most immediate and dangerous intraoperative manifestation of this crisis is severe cardiac arrhythmia, such as atrial fibrillation or supraventricular tachycardia. While hyperthermia (Option A) is a classic sign of thyroid storm, arrhythmias pose a more acute threat to hemodynamic stability during the procedure. Hypothermia (Option B) is generally associated with prolonged surgery in cold environments, not thyrotoxicosis. Hypothyroidism (Option D) is an expected long-term consequence of a total thyroidectomy but would not occur as an acute intraoperative complication. Therefore, managing heart rate and rhythm via preoperative beta-blockade and antithyroid medications is essential to prevent these intraoperative cardiac emergencies.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: For a child with myopia, presenting with symptoms such as holding books close and squinting while watching TV, which type of lenses is recommended to correct his vision?
questions.explanation: Myopia, or nearsightedness, is a refractive error where the eye is too powerful or too long, causing light rays to focus in front of the retina rather than directly on it. This results in clear near vision but blurred distance vision, explaining the child's behavior. To correct myopia, concave (minus) lenses (Option B) are required. These are "diverging" lenses that move the focal point backward, precisely positioning it onto the retinal surface. Convex (plus) lenses (Option A) are "converging" lenses used to correct hypermetropia (farsightedness). Cylindrical lenses (Option C) are used to correct astigmatism by compensating for an irregular corneal shape. A combination of concave and convex (Option D) refers to bifocal or complex multifocal lenses which are not the standard primary correction for simple childhood myopia. Therefore, the concave lens is the definitive pharmacological and physical corrective tool for a nearsighted child
questions.learning: Myopia, or nearsightedness, is a refractive error where the eye is too powerful or too long, causing light rays to focus in front of the retina rather than directly on it.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young boxer receives a blow near the eye during a boxing match. He presents to the ER with hematoma around eye, CT scan is shown below. Identify the radiological sign shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tear-drop sign

The given CT image dipicts 'tear-drop' sign and suggests a blowout fracture.

Tear-drop/ hanging drop sign is characteristic of an orbital "blow-out" fracture, which represents the orbital contents herniating through the floor of the orbit into the maxillary antrum. The most useful projection for detecting an orbital floor fracture is Water’s view.

An orbital blow-out fracture is an isolated fracture of the orbital floor when a large blunt object strikes the globe is called blow out fracture. The orbital contents herniate through the antrum. Clinical signs are periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis and subconjunctival haemorrhage (later stages).

Initial treatment consists of observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, and nasal decongestants. Indications for surgery in a blowout fracture include diplopia not resolving significantly in the early days after trauma, a fracture with a large herniation of tissues into the antrum, incarceration of tissues in the fracture, resulting in globe retraction and increased applanation tension on attempted upward gaze and enophthalmos. If any of these conditions are present, surgical correction is required within 2 weeks.

The below-given X-ray image in the Water's view shows a 'tear-drop' sign

The optimal time for surgery following a blow-out fracture is 10–14 days.

Indications for surgery in a "blow-out" fracture are as follows:

* Diplopia not resolving significantly in the early days after trauma

* A fracture with a large herniation of tissues into the antrum

* Incarceration of tissues in the fracture, resulting in  globe  retraction and increased applanation tension on attempted upward gaze

* Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

Other options:

Option A: Panda sign: A radiological finding in sarcoidosis showing bilateral symmetrical uptake in the lacrimal and parotid glands on gallium scan, creating an appearance resembling a panda's face.

Option B: Dalrymple’s sign is the commonest and earliest sign of Grave's ophthalmopathy. It is due to overactivity of levator aponeurosis and Müller's muscle. Here the upper lid margin is at level with or above the superior limbus, causing the upper sclera to become visible (scleral show).

Option C: Munson's sign is seen in keratoconus. There is a localized bulging of the lower eyelid that can be seen in a downward-looking eye.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A pediatric patient presents with respiratory distress following a suspected foreign body inhalation. To precisely localize and potentially retrieve the object, which diagnostic procedure should be initiated first?
questions.explanation: In a stable pediatric patient with a suspected foreign body inhalation, a Chest X-ray is the essential first-line investigation. While only about 10–15% of foreign bodies are radio-opaque (e.g., coins or pins), the X-ray often reveals critical indirect signs of an airway obstruction, such as localized air trapping (emphysema), atelectasis, or a mediastinal shift. These signs help the clinician localize the object to a specific bronchus. Rigid bronchoscopy (Option A) is the gold standard for definitive management and retrieval but is an invasive procedure requiring general anesthesia; it is performed after imaging supports the diagnosis. Direct laryngoscopy (Option C) only visualizes the larynx and is not suitable for bronchial objects. Flexible endoscopy (Option D) is less useful for retrieval in children compared to the rigid type. Therefore, unless the child is in extremis and requires immediate life-saving intervention, the X-ray is the standard initial diagnostic step

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A female presents with loss of vision in the right halves of both eyes. Where is the lesion located in the optic pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left optic tract

Visual loss in the right halves of both eyes is suggestive of right homonymous hemianopia. The site of the lesion in this case is the left optic tract.

Here, vision is lost in the right half of both eyes, which means:

• in the left eye, the nasal visual field is lost, and
• in the right eye, the temporal visual field is lost.

It means left temporal and right nasal fibers are destroyed, which leads to right homonymous hemianopia. Anatomically, this can be explained by the fact that each optic tract contains fibers from the ipsilateral temporal half of the retina and the contralateral nasal half of the retina.

Optic tract lesions can occur due to pituitary adenomas (most common), craniopharyngioma, tumors of the optic thalamus, large aneurysm of superior cerebellar or posterior cerebral arteries, demyelinating diseases, and infarction.

Other options:

Option B: Optic radiation lesions result in contralateral homonymous hemianopia, which means that the visual loss would occur in the left halves of both eyes rather than the right halves, as described in the question.

Option C: Lesions at the optic chiasma typically cause bitemporal hemianopia, which involves visual loss in the outer (temporal) halves of the visual field in both eyes. This is not consistent with the patient's described symptoms.

Option D: A lesion in the right optic tract would result in left homonymous hemianopia, causing visual loss in the left halves of both eyes. This does not match the patient's presentation of vision loss in the right halves of both eyes.
questions.learning: Left optic tract Visual loss in the right halves of both eyes is suggestive of right homonymous hemianopia. The site of the lesion in this case is the left optic tract.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with tuberculosis does not respond to treatment with isoniazid, rifampicin, ofloxacin, and kanamycin. What type of drug resistance is indicated in this case?
questions.explanation: The definition of drug-resistant tuberculosis is based on specific patterns of resistance. Extensively Drug-Resistant TB (XDR-TB) is defined as resistance to Isoniazid and Rifampicin (which defines MDR-TB), plus resistance to any fluoroquinolone (such as Ofloxacin) and at least one of the three injectable second-line drugs (such as Kanamycin, Amikacin, or Capreomycin). Since this patient is unresponsive to all four classes mentioned (INH, Rifampicin, a fluoroquinolone, and an injectable), they definitively meet the criteria for XDR-TB. Multidrug-resistant TB (Option A) only requires resistance to INH and Rifampicin. Rifampicin-resistant TB (Option C) is a narrower category. "Extremely" drug-resistant (Option D) is not a standard WHO classification term. XDR-TB represents a severe public health threat because it leaves very few effective treatment options remaining

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A young man with a known psychiatric illness becomes extremely aggressive after stopping his prescribed medication. He exhibits rapid, pressured speech, marked hyperactivity, and a decreased need for sleep. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's clinical triad of rapid speech (pressured speech), decreased need for sleep, and hyperactivity/aggression is diagnostic of a manic episode. Manic episodes are core features of Bipolar I Disorder and are often triggered or exacerbated by the discontinuation of mood stabilizers or antipsychotic medications. Depression (Option A) presents with the opposite symptoms, such as low energy and slowed movement. While schizophrenia (Option C) can involve disorganized behavior, it is primarily defined by chronic delusions and hallucinations rather than the episodic energy surges seen here. A substance-induced mood disorder (Option D) could mimic these symptoms, but there is no history of drug use provided, and the worsening after stopping "prescribed medication" points toward a relapse of a primary mood disorder. Thus, a manic episode is the most probable diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient's clinical triad of rapid speech (pressured speech), decreased need for sleep, and hyperactivity/aggression is diagnostic of a manic episode.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 65-year-old male, with a known case of coronary artery disease, presented for a general check-up. On examination, vital signs are normal. He has notable long limbs. Blood glucose concentration is 100 mg/dL and homocysteine concentration is 20 μmol/L. Serum lipid levels are normal. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient? Normal homocysteine concentration in blood = 5-15 μmol/L.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystathionine β-synthase

This patient with long limbs, coronary artery disease and elevated homocysteine concentration most likely has homocystinuria, and the enzyme deficiency in this condition is cystathionine β synthase.

Homocystinuria is most commonly caused by a defect in the cystathionine β synthase enzyme leading to the accumulation of homocysteine in urine and blood. They are generally normal at birth and the first sign is subluxation of the lens (ectopia lentis) seen after 3 years of age.

Manifestations of homocystinuria:

* Ectopia lentis.

* Intellectual disability and psychiatric and behavioral disorders.

* Thromboembolic episodes.

* Skeletal abnormalities resembling those of Marfan syndrome: They are tall and thin with elongated limbs and arachnodactyly.

Elevations of both methionine and homocysteine in body fluids are the diagnostic lab findings.

Other Options:

*

Deficiency of homogentisate oxidase is associated with alkaptonuria.

*

Deficiency of Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRTase) is responsible for Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

Pearl PF0079: Homocystinuria
questions.learning: Cystathionine β-synthase — This patient with long limbs, coronary artery disease and elevated homocysteine concentration most likely has homocystinuria, and the enzyme deficiency in this condition is cystathionine β synthase.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which intracellular organelle is mainly responsible for breaking down and eliminating bacteria and viruses within the cell?
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are the "digestive system" of the cell. They are specialized membrane-bound organelles containing a diverse array of over 40 acidic hydrolases (enzymes) capable of breaking down almost all types of biological polymers. Their primary role in host defense is the degradation and elimination of bacteria and viruses that have been internalized through phagocytosis or endocytosis. Peroxisomes (Option A) are involved in lipid metabolism and the neutralization of reactive oxygen species like hydrogen peroxide. The Golgi complex (Option C) is responsible for the modification and packaging of proteins. Ribosomes (Option D) are the sites of protein synthesis. Because lysosomes provide the acidic environment and potent enzymes necessary to dismantle and destroy foreign pathogens, they are the organelle definitively responsible for cellular waste elimination and microbial killing
questions.learning: Lysosomes are the "digestive system" of the cell. They are specialized membrane-bound organelles containing a diverse array of over 40 acidic hydrolases (enzymes) capable of breaking down almost all types of biological polymers.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman presents with menstrual irregularities, acne, and excessive hair growth. What is the first-line approach to management?
questions.explanation: The patient's presentation of irregular cycles, acne, and hirsutism is highly suggestive of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). For all PCOS patients, the definitive first-line management is lifestyle modification, which includes weight loss, a healthy diet, and regular exercise. Even a modest 5% reduction in body weight can significantly improve hormonal balance, restore ovulation, and enhance insulin sensitivity. Oral Contraceptive Pills (Option C) are the first-line medical therapy specifically for regulating menstrual cycles and treating hirsutism, but they follow lifestyle changes. Metformin (Option A) is an insulin sensitizer used primarily for patients with metabolic issues or insulin resistance. Clomiphene citrate (Option D) is used for ovulation induction in patients seeking fertility but is not the general first-line management for the syndrome itself. Thus, non-pharmacological interventions are prioritized to address the underlying metabolic disturbances of PCOS

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old lady presents with a hard lump in the left breast. On examination, the lump is found to be 4 cm × 6 cm in size, not fixed to the skin, but fixed to the underlying pectoralis major muscle. The T stage of this is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. cT3

The breast lump measures 4 × 6 cm, so its largest dimension is 6 cm.

Breast cancer T staging by tumor size:

• T1: ≤2 cm
• T2: >2 cm to ≤5 cm
• T3: >5 cm
• T4: Tumor of any size with extension to the chest wall and/or skin

Although the tumor is fixed to the pectoralis major muscle, involvement of the pectoralis muscle alone does not qualify as chest-wall invasion for T4 staging.

Therefore:

• 6 cm tumor + no skin involvement/chest-wall invasion → cT3

Why not the other options?

• (a) cT4a: Requires invasion of the chest wall; pectoralis muscle involvement alone is not sufficient.
• (b) cT3 — Correct: Tumor >5 cm without T4 features.
• (c) cT4b: Requires features such as ulceration, satellite skin nodules, or edema/peau d’orange.
• (d) cT2: Tumor is >5 cm, so it exceeds the T2 range.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is deficient in the mucopolysaccharidosis associated with Natowicz disease?
questions.explanation: Natowicz Disease, also classified as Mucopolysaccharidosis Type IX (MPS IX), is an extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hyaluronidase. This enzyme is responsible for the degradation of hyaluronic acid (hyaluronan); its deficiency leads to the abnormal accumulation of hyaluronic acid in various tissues. Clinical features are relatively mild compared to other MPS types and include soft tissue masses and joint stiffness. In contrast, dermatan and heparan sulfate (Options A and B) accumulate in MPS I (Hurler) and MPS II (Hunter) syndromes due to different enzyme defects. Keratan sulfate (Option C) accumulates in MPS IV (Morquio syndrome). Because Natowicz disease is specifically the "hyaluronan-accumulation" disorder, the absence of hyaluronidase makes hyaluronic acid the deficiently processed glycosaminoglycan (GAG)
questions.learning: Natowicz Disease, also classified as Mucopolysaccharidosis Type IX (MPS IX), is an extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hyaluronidase.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During surgery under halothane anesthesia, a patient develops muscle rigidity along with a rapid increase in body temperature. Which ion is primarily responsible for causing these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing malignant hyperthermia (MH), a life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle. MH is triggered by volatile anesthetic agents (such as halothane) or the depolarizing muscle relaxant succinylcholine. The core pathophysiology is an uncontrolled release of calcium ions (Ca²⁺) from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the muscle cell cytoplasm due to a mutation in the ryanodine receptor (RyR1). The sudden rise in intracellular calcium causes sustained muscle contraction (rigidity) and a dramatic increase in metabolic activity, leading to hypercapnia, metabolic acidosis, and a rapid rise in body temperature. Sodium (Option A) and magnesium (Option C) are not primary drivers of the crisis. Potassium (Option D) often increases secondarily due to rhabdomyolysis, but calcium dysregulation is the initiating event. The definitive treatment is dantrolene, which directly inhibits calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Immediate discontinuation of triggering agents, active cooling, correction of acidosis, and supportive ICU care are also essential
questions.learning: The patient is experiencing malignant hyperthermia (MH), a life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle. MH is triggered by volatile anesthetic agents (such as halothane) or the depolarizing muscle relaxant succinylcholine.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Inoculation loops are commonly sterilized by which method?
options: Heat till it become red hot
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Heat till it become red hot

Inoculating loops are sterilized by direct flaming until they become red hot.

• Red heat ensures complete destruction of all microorganisms, including spores
• This is a method of dry heat sterilization
• The loop must be allowed to cool before touching the culture to avoid killing organisms

Why not others:

• Autoclaving is used for bulk instruments, not for immediate sterilization during procedures
• Microwave is not a standard sterilization method in microbiology labs
• Passing over flame a few times without achieving red heat is inadequate

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure being performed in the image given below.
options: Intraosseous route access for giving IV fluids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intraosseous route access for giving IV fluids

The procedure being performed in the above image is intraosseous route access for transfusing IV fluids in the anterior proximal tibia.

The intraosseous route is an alternative to the intravenous (IV) route in the transfusion of fluids in shock. The marrow of long bones has a rich network of vessels that drain into a central venous canal, emissary veins, and ultimately the central circulation. So, the bone marrow functions as a non-collapsible venous access route.

Intraosseous cannulation is recommended for patients in whom IV access proves difficult or unattainable. (e.g., in cardiopulmonary arrest). In such a case, if venous access is not available within 1 min, an intraosseous needle should be placed in the anterior proximal tibia. During a resuscitation procedure, all anesthetic drugs and fluids can be administered through intraosseous cannulae.

Insertion sites for intraosseous infusion:

• In the proximal tibia, 1-2 cm anteromedial from the tibial tuberosity
• Distal tibia at the junction of the medial malleolus and the shaft of the tibia
• Distal one-third of the femur

The response time to drug administration in intraosseous infusion is close to the IV route. Fluids should be given as boluses using a 50 mL syringe.

The image below shows the procedure of intraosseous cannulation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use and recent binge drinking presents with an episode of hematemesis involving bright red blood. His vital signs are stable. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is performed, and the image is shown. Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of an alcoholic patient with binge drinking followed by hematemesis (vomiting bright red blood) is the classic presentation of a Mallory-Weiss Tear. The provided endoscopic image confirms the diagnosis, showing a longitudinal, linear mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction. These tears result from forceful vomiting or retching. Boerhaave syndrome (Option B) is a more severe, "full-thickness" rupture of the esophagus that presents with severe pain and sepsis, not typically stable vitals and isolated bleeding. Tension pneumothorax (Option A) and gastric ulcer perforation (Option D) are surgical emergencies that present with respiratory distress or "air under the diaphragm" on imaging, rather than primary hematemesis. Because the image shows a superficial mucosal tear specifically at the cardia/GE junction in a stable patient, Mallory-Weiss Tear is the definitive diagnosis. Most cases heal spontaneously with supportive care
questions.learning: The clinical history of an alcoholic patient with binge drinking followed by hematemesis (vomiting bright red blood) is the classic presentation of a Mallory-Weiss Tear.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: An HIV-positive woman on ART was prescribed ergotamine for a migraine attack 4 days back. She presented with complaints that she is unable to feel her legs from the mid-thigh to her toes, for the past two days. The angiography image is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ergotism

The clinical features and the CT angiography image showing diffuse symmetrical luminal narrowing of the lower limb vessels are suggestive of ergotism.

In this case, a patient on antiretroviral therapy is given ergotamine. HIV protease inhibitors used in ART like ritonavir, lopinavir, etc are potent inhibitors of the  CYP3A4 enzyme. This enzyme is responsible for the metabolism of ergot compounds. Hence inhibition of this enzyme leads to decreased metabolism of ergotamine. This causes the accumulation of toxic levels of ergotamine in the patient and leads to ergotism.

Ergotamine is a partial agonist and antagonist at alpha-adrenergic, 5HT1; and 5HT2 receptors. It produces sustained vasoconstriction, vasomotor center depression, and visceral smooth muscle contraction.

Adverse effects: Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain may be seen. Vasoconstriction caused by the drug is responsible for most of the adverse effects. These are usually seen with long-term therapy with higher doses.

• It may precipitate or aggravate angina pectoris or myocardial infarction due to coronary insufficiency.
• Some patients develop cold, numb, and painful extremities.
• Leg claudication may be seen
• Gangrene of the extremities

Contraindications for ergotamine:

• Peripheral vascular disease
• Coronary artery disease
• Uncontrolled hypertension
• Sepsis
• Pregnancy
• Liver and kidney diseases
questions.learning: Ergotism — The clinical features and the CT angiography image showing diffuse symmetrical luminal narrowing of the lower limb vessels are suggestive of ergotism.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A child involved in a train accident presents with stable vital signs but has a large laceration on the leg. Under disaster triage principles, which triage category does this patient fall into?
questions.explanation: In disaster triage systems, the Yellow category represents "Delayed" care. This is assigned to patients who have significant injuries but are hemodynamically stable. In this case, the child has stable vitals (no immediate life threat) but a "big laceration" that requires surgical repair and medical attention, making them a priority after the most critical cases are handled. The Red category (Option A) is for "Immediate" life-threatening emergencies like airway obstruction. Green (Option C) is for the "walking wounded" with minor cuts or sprains. The Black category (Option D) is for the deceased or those with injuries incompatible with survival. Since the child is stable but has a serious wound needing hospital care, Yellow is the appropriate classification for prioritizing treatment in a mass casualty event
questions.learning: In disaster triage systems, the Yellow category represents "Delayed" care. This is assigned to patients who have significant injuries but are hemodynamically stable.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A researcher treats cultured human cells with a histone acetyltransferase (HAT) inhibitor and observes rapid epigenetic changes. Within minutes, there is reduced transcriptional activity and chromatin appears more compact. Which of the following molecular changes is most likely to be seen immediately?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased H3K9me2/3

• HAT inhibition → ↓ histone acetylation → chromatin condensation
• Associated with repressive marks (↑ H3K9 methylation)
• Acetylation = active chromatin; methylation (H3K9me2/3) = silenced chromatin

Histone acetylation relaxes chromatin and promotes gene transcription, whereas histone deacetylation leads to chromatin condensation and gene repression.

Effect of Histone Acetylase (HAT) Inhibition:

• ↓ Histone acetylation
• Chromatin becomes more condensed
• Leads to repressive histone marks, such as H3K9 methylation (H3K9me2/3)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Blood during autopsy is preserved in?
questions.explanation: During a forensic autopsy, blood samples collected for toxicological analysis must be preserved to prevent the degradation of certain substances or the post-mortem production of alcohol. Sodium fluoride (NaF) is the standard preservative used. As established in Question 54, it acts as an antiglycolytic and an enzyme inhibitor, specifically preventing bacteria and yeast from fermenting glucose into ethanol, which would lead to a falsely elevated blood alcohol level. Sodium chloride (Option B) is simple table salt and has no preservative value in toxicology. Formalin (Option C) is used to preserve tissues for histology but would invalidate chemical testing. Rectified spirit (Option D) is concentrated ethanol and is used to preserve viscera for certain poisons but would obviously invalidate any alcohol measurement. Using NaF-preserved tubes is a mandatory forensic step to ensure the scientific validity of the autopsy's toxicological findings in legal proceedings
questions.learning: During a forensic autopsy, blood samples collected for toxicological analysis must be preserved to prevent the degradation of certain substances or the post-mortem production of alcohol.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a PCSK-9 inhibitor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Evolocumab

PCSK9 (Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin/Kexin Type 9) is a liver enzyme that regulates LDL receptor degradation.

Normally:

1️⃣ LDL receptors bind LDL cholesterol

2️⃣ LDL is taken into hepatocytes

3️⃣ LDL receptors are recycled back to the cell surface

But when PCSK9 binds LDL receptors, it causes: Receptor degradation

This results in higher LDL levels in blood.

Evolocumab is a PCSK-9 inhibitor that increases LDL receptor recycling on hepatocytes. This leads to marked reduction in LDL-cholesterol, especially in high-risk ASCVD patients.

| Drug | Type

| ---- | ----

| Evolocumab | Monoclonal antibody

| Alirocumab | Monoclonal antibody

Indications include:

• Familial hypercholesterolemia
• Very high-risk ASCVD
• Patients not controlled with statins + ezetimibe

Ezetimibe inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption, evinacumab targets ANGPTL3, and everolimus is an mTOR inhibitor.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent epistaxis and a firm, purplish mass arising from the left posterior choana, with no history of trauma. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation: The presentation of an adolescent male with recurrent epistaxis and a firm purplish mass in the posterior nasal aperture (choana) is the classic clinical picture of a Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA). JNA is a benign but locally aggressive vascular tumor. The most suitable and definitive management approach is Surgical excision, typically performed after preoperative embolization to minimize bleeding. Both Needle biopsy (Option A) and FNAC (Option B) are strictly contraindicated in a suspected JNA, as these tumors are extremely vascular and lack a muscular coat in their vessels, leading to profuse, uncontrollable hemorrhage if punctured. Radiotherapy (Option C) is generally reserved for recurrent or inoperable cases with intracranial extension. Modern management often utilizes an endoscopic approach or a combined approach for larger tumors. Rapid diagnosis through imaging (CT/MRI showing the "Holman-Miller sign") and urgent surgical planning are essential to prevent life-threatening nosebleeds and permanent facial disfigurement
questions.learning: The presentation of an adolescent male with recurrent epistaxis and a firm purplish mass in the posterior nasal aperture (choana) is the classic clinical picture of a Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During the examination of a patient, a professor asks the patient to invert his foot and points to a prominent tendon located behind the medial malleolus. Which tendon is being highlighted?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tibialis posterior

The tendon being highlighted here is of the tibialis posterior.

It passes behind the medial malleolus and is a key muscle responsible for foot inversion. The tendon of this muscle becomes prominent in this area during foot inversion. Dysfunction of this tendon can lead to flatfoot deformity.

The given image shows the tarsal tunnel and position of the tendon of tibialis posterior:

Other options:

Option A: Tibialis anterior lies anterior to the medial malleolus and aids in dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot but is not located behind the medial malleolus.

Option B: Extensor digitorum is involved in extending the toes and runs anteriorly to the foot, not behind the medial malleolus.

Option D: Extensor hallucis longus extends the big toe and runs along the anterior portion of the foot, also not behind the medial malleolus.
questions.learning: Tibialis posterior — The tendon being highlighted here is of the tibialis posterior. It passes behind the medial malleolus and is a key muscle responsible for foot inversion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Ménétrier’s disease: 1. There is excessive production of Transforming Growth Factor-alpha (TGF-α). 2. Majority of the patients present with features of protein-losing enteropathy. 3. Mucus secreting cells are replaced by parietal and chief cells. 4. The mucosal folds of the body and fundus of the stomach are greatly enlarged. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

• 1. Excessive production of TGF-α: Correct

• Ménétrier disease is associated with overexpression of transforming growth factor-α (TGF-α), which activates EGFR signaling and causes gastric foveolar hyperplasia.

• 2. Protein-losing enteropathy: Correct

• The enlarged gastric mucosa causes excessive protein loss into the gastric lumen, resulting in hypoalbuminemia and edema.
• Protein-losing gastropathy is a characteristic clinical feature.

• 3. Mucus-secreting cells are replaced by parietal and chief cells: Incorrect

• The opposite occurs: parietal and chief cells are reduced/replaced by proliferating mucus-secreting foveolar cells.

• 4. Enlarged mucosal folds of body and fundus: Correct

• There is marked giant gastric rugal/fold enlargement, predominantly involving the body and fundus, with relative sparing of the antrum.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 54-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to several hours of severe epigastric abdominal pain radiating to her back. She has also had nausea and several episodes of vomiting. The patient has a history of occasional upper abdominal pain after eating but has never had such severe symptoms. She has no other medical issues and takes no medications. Temperature is 37.6⁰C (99.6⁰F), blood pressure is 110/66 mm Hg, pulse is 118/min, and respirations are 24/min. The patient appears to be in moderate distress. Mucous membranes are dry. The abdomen is distended with marked epigastric tenderness. Bowel sounds are decreased. Laboratory results are as follows: Hematocrit: 48% Leukocytes: 18,800/mm³ Total bilirubin: 2.2 mg/dL Alkaline phosphatase: 370 U/L Lipase: 2,192 U/L Which of the following sets of renal findings are most expected in this patient?
options: Renin secretion high, Efferent arteriolar resistance high, Tubular sodium resporption high
Renin secretion high, Efferent arteriolar resistance low, Tubular sodium resporption high
Renin secretion low, Efferent arteriolar resistance low, Tubular sodium resporption low
Renin secretion low, Efferent arteriolar resistance high, Tubular sodium resporption low
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Renin secretion high, Efferent arteriolar resistance high, Tubular sodium resporption high

Acute pancreatitis with vomiting and third-spacing leads to hypovolemia and decreased renal perfusion, causing prerenal azotemia.

Prerenal state activates RAAS, resulting in:

• ↑ Renin secretion
• ↑ Angiotensin II → ↑ efferent arteriolar resistance (to maintain GFR)
• ↑ Aldosterone → ↑ tubular sodium and water reabsorption

Thus, expected renal findings are high renin, high efferent arteriolar resistance, and high tubular sodium reabsorption.
